### Article 1: MEMOTE for Standardized Genome-Scale Metabolic Model Testing (openCOBRA-Consortium Community Paper)

- **Full citation:** Lieven, C., Beber, M. E., Olivier, B. G., ... **Mahadevan, R.** ... (≈60 co-authors total). (2020). MEMOTE for standardized genome-scale metabolic model testing. *Nature Biotechnology*, 38(3), 271–278. DOI: 10.1038/s41587-020-0446-y. **Article type:** Correspondence in *Nature Biotechnology* — short-format community-consensus paper, not full research article.
- **Authorship caveat — important:** This is a **~60-author openCOBRA-consortium community paper**. Co-first authors are Christian Lieven and Moritz E. Beber (DTU Biosustain). Corresponding author is **Nikolaus Sonnenschein** (DTU Biosustain). **Mahadevan is signatory #22 of the ~60-author list**, listed alphabetically / affiliation-grouped with the other community contributors — **NOT first, last, or corresponding author**. Same authorship-class issue as Sánchez-Lengeling Article 1 and Moosavi Article 1 (high-quality paper with weak PI-specific lab signal). **The 7.3 article-level score reflects portfolio feasibility for a project inspired by this paper, not the strength of Mahadevan's authorship signal.** *Strongly recommend processing at least one Mahadevan-first-or-corresponding-author paper before treating the rollup as a stable advisor signal.*
- **Problem in plain English:** A **genome-scale metabolic model (GEM)** is a large mathematical model of an organism's metabolism — typically thousands of metabolites + thousands of reactions, organised as a stoichiometric matrix S ∈ ℝ^{m×n} plus gene-protein-reaction (GPR) rules and biomass-objective-function definitions — used to predict cellular phenotypes (growth rate, gene knockouts, drug targets, metabolic-engineering interventions) under different environmental conditions. The field has produced 10,000+ published GEMs across multiple software ecosystems (cobrapy, COBRA Toolbox, OptFlux, KBase, etc.) but quality varies wildly: stoichiometric inconsistencies, missing GPR rules, ATP-from-nothing energy-cycle artifacts, and incomplete annotations are common. The paper introduces **MEMOTE** ("metabolic model tests"), an open-source Python test suite that runs ~150 deterministic consensus tests on any SBML3FBC-format GEM across four areas — annotation, basic structural tests, biomass reaction, stoichiometry — and produces a quantitative 0–100 quality score plus a human-readable report. Validates MEMOTE on **10,780 GEMs** drawn from 7 collections (AGORA, CarveMe, Path2Models, KBase, BiGG, Ebrahim et al., OptFlux), showing dramatic across-collection quality variation: ~70% of BiGG models have ≥1 stoichiometrically unbalanced metabolite, up to 50% of Path2Models models are stoichiometrically inconsistent, ~15% of reactions across all collections lack GPR rules.
- **ML task type:** **No supervised ML in the paper.** MEMOTE itself is a rule-based / deterministic test suite — no learned model, no training. The only "ML-adjacent" component is **t-SNE for unsupervised dimensional reduction** of the 10,780-model × ~150-test feature matrix in Fig. 2a. Several natural ML reframes for a portfolio project:
  1. **Tabular regression / classification** on the 10,780-model × ~150-MEMOTE-test feature matrix (publicly available on Zenodo). Predict overall MEMOTE score from a subset of features; identify which tests dominate the score; cluster the 10,780 models by MEMOTE-feature profile and characterise clusters by collection / organism.
  2. **GEM-quality prediction from organism metadata.** Inputs: organism taxonomy (kingdom / phylum / class), genome size (Mb), GC content, number of ORFs, source collection. Output: predicted MEMOTE score before generating the GEM — a "should we trust an automatically-built GEM for this organism?" recommender.
  3. **Graph neural networks on the bipartite metabolite-reaction graph** for gap-filling / missing-reaction prediction. PyTorch Geometric on each model's S-matrix interpreted as a bipartite graph; train a link-predictor on a held-out subset of reactions per model. This is an active research direction in the field (Yang et al. 2019, Kim et al. 2022, etc.).
  4. **Metabolic-engineering target prediction** using cobrapy + MEMOTE-validated GEMs. Predict which gene knockouts / overexpressions yield the highest production of a target metabolite — closer to Mahadevan's actual research direction (strain design / adaptive evolution).
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality (paper): GEMs encoded in SBML3FBC (SBML level 3 with the Flux Balance Constraints package). Each model = stoichiometric matrix S ∈ ℝ^{m×n} + GPR boolean rules per reaction + biomass objective function + reaction reversibility flags + flux bounds + metabolite chemical formulas / charges + cross-database annotations (KEGG, ChEBI, MetaNetX, BiGG IDs, etc.).
  - Modality (ML reframe via tabular MEMOTE outputs): each model produces a ~150-feature vector of test results (binary pass/fail or fractional metrics). 10,780 such vectors are publicly available on Zenodo.
  - Modality (ML reframe via GNN): bipartite graph with metabolite-nodes + reaction-nodes; edges weighted by stoichiometric coefficient. Typical model: ~1,000–3,000 nodes per graph for a bacterial GEM, larger for eukaryotic / human GEMs.
  - Shape / size if stated (paper): 10,780 GEMs total across 7 collections; BiGG = ~80 manually curated models; AGORA = 773 human-gut-microbiota models; CarveMe = ~5,500 bacterial models; KBase + Path2Models substantially larger.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: SBML parsing via `libsbml`; `cobrapy` for constraint-based analysis primitives; MEMOTE applies its ~150 tests; t-SNE on normalised test-result matrix for the 2D visualisation in Fig. 2a.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts (paper): a per-model MEMOTE score (0–100) plus per-test pass/fail / fractional-metric outcomes; rendered as a human-readable HTML report (snapshot, diff, or history report).
  - What the model would predict (ML reframe): for the tabular reframe, scalar MEMOTE score or per-cluster categorical label; for the GNN reframe, link-prediction probability for held-out reactions; for the metadata reframe, predicted MEMOTE score from organism descriptors.
  - Units / label space: MEMOTE score ∈ [0, 100]; per-test outcomes either binary or fractional ∈ [0, 1].
- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML in the paper. MEMOTE = rule-based Python test suite built on `cobrapy`. Portfolio reframes: LightGBM or random-forest regressor on tabular MEMOTE features (recruiter-default benchmark); GNN (GCN, GAT, or GraphSAGE in PyTorch Geometric) on bipartite metabolite-reaction graphs; sklearn / XGBoost on organism-metadata regression.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: 7-collection GEM benchmark — AGORA + CarveMe + Path2Models + KBase + BiGG + Ebrahim et al. 2015 + OptFlux models.
  - Size: **10,780 GEMs total**, with per-test result vectors for each.
  - Source: Authors compiled from public collections.
  - Public? **YES — outstanding.** Both the model collection (Zenodo `10.5281/zenodo.2636858`) and the per-model test-result tables + analysis code (Zenodo `10.5281/zenodo.2638234`) are publicly deposited. MEMOTE source code is **Apache-2.0** on GitHub (`opencobra/memote`); web service at `memote.io`; documentation at `memote.readthedocs.io`. **This is the highest-reproducibility paper in the entire survey so far** (matches Sánchez-Lengeling Articles 1 and 2 at perfect-10).
  - Link: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.2636858 (models) + https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.2638234 (results + analysis code).
- **Reported headline metric:** No single supervised-ML metric (no ML). Headline empirical findings: **~70% of BiGG models** have ≥1 stoichiometrically unbalanced metabolite; **up to 50% of Path2Models models** are stoichiometrically inconsistent; **~15% of reactions across all collections** lack GPR rules; AGORA and KBase contain ~30% blocked reactions, BiGG and OptFlux ~20%, CarveMe and Path2Models very few; only AGORA / KBase / BiGG have SBML-compliant metabolite + reaction annotations; only KBase + selected BiGG models include gene annotations.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **The MEMOTE Zenodo deposit itself** — 10,780 models + per-model ~150-feature MEMOTE result vectors — match: **EXACT** (it *is* the dataset for any tabular-feature ML reframe) — access: **EASY** (single Zenodo DOI, direct download, free).

  - **CarveMe** (Machado et al. 2018 *Nucleic Acids Res*) — automated reconstruction tool + ~5,500 bacterial GEMs — match: **CLOSE** for bacterial-strain-design projects — access: **EASY**.
  - **KBase** (kbase.us, Argonne / DOE) — thousands of automatically-reconstructed GEMs + a full reconstruction-and-analysis platform — match: **CLOSE** for end-to-end-pipeline projects — access: **EASY** (free account).
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **Easy** — the entire 10,780-model dataset + per-model ~150-feature test-result vectors are on Zenodo with a single-click DOI and an Apache-2.0-licensed reproducible analysis pipeline. **Highest-tier data access of any paper in the entire survey.**
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **Heaviest new-domain-tooling lift in the survey for a non-image / non-atomic-structure article.** Standard carry-over: pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, PyTorch, matplotlib. **New systems-biology stack** (none of which appear in any prior professor's section):

The student's chemistry-undergrad background gives partial overlap (mass-balance / stoichiometry intuition transfers; LP optimisation does not).
  - **For the GNN reframe:** PyTorch Geometric on bipartite metabolite-reaction graphs (new, but well-documented).

README claim: *"Reproduces the t-SNE clustering reported by Lieven et al. 2020 and adds an interpretable ML model that flags which MEMOTE tests dominate the overall quality signal."* Tooling cost: low (sklearn / LightGBM / pandas only). ### Article 2: Heavy Metal Removal by Bioaccumulation Using Genetically Engineered Microorganisms (BioZone Review Article)

- **Full citation:** Diep, P., **Mahadevan, R.**, & Yakunin, A. F. (2018). Heavy Metal Removal by Bioaccumulation Using Genetically Engineered Microorganisms. *Frontiers in Bioengineering and Biotechnology*, 6:157. DOI: 10.3389/fbioe.2018.00157. **Article type:** Review article, 3-author U of T-internal piece anchored at BioZone (Centre for Applied Biosciences and Bioengineering, Department of Chemical Engineering and Applied Chemistry).
- **Authorship caveat — important:** Patrick Diep is **first author** (U of T PhD student at BioZone) and **Alexander F. Yakunin is corresponding author** (`a.iakounine@utoronto.ca`). **Mahadevan is middle author (#2 of 3)**. The author-contributions statement is explicit: *"PD conceived, wrote, and approved the review for publication. RM and AY helped revise the manuscript for submission."* So Mahadevan's role here is **co-supervisor / reviser, not lead PI** — Yakunin is the senior corresponding author on this one. **Lab-signal is moderate** — better than Article 1's 60-author community-paper signatory situation (this is a 3-author U of T-internal paper with an explicit Mahadevan revising role), but still NOT Mahadevan-led. **Both Mahadevan articles processed so far have weak Mahadevan-specific authorship signal.** *Strongly recommend processing at least one Mahadevan-first-or-corresponding-author paper before treating the rollup as a stable advisor signal.*
- ⚠️ **Critical terminology clash to flag up front:** This article uses "**GEMs**" to mean **Genetically Engineered Microorganisms**. Mahadevan's Article 1 (the MEMOTE paper) uses "**GEMs**" to mean **Genome-Scale Metabolic Models**. **Same acronym, completely different meaning.** When reading both Mahadevan papers consecutively, this is a real source of confusion — flag it explicitly. The two senses of "GEMs" are arguably both within Mahadevan's research domain (he uses metabolic models to design engineered microorganisms), but they are *distinct* acronym uses in *distinct* sub-fields.
- **Problem in plain English:** Wastewater from mines, metal smelters, and oil/gas refineries is laden with toxic heavy metal ions (HMs: Cd, Co, Cu, Hg, Ni, As, U). Conventional removal techniques (chemical precipitation, activated carbon, ion exchange) generate sludge waste, use non-renewable adsorbents, and cannot reliably hit the new strict regulatory limits (1.2–5 µg L⁻¹ for aquatic life). **Microbial bioaccumulation** uses metabolically-active engineered microbes to **import** HMs across the cell membrane via transporter proteins (channels, secondary carriers, primary active transporters — Table 2 of the paper) and **sequester** them inside the cell using metal-binding proteins like metallothioneins, phytochelatins (peptide chains synthesised by phytochelatin synthase), and polyphosphates (Tables 3 and 4 of the paper). The review consolidates ~50 published bioaccumulation studies across 20+ years into a biochemical framework, identifies recurring strategies that worked and didn't, and proposes pivoting from "bioremediation" (just removing the metals) to **bioextraction** (recovering valuable metals such as gold, platinum, and strategic metals from waste streams as the "mine of tomorrow"). Industrial adoption has been "virtually non-existent" despite 25+ years of academic work.
- **ML task type:** **No ML in the paper** (it's a review). The most ML-portfolio-relevant artifacts are **Tables 1 (~50 bioaccumulation studies with measured capacities)**, **Table 2 (importer proteins by transporter class with UniProt IDs)**, **Table 3 (~30 metal-binding storage proteins with UniProt IDs)**, and **Table 4 (phytochelatin-synthesis enzymes with UniProt IDs)**. Several natural ML reframes:
  1. **Tabular regression on Table 1.** Predict bioaccumulation capacity Q_m (mg_HM g_DW⁻¹) from features: HM type (Cd / Co / Cu / Hg / Ni / As / U / multi-metal), chassis (E. coli vs S. cerevisiae vs M. huakuii vs D. radiodurans vs ...), strategy (import-only / storage-only / both), starting concentration, time, transporter class. ~50 rows directly digestible from Table 1.
  2. **Protein-sequence ML using the ~30 UniProt IDs in Tables 2 and 3.** Fetch sequences via UniProt REST API, train a classifier (or fine-tune a pretrained protein language model — **ESM-2** from Meta AI, **ProtBERT** from Rostlab) to predict "metal binder vs not" or specifically "Cd binder vs Hg binder vs Ni binder vs negative control." Direct connection to the protein-language-model field which is a hot ML topic in 2024–2026.
  3. **Literature-mining extension** across the ~70 cited primary papers to expand Table 1 to ~150–200 rows.
  4. **Cross-link with Article 1** — combine MEMOTE-validated GEMs (Article 1's sense) with bioaccumulation strain-design data (Article 2's sense) into a unified portfolio. This is the strongest cross-paper narrative within Mahadevan's section so far.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality (paper): Tabulated literature data — Table 1 has ~50 entries × ~7 columns; Tables 2, 3, 4 have UniProt IDs + organism + target HM. PDB structures referenced in Fig. 1 (1LDA, 4GBY, 3J09, 2OMF, 1T2Y).
  - Modality (tabular ML reframe): ~7 features per row from Table 1 (HM, chassis, strategy, conc_in, conc_ads, time, transporter class).
  - Modality (protein-sequence ML reframe): amino-acid strings of ~30 importer/storage proteins from Tables 2, 3, 4 (typical lengths: 5 kDa metallothioneins ~50 aa, transporters ~300–500 aa, phytochelatin synthases ~500 aa).
  - Shape / size if stated (paper): Table 1 = ~50 bioaccumulation studies; Tables 2–4 = ~30 distinct UniProt-cataloged proteins.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: none — it's a review.

### Article 3: EMILiO — A Fast Algorithm for Genome-Scale Strain Design (FIRST Mahadevan-Corresponding-Author Paper in This Section)

- **Full citation:** Yang, L., Cluett, W. R., & **Mahadevan, R.** (2011). EMILiO: A fast algorithm for genome-scale strain design. *Metabolic Engineering*, 13, 272–281. DOI: 10.1016/j.ymben.2011.03.002. **Article type:** Primary research paper in *Metabolic Engineering* (top-tier systems-biology / metabolic-engineering journal).
- **Authorship — finally a clean Mahadevan lab signal:** Laurence Yang is **first author** (Mahadevan's PhD student at U of T Chemical Engineering and Applied Chemistry); William R. Cluett is middle author (U of T Chem Eng faculty co-supervisor); **Mahadevan is corresponding author** (`krishna.mahadevan@utoronto.ca`). Three-author U-of-T-only paper. **This is the first Mahadevan-CORRESPONDING-author paper processed in this section** — it resolves the open-items concern from Articles 1 and 2 that "neither article is Mahadevan-led" and confirms the previously-inferred research direction (computational strain design + constraint-based modeling + bilevel optimization for metabolic engineering). **Strongest Mahadevan-specific lab signal in the section.**
- **Beautiful unification of the two earlier articles in Mahadevan's section:** EMILiO **uses genome-scale metabolic models** (Article 1's "GEMs" sense — the iAF1260 *E. coli* model from Feist et al. 2007) to **design genetically engineered microorganisms** (Article 2's "GEMs" sense — succinate / L-glutamate / L-serine over-producing *E. coli* strains). The acronym clash flagged in Articles 1 and 2 is resolved by Article 3: both senses of "GEM" are tied together through Mahadevan's actual research programme, where genome-scale metabolic models are the *substrate* for designing engineered microorganisms.
- **Problem in plain English:** Metabolic engineers want to genetically modify microbes (typically *E. coli* or yeast) to over-produce target chemicals — succinate (~$10B-market biopolymer precursor), amino acids (L-glutamate, L-serine), biofuels, drug intermediates. With ~2000 reactions in a genome-scale *E. coli* model, choosing even 5 modifications gives ~8 trillion combinations; choosing the *flux level* of each modified reaction adds continuous-search complexity on top. Existing algorithms (**OptKnock** 2003 for knockouts only, **OptReg** 2006 for ±regulation, **GDLS** 2009 for local search) had two limitations: (1) only discrete modifications (delete / overexpress / suppress), but Alper et al. 2005 showed lycopene production in *E. coli* is maximized at *intermediate* dxs expression — not full deletion or full overexpression; (2) the underlying mixed-integer linear programs become combinatorially expensive for >3 modifications. **EMILiO** (*E*nhancing *M*etabolism with *I*terative *L*inear *O*ptimization) solves both: (a) handles continuous flux levels by importing **successive linear programming (SLP)** from the petrochemical industry's 50-year-old toolbox; (b) reformulates the bilevel optimization as a single-level mathematical program with complementarity constraints (MPCC) using KKT conditions; (c) uses a 3-stage pipeline (SLP → recursive LP-pruning → MILP) to extract minimal sets of modifications. Result: 100% maximal succinate production with 3 modifications in **2 minutes CPU time**, vs OptReg* taking 4 days to reach 83.26% and OptReg*LS local-search taking 4 hours for 82.13%.
- **ML task type:** **No supervised ML in the paper.** The paper is constrained-optimization (LP + MILP + bilevel + MPCC + KKT) plus **affinity-propagation clustering** (Frey & Dueck 2007, unsupervised) of the 234 strain designs in Fig. 5. ML reframes for a portfolio project:
  1. **Tabular regression on the 234-strain-design output dataset.** Predict succinate production (% of theoretical maximum) from a feature vector encoding which of ~100+ reactions are modified and how (knockout / up-regulate to flux X / down-regulate to flux Y). Cleanest supervised setup of any Mahadevan article processed so far. Could also reproduce + extend Fig. 3's "landscape of strain designs" using t-SNE / UMAP / hierarchical clustering instead of affinity propagation.
  2. **Reinforcement learning / Bayesian optimization for strain design.** Replace EMILiO's SLP/MPCC formulation with a learned policy (PPO / SAC) that proposes strain modifications and uses cobrapy + iAF1260 as the simulator/reward. This is genuinely an active research direction in 2024–2026 (e.g., learned bilevel-optimization for metabolic engineering, AlphaFold-style search over strain-design space).
  3. **FBA-surrogate neural network.** Train a feed-forward NN (or graph NN on the metabolite-reaction bipartite graph from Article 1) to predict FBA outputs (max growth rate, max product flux) from input modifications + media conditions, eliminating most of the inner LP solves during exploration. Speeds up RL-style strain design by ~100×.
  4. **Cross-paper unification** with Articles 1 and 2. **Strongest narrative:** use MEMOTE-validated GEMs (Article 1) as the model substrate → run EMILiO-style strain-design (Article 3) targeting heavy-metal bioaccumulation (Article 2) → fine-tune ESM-2 (Article 2) on the resulting predicted-overexpressed metal-binding proteins. **All three Mahadevan articles connect through cobrapy + the iAF1260 model + strain design** — this section is the strongest within-section narrative arc of any professor in the survey aside from Frank Gu's Article 3 → Article 1 review-then-experiment pair.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality (paper): `iAF1260` genome-scale model of *E. coli* (Feist et al. 2007) — ~1260 ORFs, ~2000 reactions, stoichiometric matrix S ∈ ℝ^{m×n}, GPR rules, biomass objective. Plus media conditions (max glucose / oxygen uptake = 20 mmol/gDW/h), minimum growth rate (0.1 h⁻¹), restricted target-reaction set (excluding cell-envelope / glycerophospholipid / transport reactions per Feist et al. 2010).
  - Modality (ML reframe via tabular outputs): each of the 234 strain designs in Dataset S2 = ~100-dim binary/continuous feature vector (which reactions modified + their target flux levels) + scalar target (succinate% / L-glutamate% / L-serine% of maximum).
  - Modality (ML reframe via RL): state = current (set-of-modifications + iAF1260 model); action = add/remove a modification with a flux level; reward = FBA-predicted product flux at max growth.
  - Shape / size if stated (paper): 234 strain designs for succinate; additional designs for L-glutamate (multiple) and L-serine (multiple, including a 99.65%-maximal design with non-intuitive PPA / PPKr modifications).
  - Preprocessing in the paper: model reduction via reduced row echelon form of S; restriction of target-reaction set; conversion of bilevel optimization → MPCC via KKT; iterative SLP with a single tunable parameter K_p (objective weight on product maximization).
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts (paper): set of reactions to modify + how (knockout vs continuous flux level v_L / v_U) + predicted % of maximum product flux.
  - What the model would predict (ML reframe): scalar product-flux% from tabular reframe; modification policy from RL reframe; FBA outputs from surrogate-NN reframe.
  - Units / label space: product-flux% ∈ [0, 100]; flux levels in mmol/gDW/h (succinate v_max = 32.25 mmol/gDW/h for the iAF1260 baseline).
- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML. EMILiO = 3-stage pipeline: (1) **Successive Linear Programming (SLP)** to identify large set of active flux-bound constraints; (2) recursive **LP-based pruning** to find subsets of constraints that achieve user-defined production threshold; (3) final **MILP** minimizing number of modifications. Implemented in MATLAB with CPLEX 11.2. ML reframes: LightGBM / XGBoost for tabular regression; Stable-Baselines3 PPO / SAC for RL; small MLP or PyTorch Geometric GraphSAGE for FBA-surrogate.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: 234 EMILiO-generated strain designs for succinate production + supplementary L-glutamate / L-serine designs.
  - Size: 234 succinate strains (Dataset S2) + ~5–10 amino-acid strains (Dataset S4) + literature comparison (Dataset S3) + per-strain flux deviation vectors (Dataset S1).
  - Source: Generated by EMILiO using the public `iAF1260` model from Feist et al. 2007 (also public on BiGG).
  - Public? **YES** — Datasets S1, S2, S3, S4 are journal supplementary information, openly downloadable from the *Metabolic Engineering* article page. The `iAF1260` model itself is on BiGG (free download). MATLAB / CPLEX implementation is described in detail in the paper's Methods + a cited follow-up (Yang et al. 2010 Symposium proceedings) but **no GitHub code release** (this is a 2011 paper, before GitHub-as-deposit became standard).
  - Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymben.2011.03.002 (paper + supplementary); BiGG = http://bigg.ucsd.edu/models/iAF1260.
- **Reported headline metric:** **EMILiO finds 100% maximal succinate production with 3 modifications (SUCDi knockout + FRD2 up-regulation + aconitase up-regulation) in 2 minutes CPU time on a 3.2 GHz Intel Xeon.** OptReg* (modified reference algorithm with the same objective) terminated after 4 days at 83.26%; OptReg*LS local-search reached 82.13% in 4 hours. Across the 234 alternate succinate strains: range 75–100% maximal production, 15 affinity-propagation clusters distinguished by which subset of citric-acid-cycle / glyoxylate-shunt / acetate-metabolism reactions are modified. L-glutamate: 100% maximal flux strain found (knockout AKGDH + GLUDC + activate forward ICDH). L-serine: 99.65% maximal flux strain found (using non-intuitive PPA / PPKr modifications).
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **EMILiO supplementary datasets S1–S4** — match: **EXACT** for the tabular-regression reframe — access: **EASY** (journal supplementary download).
  - **`iAF1260` model on BiGG** — match: **EXACT** for any reimplementation in cobrapy — access: **EASY** (free, single download, MIT-licensed).
  - **Cross-link with Article 1's MEMOTE Zenodo deposit** (10,780 GEMs incl. iAF1260 itself) — match: **CLOSE** for unified portfolio — access: **EASY** (already in survey).
  - **OptKnock paper data** (Burgard et al. 2003 *Biotechnol Bioeng*) — earlier work, public — match: **CLOSE** for any "evolution-of-strain-design-algorithms" historical project — access: **EASY**.
  - **`cobrapy` itself** with example strain-design tutorials — match: **CLOSE** for reimplementing EMILiO in modern Python — access: **EASY** (well-documented, MIT-licensed).
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **Easy** — Datasets S1–S4 are supplementary downloads; iAF1260 is on BiGG. **One step easier than Article 2** (which needs Table 1 hand-transcription) but with the **same tooling-lift cost as Article 1** (cobrapy + libsbml + LP/MILP solver) if you want to actually run / extend EMILiO rather than just analyze its outputs.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **Same systems-biology stack as Article 1** — cobrapy, libsbml, SBML3FBC, FBA / FVA, constraint-based-modeling concepts. **Plus mathematical optimization concepts new to the chemistry student:** linear programming, mixed-integer linear programming, bilevel optimization, KKT conditions, MPCCs. Free academic licenses: CPLEX (IBM), Gurobi (free academic), GLPK (open-source). For ML reframe: pandas / sklearn / LightGBM (familiar) for tabular; Stable-Baselines3 + Gym for RL; PyTorch Geometric for FBA-surrogate GNN. **No avoiding the cobrapy stack here** (unlike Article 2, which had a cobrapy-free protein-sequence reframe). Heaviest tooling lift of the three Mahadevan articles, tied with Article 1.
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** Three viable framings, in increasing order of ambition:
  1. **Lightest — tabular regression on Dataset S2.** Download Dataset S2 (234 succinate strain designs); convert each strain's modifications into a feature vector; train LightGBM / XGBoost to predict succinate% from modifications; produce SHAP plots ranking which reactions matter most for production; reproduce the affinity-propagation clusters from Fig. 5 using UMAP / t-SNE / hierarchical clustering. README claim: *"Reproducible ML benchmark on the EMILiO 234-strain-design dataset, recovering the citric-acid-cycle / glyoxylate-shunt cluster structure reported by Yang, Cluett & Mahadevan 2011 from a learned regressor."* Tooling cost: low (sklearn / LightGBM only).
  2. **Medium — reimplement EMILiO in cobrapy.** Port the SLP / MPCC / MILP pipeline from MATLAB+CPLEX to Python+cobrapy+Gurobi-or-GLPK; verify reproduction of the 100%-maximal succinate strain in <2 minutes; release on GitHub as `emilio-py`. ### Summary for this professor

- **Common thread across their work (based on Articles 1, 2, and 3):** **Computational strain design + constraint-based metabolic modeling for synthetic biology / metabolic engineering**, now **confirmed by Article 3** (the first Mahadevan-corresponding-author paper). The three articles span Mahadevan's research programme cleanly: Article 1 = the bioinformatics infrastructure (10,780-GEM MEMOTE quality-control benchmark) that ensures genome-scale models are usable; Article 2 = an application domain (heavy-metal bioaccumulation in engineered microbes) that motivates strain-design work; Article 3 = the **algorithmic core** (EMILiO computational strain design via successive linear programming + bilevel optimization + KKT reformulation, Yang–Cluett–Mahadevan 2011). **The "GEMs" acronym clash that confused Articles 1 and 2 is resolved by Article 3:** EMILiO **uses genome-scale metabolic models** (Article 1's "GEMs") to **design genetically engineered microorganisms** (Article 2's "GEMs"). Methodologically a mix of **composite-index construction** (LCA-EIS in Article 1, CalEnviroScreen-style EJI in Article 2), **community-integrated GIS / CBPAR**, and **qualitative ethnographic + interview + document-analysis fieldwork** (Article 3). The unifying theoretical commitment across all three articles is a **principled critique of pure-quantitative / pure-ML approaches to environmental and climate problems** ("information determinism" in Article 3, "weapons of math destruction" in Articles 2 and 3, "environmental data justice" in Articles 2 and 3) in favor of **plural, situated, equity-focused, community-engaged knowledge practices**.

### Article 1: Canadian Food Life Cycle Inventory database + Environmental Impact Score / EIS-Nutrition composite index (one-page conference abstract)

- **Full citation:** Jarvis, S., Hadjikakou, M., Wu, J., **Classens, M.**, Chiavaroli, L., Sievenpiper, J., L'Abbe, M., Jenkins, D., & Malik, V. (2024). Integrating health, nutrition, and environmental impacts of foods: a life cycle impact assessment and modelling analysis of foods in Canada. *The Lancet Planetary Health*, published online April 15, 2024 (Abstracts section, p. 18). CC BY 4.0 Open Access.
- **Authorship caveat:** This is a **one-page conference / proceedings abstract**, not a full peer-reviewed methods paper. **Classens is the 4th of 9 authors (middle position)**. First author Sarah Jarvis is a PhD candidate in Nutritional Sciences (Temerty Faculty of Medicine); Principal Investigator and final-author is Vasanti Malik (Nutritional Sciences + Harvard T.H. Chan). Per the explicit contributions statement: *"MC shared expertise in sustainability pedagogy and food systems transformation to guide the goal and scope of life cycle assessment and provided knowledge translation guidance."* **Classens's role is advisory framing on sustainability + knowledge translation — not data, methods, modeling, or analysis.** The technical work (LCA database + composite index) is led by Jarvis under Malik's supervision with Hadjikakou (Deakin University, environmental science) and Wu (UNSW, George Institute) providing LCA / environmental-science methods expertise. **This single abstract is a weak signal for what a Classens-supervised master's thesis would actually look like** — the apparent computational angle is owned by other authors.
- **Problem in plain English:** Food-system transitions toward sustainability require trading off nutritional quality against environmental impact, but **no Canada-specific database** combines both views of foods. Canada's geography, agro-climate, domestic production / import shares, and emissions profile differ enough from US / EU / global LCA databases that those datasets distort estimates for Canadian dietary policy work. The team builds a **Canadian Food Life Cycle Inventory** keyed to the Canadian Nutrient File nomenclature, computes a per-food **Environmental Impact Score (EIS)** across 7 cradle-to-grave indicators (greenhouse-gas emissions, eutrophication, particulate matter, freshwater usage, land use, non-renewable energy consumption, food loss + waste), then folds in nutrition via the **EIS-Nutrition (EIS-N)** composite — defined explicitly as the *ratio of EIS to Nutri-Score*. Headline preliminary finding: animal-based foods (especially beef) have the worst environmental scores, and higher-nutrition foods generally have better environmental scores too (with category-specific exceptions).
- **ML task type:** **Not an ML paper.** As written, this is a database-construction + composite-index paper using standard LCA methodology + an established food-nutrient-profiling tool (Nutri-Score). The methods involve no machine learning. **An ML reframe is possible but would be entirely my construction**, e.g.: (i) **regression** — predict each EIS sub-indicator (or the composite EIS-N) from Canadian Nutrient File macro/micro-nutrient fields + food-category metadata, on Agribalyse / Poore-Nemecek / dataFIELD as public substrates; (ii) **clustering / dimensionality reduction** — PCA / UMAP / k-means / Gaussian mixture on the 7-indicator EIS vectors to discover sustainability-and-nutrition tiers of foods; (iii) **gap-imputation** — fill missing LCA values for Canadian-specific foods by training a regressor on Agribalyse and applying it to the Canadian Nutrient File. **All three are my framings, not the paper's.**
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: **Tabular**. Per food item: ~7 LCA indicator values (continuous, mixed units — kg CO₂-eq, kg P-eq, kg PM2.5-eq, m³ water, m² land, MJ non-renewable energy, % food loss/waste) + Canadian Nutrient File nutrient profile (continuous, ~150 fields including macros, micros, sodium, sugars) + categorical food-category metadata.
  - Shape if stated: **Not specified in paper** — abstract does not report row count or column count.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: Aggregation of indicator values across the spectrum of agricultural practices weighted by Canadian domestic production + import shares (cradle-to-grave). Structuring per Canadian Nutrient File nomenclature for join-ability.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: **Not a model — a derived score.** EIS = environmental impact score per impact category per food (dimensionless, derivation of the weighting scheme not detailed in the abstract). EIS-N = EIS ÷ Nutri-Score (dimensionless ratio). Lower EIS-N = better.
  - Units or label space: Continuous; per food item.
- **Model architecture (brief):** **None — LCA + scoring rules, not a machine-learning model.** The paper's "model" is the composite-index definition: cradle-to-grave LCA → per-category EIS → ratio with Nutri-Score → EIS-N.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: **Canadian Food Life Cycle Inventory database** (newly constructed for this work) + **Canadian Nutrient File** (existing public Government-of-Canada nutrition database) + **Nutri-Score** (existing public nutrient-profiling system).
  - Size: **Not specified in paper.** Abstract does not state the number of foods, indicator coverage, or temporal range.
  - Source: Canadian-specific LCA inventories built by the team; nutrition keyed to the Canadian Nutrient File.
  - Public? **Unclear from the abstract.** The abstract is forward-looking about utility ("have potential to serve as powerful tools"); it does not state whether the database has been released. The Canadian Nutrient File and Nutri-Score system rules are public.
  - Link: **Not provided in paper.** Search Government-of-Canada Open Data + the corresponding-author email (sarah.jarvis@mail.utoronto.ca) for current release status.
- **Reported headline metric:** **None in a quantitative-ML sense.** "Preliminary results show the greatest environmental impacts for animal-based foods, particularly beef" + "Foods with greater nutritional quality also generally show greater environmental sustainability, with some exceptions." No held-out test set, no error metrics, no benchmark comparison.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **Agribalyse 3.x (ADEME, France)** — ~2,500 foods × per-food LCA indicators (climate change, eutrophication, water use, land use, particulate matter, others) — match: **close** (same methodology family, French rather than Canadian agro-climate) — access: **easy — direct download** (CSV / Excel from agribalyse.ademe.fr) — https://agribalyse.ademe.fr/
  - **Poore & Nemecek (2018) Science meta-analysis supplementary data** — ~38,700 farms × ~40 products × LCA fields globally — match: **close** (global rather than Canada-specific; per-farm rather than per-food-category) — access: **easy — direct download** (Science SI XLSX) — Poore J. & Nemecek T. *Science* 360:987–992
  - **dataFIELD (University of Michigan; Heller et al.)** — US foods × LCA indicators — match: **close** (US not Canada) — access: **medium** — public reports; some data via Sustainable Minds; some by request
  - **Canadian Nutrient File** — official public Government-of-Canada nutrition database, ~5,800 foods × ~150 nutrient fields — match: **direct** (this is *exactly* the nutrition side of the paper) — access: **easy** — open download — https://food-nutrition.canada.ca/cnf-fce/
  - **Nutri-Score scoring rules** — public deterministic algorithm (positive points for fiber / protein / fruit-vegetable-legume / nuts; negative points for energy / saturated fat / sugar / sodium); reimplementable in ~50 lines of pandas — match: **direct** — access: **easy** — described in Hercberg et al. 2014 + EU SAINS scientific opinion documents
  - **Open Food Facts** — crowdsourced food product database (~3M items) with Nutri-Score, NutriScore-grade, ingredient lists, and emerging environmental Eco-Score — match: **close (broader scope)** — access: **easy — direct download** (Parquet, JSON, MongoDB dumps) — https://world.openfoodfacts.org/data
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **Unclear → likely medium.** The abstract does not link a release of the Canadian Food LCI database. Best-case: it has been or will be released alongside a forthcoming methods paper. Worst-case: in-house and not redistributed. The two underlying public anchors (Canadian Nutrient File, Nutri-Score rules) are easy. **Use Agribalyse + Canadian Nutrient File + Nutri-Score as a reproducible substitute** rather than waiting for the team's database.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **Almost entirely within current toolset.** pandas + numpy + scikit-learn / LightGBM / XGBoost for any tabular regression-or-clustering reframe. No new chemistry-specific tooling (no RDKit / cobrapy / SMILES tokenization / GNN libraries). New domain concepts to read up on briefly: LCA methodology (cradle-to-grave system boundaries, characterization factors, functional units, ReCiPe / IMPACT 2002+ / EF 3.0 impact-method families), Nutri-Score scoring rules. **By far the lightest tooling lift in the survey** — comparable to the simplest tabular framings of Galatro Article 1 / Edwards Article 2 / Mahadevan Article 2.
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** Three viable framings, all my construction (the paper itself frames no ML task):
  1. **EIS-N regression from nutrient profile alone (most direct).** *"Predicting the environmental-impact-to-nutrition ratio of foods from their Canadian Nutrient File entry — a sklearn / LightGBM regression baseline."* Train on Agribalyse foods (where both LCA and nutrition fields exist), predict EIS-N from nutrient features alone, evaluate on a held-out subset; then explore whether the regressor generalizes to Canadian Nutrient File rows that lack LCA values (gap-imputation framing). Notebook + README + a small Streamlit / Gradio demo where a user pastes a nutrient profile and sees a predicted EIS-N. README claim: *"A nutrient profile alone predicts ≈X% of the variance in environmental footprint across N foods."*
  2. **Sustainability-tier clustering of foods.** *"Discovering sustainable-and-nutritious food clusters via PCA / UMAP / Gaussian mixture on Agribalyse + Open Food Facts."* Cluster foods in joint LCA-nutrition space, visualize tiers, label canonical members per cluster. Lighter ML content, heavier EDA + visualization — a strong README-narrative project for a recruiter who wants to see communication skills.
  3. **Eco-score-from-image (stretch).** *"Predicting the Open Food Facts environmental Eco-Score from packaged-food product images via a small CNN fine-tune."* Uses Open Food Facts product images + Eco-Score grades (A–E) as a multi-class image classification target. Heavier compute (Colab GPU) but visually compelling on a portfolio site. Note: the paper does not anchor this — it is purely my construction.
  
  **Strongest single recommendation: Framing 1** (regression baseline + gap-imputation). It is the lightest tooling lift in the survey, runs on a laptop, uses only public datasets with permissive licenses, and tells a clean recruiter-legible story ("I built a regressor that predicts environmental footprint from nutrient profile"). **The portfolio-impact ceiling is moderate** — sustainability-ML is a real area but the work is more legible to ESG / food-tech / climate-policy audiences than to ML / pharma / materials-science recruiters.

### Article 2: Mapping for Change — Peterborough Environmental Justice Index + Participatory Mapping (community-integrated GIS)

- **Full citation:** Rutherford, S., **Classens, M.**, & Chan, P. L. R. (2025). Mapping for change: Balancing big and small data in documenting environmental (in)justice in a small Canadian city. *Canadian Geographies / Géographies canadiennes*, 69, e70039. DOI: 10.1111/cag.70039. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 Open Access. **Funded by Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC) grant 890-2021-0015.**
- **Authorship signal — substantially stronger than Article 1.** **3-author paper, Classens is the 2nd of 3 authors (middle in a 3-author paper), and the ONLY U of T author.** First author and corresponding author Stephanie Rutherford (Trent University, School of the Environment, Peterborough); third author P. L. Roshelle Chan (Trent). **The funder is SSHRC** — the Canadian council that funds humanities + social sciences, **NOT NSERC** (which funds STEM). This is a critical structural signal: **a Classens-supervised master's thesis would plausibly be SSHRC-funded, in the social-science / community-engaged-research register, not NSERC-funded engineering / chemistry**. Article 2 confirms that Classens's actual research direction *is* community-engaged spatial environmental-justice work — not just generic "sustainability advisory" as Article 1's contributions statement suggested.
- **Problem in plain English:** Indigenous, racialized, and poor communities across Canada experience disproportionate environmental risk (proximity to polluting facilities, flood risk, heat-wave exposure, lack of tree canopy, traffic / rail / airport pollution, ageing housing) that compounds with social and health vulnerabilities. Existing **Statistics Canada census data** are too aggregated and too distanced from lived experience to reveal this fully ("big data" alone is insufficient), but **purely qualitative / participatory data** lacks the population-level coverage that policymakers can act on ("small data" alone is insufficient). The team builds a **community-integrated GIS (CIGIS)** project for Peterborough, Ontario (population 83,651) combining (a) a Peterborough **Environmental Justice Index (EJI)** computed from 39 indicators across environmental burden + social vulnerability + health vulnerability at the Dissemination-Area level, with (b) a year-long **participatory mapping** project (19 community participants leaving photos + reflections + map pins on a shared Google Map). The headline finding: cumulative burden concentrates in the downtown core where renters, low-income households, single-parent families, and people with chronic-health conditions are spatially co-located within 1 km of polluting facilities and lacking tree canopy.
- **ML task type:** **Not an ML paper** — explicitly methodologically a **community-integrated GIS + community-based participatory action research (CBPAR)** project. The composite-index construction is **deterministic** (percentile-rank → category-mean → scale-to-0-10 → sum), inspired by CalEnviroScreen + ENRICH + EJScreen + Ontario Marginalization Index + Canadian Marginalization Index. **An ML reframe is possible but again would be my construction**, e.g.: (i) **unsupervised clustering** — k-means / Gaussian mixture / UMAP+HDBSCAN on the 39-indicator DA vectors to discover natural vulnerability typologies that the linear EJI averages over; (ii) **spatial regression** — geographically-weighted regression / spatial-lag / spatial-error models predicting health outcomes from environmental + social features (mgwr, libpysal/spreg); (iii) **satellite-image regression** — predict per-DA tree canopy % or heat-wave exposure from Sentinel-2 / Landsat tiles via a CNN, then ingest into an EJI variant (the "remote-sensing-augmented EJI" framing); (iv) **cross-city transfer** — train an EJI predictor on California (CalEnviroScreen, ~8,000 tracts × 21 indicators) and evaluate transferability to Ontario DAs; (v) **NLP on participatory-mapping notes** — small-N topic modelling / sentiment analysis on the year of community reflections. **Note that the paper is explicitly skeptical of "big data" in EJ work** (citing O'Neil's *Weapons of Math Destruction*, Mah 2017, and Vera et al. 2019 on data-justice critiques) — so a pure-ML reframe runs against the paper's stated epistemology and would need careful framing in any thesis.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: **Tabular spatial data at the Statistics Canada Dissemination-Area (DA) level**, the smallest standard Canadian census geography. **39 indicators** spanning three domains:
    - **Environmental Burden** (11 indicators): flood risk, heat-wave exposure, proximity to polluting facilities, proximity to landfills, proximity to hazardous waste receivers, proximity to major roads + highways, proximity to railways + airports, lack of tree canopy, houses built before 1980, proximity to amenities, proximity to healthy food outlets.
    - **Social Vulnerability** (16 indicators): no certificate / diploma / degree, unemployment rate, labour force participation, lone-parent families, individuals living alone, dependency ratio, multigenerational households, major-repair housing, renters, shelter-cost-to-income ratio, crowded home, residential mobility, recent immigrants, Indigenous identity, visible minority, first/second-generation, linguistic isolation, low income, government transfer payments.
    - **Health Vulnerability** (8 indicators): self-perceived poor mental health, heart disease, cancer, diabetes, asthma, difficulty walking / climbing steps, severe household food insecurity, no regular healthcare provider.
  - Shape if stated: **Not specified in paper** — abstract does not state the DA count for Peterborough, but Statistics Canada open data reports ~150-200 DAs for the city of 83,651 people. Ontario-wide there are ~20,000 DAs; Canada-wide ~57,000.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: All values rank-percentile-scaled (0-100) within each indicator before averaging — this normalizes mixed-unit indicators (% of households, m to nearest highway, kg/m³ PM2.5) into a single comparable scale. Iterative refinement of the indicator list through advisory-circle consultations.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: **Not a model — a derived score.** Final per-DA EJI = (Environmental-Burden composite scaled to 0-10) + (Population-Characteristics composite scaled to 0-10), then percentile-ranked across all DAs in the study area. Higher = greater cumulative impact.
  - Units or label space: Continuous 0-100 percentile rank per DA.
- **Model architecture (brief):** **None — composite-index methodology, not a machine-learning model.** Score-construction algorithm: percentile-rank each indicator → average percentile-ranks within each of the 3 categories → average social + health composites into a Population-Characteristics composite → scale Environmental-Burden and Population-Characteristics composites to 0-10 by dividing by the max observed value × 10 → sum the two scaled composites → percentile-rank the final EJI scores. Implementation: **ArcGIS Pro 3.2.2** for spatial processing; **ArcGIS Online Experience Builder** for the public web map.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: **Peterborough Environmental Justice Index** (newly constructed for this work) + **Statistics Canada Census of Population 2021** + **Statistics Canada Canadian Community Health Survey 2023** + various Ontario / municipal open-data layers (polluting-facility locations, road / rail / airport networks, floodplain shapefiles, tree-canopy raster, conservation-authority data) + **19 participants × ~1 year of crowd-sourced Google-Map points** with photos + written reflections.
  - Size: ~150-200 DAs for Peterborough × 39 indicators (~6,000-8,000 cells) for the EJI; participatory mapping is small-N (19 participants).
  - Source: Statistics Canada Census Profile 2021 + CCHS PUMF 2023; Ontario Marginalization Index (Matheson et al. 2023) + Canadian Marginalization Index (Matheson et al. 2012) used as method anchors; municipal + provincial open-data downloads for environmental layers.
  - Public? **Partial.** The Peterborough EJI itself **is publicly accessible** as an interactive ArcGIS Online Experience Builder map (the paper says raw + percentile-ranked indicator values + composite scores can be explored on the map and a URL is referenced as "the full map can be accessed here"). Whether bulk-downloadable as a CSV / shapefile is unclear from the paper alone. The underlying Statistics Canada layers + ON-Marg / CAN-Marg are fully public.
  - Link: Search for "Mapping for Change Peterborough EJI" on ArcGIS Online; supporting information of the Wiley DOI may include the URL. Contact corresponding author Stephanie Rutherford (srutherford@trentu.ca) if direct download is needed.
- **Reported headline metric:** **None in a quantitative-ML sense — qualitative + descriptive findings only.** Cumulative burden concentrates in downtown DAs (top-5% percentile rank). 22% of downtown households low-income (vs. 14.4% citywide); 75% renters; 34% spending >30% income on housing; 11% unemployment; 92% of high-burden DAs within 1 km of a polluting facility; 60% within 50 m of a major road; only 17% tree canopy; 30% on a floodplain; 56% of dwellings built before 1960. **No held-out test set, no formal evaluation, no benchmark comparison.** The paper's "validation" is the qualitative agreement between the EJI map and the participatory-mapping insights from 19 community members.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **CalEnviroScreen 4.0** (California OEHHA) — **the gold-standard public EJ index**: ~8,000 census tracts × 21 indicators (8 pollution + 5 environmental-effects + 5 sensitive-population + 3 socioeconomic). Match: **direct** — explicitly cited as inspiration in the paper. Access: **easy** — full CSV / Excel + shapefile + scoring methodology PDFs from oehha.ca.gov. https://oehha.ca.gov/calenviroscreen
  - **EJScreen 2.x** (US EPA) — ~73,000 census block groups × 12 environmental + 6 demographic indicators with national + regional percentile rankings. Match: **direct** — also cited as inspiration. Access: **easy** — public CSV + shapefile + ArcGIS layer + REST API. https://www.epa.gov/ejscreen
  - **Ontario Marginalization Index 2021** (ON-Marg, Public Health Ontario) — DA-level for all of Ontario × 4 dimensions (residential instability, ethnic concentration, dependency, material deprivation). Match: **close** (social vulnerability piece only, not environmental). Access: **easy** — direct download from Public Health Ontario. https://www.publichealthontario.ca/en/Data-and-Analysis/Health-Equity/Ontario-Marginalization-Index
  - **Canadian Marginalization Index** (CAN-Marg, Matheson et al.) — DA-level for all of Canada × 4 dimensions (same as ON-Marg). Match: **close**. Access: **easy** — direct download.
  - **Statistics Canada Census Profile 2021** — full DA-level data for ~57,000 DAs nationally × ~150 census variables (income, household, education, ethnicity, housing). Match: **direct** for the social-vulnerability + population-characteristics indicators. Access: **easy** — public from statcan.gc.ca. https://www12.statcan.gc.ca/census-recensement/2021/dp-pd/prof/
  - **Statistics Canada Canadian Community Health Survey (CCHS) PUMF** — health-vulnerability indicators (chronic conditions, food insecurity, healthcare access). Match: **direct**. Access: **medium** — free account + Public-Use Microdata File download. Note that DA-level CCHS is restricted; only health-region-level is in the PUMF. Direct DA-level requires a Statistics Canada Research Data Centre application.
  - **Sentinel-2 + Landsat-8/9** (Copernicus + USGS) — multispectral satellite imagery for tree-canopy / land-cover / urban-heat-island modelling — match: **close** for the environmental-burden indicators that can be derived from imagery (tree canopy %, heat-wave proxy, impervious-surface). Access: **easy** — Google Earth Engine or sentinelsat / pystac.
  - **OpenStreetMap** (OSM) — global road / rail / amenity / pollution-source data. Match: **close** for proximity-to-major-road / proximity-to-amenity indicators. Access: **easy** — Overpass API + osmnx / geopandas.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **Medium.** The Peterborough EJI is on a public ArcGIS Online map (interactive view + per-DA drill-down), but bulk download as a clean CSV / shapefile is not confirmed by the paper alone — likely requires emailing Rutherford or scraping the ArcGIS REST endpoint. The two underlying public anchors (Statistics Canada + ON-Marg) are easy.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **Mixed lift.** Tabular ML on the 39-indicator DA vectors is pandas + sklearn / LightGBM only — fine. **But anything that takes advantage of the spatial structure** (the *whole* point of EJ work) requires the Python geospatial stack: **geopandas** (spatial dataframes), **shapely** (geometric operations), **rasterio** (raster I/O), **pyproj** (coordinate-reference-system transforms), **folium** / **leaflet** / **kepler.gl** (interactive web maps), **libpysal** + **esda** + **splot** (spatial-autocorrelation: Moran's I, Getis-Ord Gi*, LISA), **mgwr** (geographically-weighted regression). For satellite-image extensions: **Google Earth Engine Python API**, **stackstac**, **xarray**, **torchgeo**. **The paper used ArcGIS Pro 3.2.2** which is paid + Windows-only — for a free / portable GitHub portfolio, substitute QGIS or geopandas-only workflows. **This is a substantial new ecosystem if the student has not done geospatial Python before** (heavier than Article 1's pure-tabular framing, lighter than the cobrapy / RDKit / GNN tooling for the chemistry / biology professors).
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** Five viable framings, all my construction (the paper itself is methodologically a deterministic composite-index, not an ML model):
  1. **Reproduction in QGIS / geopandas (the cleanest, most direct-replication framing).** *"Reimplementing the Peterborough EJI using only open-source Python (geopandas + folium) and Statistics Canada open data."* Take the 39-indicator list from Table 1, pull every accessible indicator from public sources, reproduce the percentile-rank-and-sum methodology, render an interactive web map with Folium / Leaflet. Notebook + README + a deployed Streamlit app. **README claim:** *"An open-source Python reimplementation of the Peterborough Environmental Justice Index, replacing ArcGIS Pro with geopandas + folium and reproducing within X% of the published scores."* This is **the strongest pure-Article-2 framing** because it directly replicates the paper's method, has a clear Did-it-match? success criterion, and demonstrates geospatial-Python fluency to a recruiter.
  2. **Cross-city EJI for Toronto (or another Canadian city).** *"Extending the Peterborough Environmental Justice Index methodology to the City of Toronto."* Apply the same indicator structure + scoring algorithm to Toronto DAs (~3,700 DAs in the Greater Toronto Area). Compare Toronto's spatial pattern of cumulative burden to Peterborough's. **README claim:** *"A reproducible pipeline that applies the Peterborough EJI methodology to any Canadian city given a list of DAs and the Statistics Canada open-data layers."* This framing is recruiter-legible *and* personally relevant (Toronto is the user's likely thesis context).
  3. **Unsupervised clustering of vulnerability typologies.** *"Discovering natural vulnerability typologies via UMAP + HDBSCAN on the 39-indicator DA vectors."* Linear composite indices average over heterogeneous indicators; clustering finds whether DAs in the top-5% by EJI all look the same or form distinct typologies (e.g., "renter-heavy + downtown-pollution" vs "rural-First-Nations + healthcare-access"). Notebook + cluster-by-cluster narrative + interactive UMAP plot. **README claim:** *"A composite EJI score conflates distinct vulnerability profiles; UMAP+HDBSCAN reveals N typologies that policy interventions should treat differently."*
  4. **Cross-country EJI transfer (CalEnviroScreen → ON-Marg).** *"Training a per-tract vulnerability regressor on CalEnviroScreen and evaluating its transferability to Ontario DAs."* Use CalEnviroScreen as the labeled training set (~8,000 tracts × 21 indicators, fully public CSV); train a LightGBM regressor; evaluate on whatever overlapping indicators are recoverable for Ontario DAs from Statistics Canada + ON-Marg. **README claim:** *"How well do US-trained environmental-justice models transfer to Canadian census geographies? A LightGBM benchmark."*
  5. **Satellite-image-augmented EJI (stretch — heavier compute).** *"Predicting per-DA tree canopy % from Sentinel-2 imagery via a CNN, then re-running the EJI with the predicted layer."* Tree canopy is one of the 11 environmental-burden indicators in Table 1 and is hard to obtain at fine spatial resolution from official sources; Sentinel-2 + a small NDVI-derived classifier or a torchgeo CNN can produce it. **README claim:** *"A satellite-image-augmented Environmental Justice Index for Peterborough, replacing the official tree-canopy layer with a Sentinel-2 CNN derivation."*
  
  **Strongest single recommendation: Framing 1 (open-source reimplementation)** — it is the cleanest direct replication of an actual Classens-co-authored paper, demonstrates geospatial-Python fluency clearly, and the success criterion (matching published scores within tolerance) is unambiguous. **Framing 2** (Toronto extension) is a strong follow-up because it transitions naturally from the replication into a "useful real-world artifact" for the user's home city. **Framings 3-5 add ML novelty** but at the cost of moving away from the paper's own methodology. **Note again:** Article 2 is explicitly skeptical of pure-ML approaches (cites *Weapons of Math Destruction* and the data-justice literature), so a thesis under Classens that uses these framings would need to be carefully positioned as *complementing*, not *replacing*, the participatory + qualitative methodology.

**Article 2 verdict:** A **substantially stronger Classens signal than Article 1**, and a **clearer template for a possible Classens-supervised thesis**. The work is community-engaged, environmental-justice-focused, mixed quantitative-qualitative GIS — exactly the kind of work the School of the Environment supports. **For ML-portfolio purposes**, the open-source reimplementation framing (Framing 1) is the cleanest recruiter-legible project and demonstrates real geospatial-Python skill. **The structural caveat from Article 1 holds**: the paper is not an ML paper, the paper is *explicitly skeptical* of pure-quantitative approaches to social vulnerability, and Classens's funding stream is SSHRC (humanities + social sciences) rather than NSERC. **A successful Classens-supervised ML thesis would need to position ML as complementary to participatory + qualitative methods, not replacing them** — the user should expect to read Cope & Elwood's *Qualitative GIS*, Liboiron's *Pollution Is Colonialism*, and Vera et al.'s *environmental data justice* before sitting down with him.

### Article 3: Climate Data Practices — A Research Approach for HCI and Climate Justice (ACM TOCHI critical-HCI paper)

- **Full citation:** Soden, R., Agrawaal, T. S., Lord, A., Chanen, C., Flawn, L., Seaifan, Z., **Classens, M.**, & Easterbrook, S. (2025). Climate Data Practices: A Research Approach for HCI and Climate Justice. *ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction*, 32(4), Article 34, 27 pages. DOI: 10.1145/3719346. Published August 2025.
- **Authorship signal — third disciplinary register added.** **8-author paper, Classens is the 7th of 8 authors** (penultimate, between U of T students and senior CS faculty). Corresponding author Robert Soden (U of T Computer Science, soden@cs.toronto.edu); senior author Steve Easterbrook (U of T Computer Science) — **a critical-HCI / climate-informatics CS group**, NOT a quantitative-ML group. All 8 authors are at U of T. Middle authors include Taneea S. Agrawaal (CS), Austin Lord (postdoc), and several mail.utoronto.ca students. **Classens is brought in as the environmental-studies subject-matter expert**, bridging Soden's CS-HCI team to environmental-justice scholarship. **This adds a third disciplinary register to Classens's collaborative network**: Article 1 = Nutritional Sciences (Temerty Faculty of Medicine), Article 2 = SSHRC Geography (Trent), Article 3 = U of T Computer Science (critical HCI / climate informatics). **The pattern across all three articles**: Classens collaborates as the environmental-studies / critical-data-studies bridge for teams whose primary disciplinary home is elsewhere.
- **Problem in plain English:** Despite massive growth in climate data over the past decades (remote sensing, IoT sensors, ML, big data), governments and civil society have not made commensurate progress on climate action. The authors argue this is because **"information determinism"** — the false belief that more data alone produces social change — misattributes agency to data while ignoring the **social practices** through which data is created, used, shared, and made meaningful. They introduce **"climate data practices"** as a conceptual lens for HCI research at the intersection of critical data studies, practice theory, and climate / environmental justice. Drawing on a year-long collaborative ethnographic study of activists, City of Toronto staff, and non-profits, they present **six vignettes** of climate data practices and connect them to HCI theory.
- **ML task type:** **Not an ML paper — explicitly anti-ML in its theoretical framing.** Methodologically a **qualitative + interpretive critical-HCI study**: ethnographic fieldwork, semi-structured interview studies, and document analysis. The conceptual contribution is a framework (practices + scenes + infrastructures) for *critically interrogating* data and ML systems, not for building them. The paper explicitly cites: **information determinism** (Srinivasan, Finn & Ames 2017), **Weapons of Math Destruction** (O'Neil 2016 — also cited in Article 2), **Pollution Is Colonialism** (Liboiron 2021 — also cited in Article 2), **environmental data justice** (Vera et al. 2019 — also cited in Article 2), **algorithms-of-oppression** (Noble 2018), **forgetting practices in data sciences** (Muller & Strohmayer 2022), and **"beyond technical fixes"** (Nightingale et al. 2020). **An ML reframe is possible but more theoretically fraught than for Articles 1 or 2** — any ML reframing of this paper is *against* its central argument. Possible framings: (i) **build the equity-overlay dashboard the paper critiques** — pull City of Toronto Open Data climate indicators, add CalEnviroScreen-style equity layers (per-capita rather than per-acre emissions, demographic overlays, vulnerability composites), publish as a Streamlit / Folium app framed as a response to Soden et al.'s critique; (ii) **NLP analysis of TCFD corporate climate-financial-disclosure filings** — extract climate-financial framing patterns from public corporate filings, audit how companies report climate risk; (iii) **LLM audit of climate framings** — evaluate how GPT-4 / Claude / open-source LLMs frame climate change (do they reify carbon-emissions-only views, miss recognition justice, fail on Indigenous knowledge?) — connects to AI-ethics / FAccT / responsible-AI recruiter audience; (iv) **Mapillary / Street View CNN classification** of pop-up vs car-dominated street infrastructure (transferable from Article 2's geospatial framing); (v) **topic modelling on Climate Action Tracker / CDP corporate-disclosure text corpora**. **All five are my constructions; the paper itself frames no ML task and is explicitly anti-information-determinism.**
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: **Qualitative ethnographic + interview data** — the paper's primary data is private interview transcripts (City of Toronto staff in environment + finance divisions, climate-justice activists, non-profit organization staff including Muslim-women-bicycling community center, urban farmers, transit planners) and document analysis (City of Toronto climate dashboards, financial reports, TCFD filings, data-for-equity strategy documents).
  - Shape if stated: **Not specified.** The paper says the team met biweekly or monthly from September 2022 to August 2023, with multiple individual studies feeding the synthesis; total participant count not stated.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: Standard qualitative-research workflow (collaborative thematic discussion, vignette construction). No specific software named; presumably NVivo / Atlas.ti for coding (not mentioned).
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: **Not a model — six descriptive vignettes + a conceptual framework.** Output is theoretical: the *climate data practices* approach + the *practices/scenes/infrastructures* trio.
  - Units or label space: N/A.
- **Model architecture (brief):** **None — qualitative + interpretive critical-HCI methodology**, not a machine-learning model.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: Private interview + ethnographic + document-analysis dataset on climate data practices in the City of Toronto. **Public document references** include the City of Toronto's net-zero-2040 emissions dashboard, the City's Data for Equity Strategy, City Financial Reports (2018–2019 with TCFD disclosures), and the Toronto seed library / Seedy Saturday/Sunday events.
  - Size: **Not specified.** Year-long study with ~7 individual researcher work-streams.
  - Source: City of Toronto staff + Toronto-area activists + non-profits + urban farmers (year-long Toronto fieldwork, 2022-2023).
  - Public? **No — the primary qualitative dataset is private** (standard for ethnographic IRB-approved research). **Topic-adjacent public datasets** that the paper *references* are public: City of Toronto Open Data, TCFD corporate filings, CDP, Climate Action Tracker.
  - Link: **Not provided in paper** for the primary dataset. Public references: https://open.toronto.ca/, https://www.fsb-tcfd.org/, City climate dashboard linked in Figure 1-2.
- **Reported headline metric:** **None — qualitative descriptive + theoretical contribution.** No formal evaluation, no benchmark, no held-out test set, no error metrics. "Validation" is internal coherence of the conceptual framework + connection to prior HCI / STS / practice-theory literature.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **City of Toronto Open Data** — the City's official climate + emissions dashboard data + 100+ open datasets (transit, social services, demographics). Match: **direct** for the dashboarding vignette + the equity-overlay framing. Access: **easy — direct download** (CKAN portal). https://open.toronto.ca/
  - **Climate Action Tracker (CAT)** — country-level climate-policy assessments. Match: **loose** (national rather than urban scope). Access: **easy** — public data + scraping. https://climateactiontracker.org/
  - **CDP (Carbon Disclosure Project)** — corporate + city climate-disclosure database. Match: **close** for the financialization + TCFD framings. Access: **medium** — free account + portal access; bulk downloads sometimes restricted. https://www.cdp.net/
  - **TCFD-aligned corporate filings** — scattered across SEC / SEDAR / company sustainability-report repositories. Match: **direct** for the financialization vignette. Access: **medium-hard** — issuer-by-issuer scraping; harmonization non-trivial.
  - **Mapillary** + **Google Street View** — street-level imagery for the pop-ups vignette (school streets, traffic-calming interventions). Match: **close**. Access: **easy** (Mapillary free, Street View Static API has rate-limited free tier). https://www.mapillary.com/
  - **Open Food Facts** + **Seedy Saturday/Sunday catalog data** — for the seed-sharing vignette. Match: **loose** (broader food-packaging + seed-library scope). Access: **easy** (Open Food Facts) / **medium** (Seedy events typically lack a centralized catalog). https://world.openfoodfacts.org/data
  - **City of Toronto's published equity-overlay maps + 2023 Data for Equity Strategy** — gives the City's own equity-strategy framing as a public anchor. Match: **direct** (the paper critiques this strategy explicitly). Access: **easy**. https://www.toronto.ca/city-government/accessibility-human-rights/equity-diversity-inclusion/data-for-equity/
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **Very hard / N/A** — the primary qualitative dataset is private interview + ethnographic data and is not redistributable. Topic-adjacent public data is **easy-to-medium**.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **Mostly within current toolset**, with one or two additions per chosen framing. Standard ML stack (pandas / sklearn / lightgbm) for tabular framings; **Hugging Face transformers (BERT / RoBERTa / Climate-BERT)** for the TCFD / corporate-disclosure NLP framings; **Folium / Streamlit / Plotly Dash** for the equity-overlay-dashboard framing; **OpenAI / Anthropic API + LangChain / instructor** for the LLM-audit framing; **Mapillary API + torchvision** for the street-imagery framing. **No new heavy ecosystem** (no cobrapy / RDKit / SBML / DFT). **Conceptual reading is heavier than tooling** — to do this work credibly requires familiarity with critical data studies (Loukissas, Mah, D'Ignazio & Klein, Liboiron) + practice theory (Bourdieu, Schatzki, Reckwitz, Shove) + critical HCI (Soden's own prior work, Bardzell, Light & Shklovski).
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** Five viable framings, all my construction (the paper itself is methodologically anti-ML and explicitly critiques information determinism):
  1. **Equity-overlay climate dashboard for Toronto (most direct response to the paper).** *"Building the per-capita, equity-overlaid climate dashboard that Soden et al. (2025) argue Toronto needs."* Pull City of Toronto Open Data climate indicators (GHG emissions, transit + housing + health vulnerability), reframe per-capita rather than per-acre, overlay CalEnviroScreen-style demographic vulnerability layers from the Article-2 framing, and deploy as a Streamlit / Folium app. **README claim:** *"A community-equity-overlay variant of the City of Toronto climate dashboard, built in response to Soden et al.'s (2025) critique of carbon-emissions-only framings."* This is **the strongest pure-Article-3 framing** because it directly engages the paper's own dashboarding critique while producing a tangible, recruiter-legible artifact.
  2. **LLM audit of climate-change framings.** *"How do GPT-4, Claude Opus, and open-source LLMs frame climate change? An audit informed by Soden et al.'s climate data practices framework."* Evaluate how off-the-shelf LLMs respond to climate-related prompts (carbon-emissions-only vs equity-aware framings, treatment of Indigenous knowledge, recognition justice, distributional vs procedural framings). Notebook + structured prompt-evaluation harness + qualitative + quantitative analysis. **README claim:** *"An empirical audit of how large language models frame climate change, drawing on Soden et al. (2025)'s climate-data-practices framework."* **Strongest portfolio-impact framing for AI-ethics / FAccT / responsible-AI recruiter audiences** (Anthropic policy team, Hugging Face, Vector Institute, MILA AI ethics, Google Research responsible-AI, OpenAI policy).
  3. **TCFD / CDP corporate-disclosure NLP analysis.** *"Topic modelling and framing analysis of climate-financial disclosures across Canadian municipalities + Fortune 500 corporations."* Scrape public TCFD-aligned filings, fine-tune a Climate-BERT / SciBERT classifier on greenwashing-vs-substantive framings, analyze patterns. **README claim:** *"A quantitative analysis of climate-financial-disclosure framing patterns across N corporations + M cities."* Direct response to the financialization vignette in the paper; legible to ESG / sustainability-finance / climate-policy recruiters.
  4. **Mapillary CNN classifier for active-transportation infrastructure.** *"Predicting pop-up-style traffic-calming interventions from street-level imagery."* Train a torchvision CNN on Mapillary tiles annotated as pop-up vs car-dominated, transfer to other Canadian cities. Connects directly to the pop-ups vignette + Article 2's geospatial framing. **README claim:** *"A CNN-based detector for active-transportation infrastructure from Mapillary imagery, applied to Toronto's pop-up program evaluation."*
  5. **Practice-theory-informed LLM-application audit (most theoretical).** *"Auditing AI climate-action chatbots / recommenders against Soden et al.'s practices/scenes/infrastructures framework."* Pick 2-3 public AI climate tools (e.g., ClimateGPT, ClimateBERT-based dashboards, climate-action chatbots), audit each against the paper's six practices + critical-data-studies framework. Less ML-building, more ML-auditing. **README claim:** *"A practice-theory-informed audit of three public climate AI tools, evaluated against Soden et al. (2025)'s framework."* Strongest *theoretical depth* framing.
  
  **Strongest single recommendation: Framing 2 (LLM climate audit)** — it is the highest portfolio-impact framing for the responsible-AI / AI-ethics recruiter audience that *most matches* Classens's actual research direction across all three articles. **Framing 1 (equity-overlay dashboard)** is the most concrete + recruiter-legible to civic-tech / public-health / ESG audiences. **Framings 3-5 are stretch options** with progressively heavier theoretical load. **Note again:** Article 3 is *the most explicitly anti-ML of the three Classens articles* (cites information determinism, Weapons of Math Destruction, Pollution Is Colonialism, environmental data justice, beyond-technical-fixes), so any ML-building framing here must be carefully positioned as *responding to* — not replacing — the paper's critical-HCI argument.
