### Article 2: Operando Neutron Radiography of Concentration Distributions in RFBs (*Nature Communications*)

- **Full citation:** Jacquemond, R. R., **van der Heijden, M.**, Boz, E. B. (these three contributed equally), Carreón Ruiz, E. R., Greco, K. V., Kowalski, J. A., Muñoz Perales, V., Brushett, F. R., Nijmeijer, K., Boillat, P., & Forner-Cuenca, A. (2024). Quantifying concentration distributions in redox flow batteries with neutron radiography. *Nature Communications*, 15, 7434. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-50120-7. **CC BY 4.0** (open access). **Source Data Files released** + **ChemRxiv preprint with data** at https://chemrxiv.org/engage/chemrxiv/article-details/64e77958dd1a73847f6d8c15 + **two video supplementaries** online.
- **Authorship caveat:** Maxime is **co-first author** alongside Rémy Jacquemond (TU Eindhoven + DIFFER) and Emre Burak Boz (TU Eindhoven) — the three contributed equally per the explicit author-contribution statement. Forner-Cuenca is corresponding/last-author PI. **Major international collaboration**: TU Eindhoven Forner-Cuenca lab (Maxime, Boz) + DIFFER Dutch Institute for Fundamental Energy Research (Jacquemond, Nijmeijer) + Paul Scherrer Institute Switzerland (Carreón Ruiz, Boillat — neutron-imaging beamline scientists) + MIT Brushett group (Greco, Kowalski) + UC3M Madrid (Muñoz Perales) + JCESR (US DOE Energy Innovation Hub). **Funded by ERC FAIR-RFB 101042844 + Dutch NWO Veni 17324 + NWO Science XS OCENW.XS4.295 + JCESR/DOE + NSF Graduate Research Fellowship (Greco) + Swiss NSF P2EZP2_172183 (Forner-Cuenca postdoc support).** **Authored during her PhD at TU Eindhoven** — same era as Article 1, NOT yet UWaterloo-faculty work. **Co-first authorship with Jacquemond + Boz** is one tier below sole-first-authorship (Article 1's class) but the *Nature Communications* venue is several tiers above *Adv. Mater. Technol.* — net authorship-signal upgrade vs. Article 1.
- **Problem in plain English:** Standard electrochemical diagnostics (polarization curves, EIS, charge-discharge cycling) treat a redox flow battery as a "black box" — they tell you cell-level current and voltage but cannot tell you *where inside the cell* species are concentrated, where mass-transfer limitations form, or how charge carriers actually move between half-cells. To rationally design better electrodes, separators, and flow fields, the field needs an **operando, non-invasive, spatially-resolved** technique to image dissolved-species concentrations inside an *operating* flow cell. The paper introduces **operando neutron radiography** as that technique, leveraging the fact that hydrogen-rich organic redox molecules (TEMPO/TEMPO+) and boron-containing supporting ions (BF₄⁻) are highly attenuating to thermal/cold neutrons while the deuterated acetonitrile solvent (CD₃CN) and PF₆⁻ supporting ion are nearly transparent — yielding subtractive-imaging contrast between active species and supporting electrolyte.
- **ML task type:** **The paper has NO ML.** It is primary research on a new diagnostic technique (image-based concentration quantification via Lambert-Beer law + 2×2 energy-resolved matrix inversion). **Reframing required to ship an ML portfolio project — but the reframings are abundant and well-aligned because the released data is image data, the most ML-friendly modality.** The natural ML reframes are: **(1) U-Net semantic segmentation** of operando radiograph stacks (electrolyte vs. electrode vs. membrane vs. flow channels); **(2) CNN regression** mapping raw radiograph → concentration field, replacing the Lambert-Beer pixel-wise calculation with a learned decoder; **(3) Physics-informed neural network (PINN)** trained on the released ChemRxiv operando concentration data, constrained by the coupled Nernst-Planck-Poisson-Stokes reactive-transport PDEs — directly bridges Article 2 to Pulsipher's Article 3 PINN methodology.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: **2D neutron radiograph stacks** of operando flow cells. NEUTRA (thermal-neutron white beam): single grayscale 2D images per timestep, 6 μm pixel pitch, ~20 μm effective resolution, ~30 s exposure time per acquisition. ICON (cold-neutron time-of-flight): stacks of energy-binned grayscale images per timestep, 55 μm pixel pitch, ~150 μm effective resolution, 120 s per energy frame, 109 ToF frames per 11.36 ms cycle binned to High-Energy (17.0–77.3 meV, mean 28.3 meV) + Low-Energy (5.7–16.0 meV, mean 8.5 meV) frames.
  - Shape/size: NEUTRA images are 2D arrays at 6 μm pitch over a ~15 mm × 1.5 mm reactor area (~2,500 × 250 pixels per cell-area image); ICON images are 512 × 512 pixel² at 55 μm pitch (28 × 28 mm² field of view).
  - Preprocessing in the paper: 11-step image-processing pipeline — dark current correction, white-spot filtering (gamma-ray rejection), Gaussian filtering, open-beam correction, registration (correlation-based geometric transformation), intensity correction (gain + offset), scattered-background correction (via "black body" boron rods placed in front of the sample), referencing (pixel-wise division by reference cell), positioning (rotation), cell mask (region-of-interest selection), concentration calculation via Lambert-Beer law `T = exp(-σᵢ · nᵢ · δ)` with cuvette-calibrated cross-sections σᵢ. For ICON: a 2×2 matrix inversion `[ln T_LE; ln T_HE] = δ_cell · [σ_BF4_LE σ_TEMPO_LE; σ_BF4_HE σ_TEMPO_HE] · [C_BF4; C_TEMPO] · N_A` to deconvolute species concentrations pixel-wise.
- **Output representation:**
  - **Paper's outputs:** 2D pixel-wise concentration maps in mol/L for: (a) cumulative `[TEMPO]+[TEMPO+]` in the KPF6 system at NEUTRA (max ~0.5 M); (b) cumulative `[TEMPO]+[TEMPO+]+[BF4-]` in the BF4 system at NEUTRA (max ~1.0 M, includes BF4 contribution); (c) **deconvoluted `[TEMPO]+[TEMPO+]` AND `[BF4-]` separately** at ICON via energy-resolved 2×2 matrix inversion (each up to 0.5 M).
  - Units / label space: continuous regression target — concentration in mol/L (0 to 0.5 or 0 to 1.0 M depending on system); spatial dimension across reactor (μm-scale).
- **Model architecture (brief):** **No ML model in the paper.** The "model" is the Lambert-Beer law (pixel-wise scalar inversion at NEUTRA) + a 2×2 linear system (energy-resolved inversion at ICON). For the ML reframings: (i) **U-Net** (PyTorch, well-documented) for image segmentation of cell components; (ii) **2D CNN regressor** (PyTorch — standard ResNet/U-Net encoder-decoder backbone) for radiograph → concentration field; (iii) **PINN** (PyTorch + autograd-based PDE residual loss; tools like DeepXDE or NVIDIA Modulus) for Nernst-Planck-Poisson-Stokes reactive-transport modeling.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: **Operando neutron radiography stacks** of TEMPO/TEMPO+ + supporting-salt non-aqueous flow cells across two beamlines × multiple polarization conditions × multiple flow rates
  - Size: hundreds-to-thousands of images per beamline × multiple experimental conditions (6 polarization states × 2 flow rates × 2 supporting salts at NEUTRA + similar matrix at ICON); precise size depends on Source Data Files contents
  - Source: Custom — experiments at Paul Scherrer Institute SINQ facility (NEUTRA + ICON beamlines, proposal numbers 20202189 + 20202333); flow cells assembled at TU Eindhoven Forner-Cuenca lab; electrolytes synthesized in-house from TEMPO + nitrosonium tetrafluoroborate (NOBF4) / hexafluorophosphate (NOPF6); flow cells used Sigracet 39AA paper electrodes (NEUTRA) or AvCarb G100 felt electrode (ICON, 3200 μm thick to compensate for lower spatial resolution); Fumasep FAB-PK-130 anion exchange membrane (130 μm).
  - Public? **PARTIAL — Source Data Files released via Nature Communications + ChemRxiv preprint** at https://chemrxiv.org/engage/chemrxiv/article-details/64e77958dd1a73847f6d8c15 + two video supplementaries online. **MAJOR upgrade vs. Article 1's "data on request" status.** Code is on-request only ("The code used in this study can be provided by the corresponding author upon request") — drag, but the data itself IS publicly accessible.
  - Link: ChemRxiv preprint with data — https://chemrxiv.org/engage/chemrxiv/article-details/64e77958dd1a73847f6d8c15 ; Nature Comm article — DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-50120-7; Source Data Files downloadable from the published article supplementary
- **Reported headline metric:** Lambert-Beer law holds linearly across 0–0.5 M for TEMPO, TEMPO+PF₆⁻, and TEMPO+BF₄⁻ in CD₃CN (cuvette calibration, R² near 1.0). Operando: at +0.6 V WE polarization, a TEMPO+ concentration front accumulates near the membrane (Donnan exclusion); at lower flow rates the front is more pronounced (5.6 mL/min worse than 15.1 mL/min). With BF4⁻ as supporting anion, BF4⁻ migration across the anion-exchange membrane is **directly imaged** — confirms BF4⁻ is the dominant charge carrier. ICON ToF deconvolution successfully separates TEMPO and BF4⁻ concentration profiles via 2×2 matrix inversion with cuvette-calibrated LE+HE cross-sections (TEMPO: σ_LE=0.34 cm², σ_HE=0.28 cm²; BF4⁻: σ_LE=0.37 cm², σ_HE=0.25 cm²). Capacity utilization: 60% discharge at -0.6 V / 21.1 mL/min, 45% recharge at +0.6 V → 15% underutilization due to asymmetric starting BF4⁻ distribution.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **The paper's OWN released data** (Source Data Files via Nature + ChemRxiv preprint) — match: **direct, perfect** — access: **easy** (download from Nature article supplementary + ChemRxiv link)
  - **PSI ICON / NEUTRA beamline open datasets** (Paul Scherrer Institute neutron-imaging archive — some operando fuel-cell + battery datasets are publicly available) — match: **close-by-domain** — access: **medium** (PSI registration; not all data is open)
  - **ImageNet / COCO / Kaggle medical-imaging segmentation datasets** — wrong domain but useful for U-Net pretraining transfer-learning step — match: **analogy** — access: **easy**
  - **Lithium-ion battery operando neutron-radiography datasets** (Michalak 2015 *Sci. Rep.* gas evolution, Liu 2014 *Angew. Chem.* lithium transport, Lanz 2001 *J. Power Sources*) — wrong electrolyte but methodologically adjacent — match: **analogy** — access: **medium** (per-paper supplementary materials)
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **Easy-to-medium — Source Data Files + ChemRxiv preprint are publicly downloadable.** Code is request-only (drag for full reproducibility but not blocking for dataset use). **Substantial improvement vs. Article 1's "data on request" status.**
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **PyTorch** (already familiar from prior projects); **U-Net architecture** (standard CV — well-documented; many open-source implementations and tutorials); **image preprocessing pipeline** (scikit-image / OpenCV — minor new pieces for neutron-imaging-specific corrections like dark-current + scattered-background subtraction); **HDF5 / TIFF stack handling** (h5py + tifffile — standard scientific Python). **Optional stretch (PINN route): autograd-based PDE residual losses** (DeepXDE or NVIDIA Modulus — one major new framework concept; closely related to Pulsipher Article 3's PINN methodology so cross-survey-synergistic to learn). **Optional stretch (segmentation transfer learning)**: pretrained ImageNet/medical-segmentation U-Net weights as initialization.

  1. **"U-Net segmentation of operando neutron radiographs."** Train a U-Net on the released ChemRxiv stacks to segment electrolyte vs. electrode vs. membrane vs. flow channels in the operando radiographs. README headline claim: *"Pixel-accurate semantic segmentation of operando neutron-radiography stacks at 95%+ IoU, replacing the paper's 11-step manual ImageJ pipeline."* **Cleanest beginner-friendly framing.**
  2. **"CNN concentration regression replacing Lambert-Beer."** Train a 2D CNN (encoder-decoder backbone) on (raw radiograph → ground-truth concentration map) pairs from the released data, learning the cuvette-calibrated Lambert-Beer transformation end-to-end. README headline claim: *"Learned concentration decoder matches paper's Lambert-Beer baseline within ~5% RMSE without explicit cross-section calibration."* **Mid-difficulty; demonstrates ML-can-replace-physics framing.**
  3. **"Physics-informed neural network for reactive transport in an operating RFB."** Train a PINN on the released ChemRxiv concentration data, with the loss combining (a) data fitting to operando concentration maps, (b) Nernst-Planck-Poisson-Stokes PDE residuals, (c) boundary/initial conditions from the cell geometry. **Bridges directly to Pulsipher Article 3 PINN methodology** — natural co-supervision setup if Maxime + Pulsipher both at UWaterloo. ### Article 3: Foundational Pore Network Modeling Framework for RFB Electrodes (*J. Electrochem. Soc.*, "Women in Electrochemistry" Focus Issue)

- **Full citation:** **van der Heijden, M.**, van Gorp, R. (these two contributed equally), Sadeghi, M. A., Gostick, J., & Forner-Cuenca, A. (2022). Assessing the versatility and robustness of pore network modeling to simulate redox flow battery electrode performance. *Journal of The Electrochemical Society*, 169(4), 040505. DOI: 10.1149/1945-7111/ac5e46. **CC BY 4.0** (open access). **Part of "Women in Electrochemistry" Focus Issue.** Supplementary material online (Sections S1–S6).
- **Authorship caveat:** Maxime is **co-first author** alongside Rik van Gorp (TU Eindhoven, the same co-first who appears on the unprocessed van Gorp/van der Heijden 2023 *Chem. Eng. J.* GA+PNM companion paper). Forner-Cuenca is corresponding/last-author PI. **Major UWaterloo + TU Eindhoven collaboration**: Mohammad Amin Sadeghi (UWaterloo Chemical Engineering, OpenPNM core developer) + **Jeffrey Gostick (UWaterloo Chemical Engineering, OpenPNM founder/maintainer)** provided the OpenPNM framework + model debugging. Funded by Dutch NWO Veni 17324 (Forner-Cuenca). **Authored during her PhD at TU Eindhoven** — same era as Articles 1 + 2, NOT yet UWaterloo-faculty work. **Co-first authorship class** with van Gorp; same authorship class as Article 2 but with a smaller, tightly-collaborative author roster (5 authors total vs. Article 2's 11). **Chronologically the EARLIEST of Maxime's three articles** (2022, vs. Article 1's 2023 + Article 2's 2024) — Article 3 is the foundational PNM paper that the rest of her PhD-era research builds on. **Direct UWaterloo collaboration via Gostick + Sadeghi** is a particularly strong signal for a future UWaterloo-faculty-era continuation of this research thread.
- **Problem in plain English:** Designing better porous electrodes for redox flow batteries (RFBs) requires understanding how electrode microstructure (pore size distribution, fiber arrangement, porosity gradients) affects cell-level performance (current, pressure drop, mass-transfer limitations). Direct numerical simulations (lattice Boltzmann, finite-element CFD) are accurate but too computationally expensive to use for design optimization at the cell scale (~1 cm). Macroscopic continuum models are fast but volume-averaged — they can't capture local microstructural effects. Pore network modeling (PNM) is a middle-ground approach: approximate the porous space as a network of spheres (pores) connected by cylinders (throats), solve 1D analytical transport equations on the network instead of full 3D PDEs. The paper asks: **can a PNM be made versatile + robust enough to handle multiple electrode geometries (paper + cloth) and multiple electrolyte chemistries (aqueous + non-aqueous)?** And: **what is the minimum set of fitting parameters needed to accurately reproduce experimental cell performance?**
- **ML task type:** **The paper has NO ML.** It is primary research on a new computational framework (PNM for RFBs). However, **the paper's conclusion explicitly invites ML coupling**: *"Coupled with machine learning approaches, the proposed framework can be used as a predictive framework with the potential to accelerate the engineering of porous electrodes for specific electrolyte chemistries from the bottom-up."* **Reframing required, but the paper hands you the invitation directly.** The natural ML reframes are: **(1) ML surrogate for the PNM** — train an MLP / GBM / CNN on (electrode features + electrolyte properties + applied voltage) → (current, pressure drop, overpotentials) to replace the slow iterative Butler-Volmer solver with a fast learned predictor; **(2) GNN on extracted pore networks** — treat the network as a graph (nodes = pores with diameter + position + chemistry features, edges = throats with conductances), train a GNN to predict performance directly; **(3) Active learning for parameter identification** — train an ML model to identify km / j₀ / α from polarization curves automatically, replacing the manual SciPy least-squares fitting in the paper; **(4) PINN** for the same Butler-Volmer + Nernst-Planck-Poisson-Stokes physics, validated against this paper's PNM ground truth + Article 2's released ChemRxiv operando data — bridges directly to Pulsipher Article 3 PINN methodology.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: **3D pore network extracted from X-ray tomographic microscopy** of dry uncompressed electrodes via the SNOW algorithm (Gostick 2017, marker-based watershed segmentation). Each network = (pore-diameter array, throat-diameter array, pore-position array, throat-connectivity list). For the laboratory-scale 1.7 cm electrode, multiple ~1 mm subsamples are placed in series ("network-in-series" approach) to match the full electrode length while preserving microstructural fidelity.
  - Shape/size: 2 electrode types — Freudenberg H23 paper (~1 mm × 1 mm × 198 μm subsample, ~thousands of pores; unimodal PSD ~15 μm) + ELAT Cloth woven (~1 mm × 1 mm × 375 μm subsample, ~thousands of pores; bimodal PSD with small inter-fiber pores + larger inter-bundle pores up to 260 μm). XTM resolution 3.3 μm/voxel.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: 2D median filter (radius 2.0 px) → K-means cluster segmentation → SNOW algorithm with marker-based watershed → trim boundaries (1 mm × 1 mm × full-thickness selection from center of tomogram) → extract pore + throat properties via OpenPNM.
- **Output representation:**
  - **Paper's outputs:** at each applied voltage (0 to -1V in -0.05V steps), the iterative algorithm computes per-pore concentration, per-pore current, per-pore overpotential, per-pore pressure → integrated to: (a) total current at applied voltage = polarization curve point, (b) total pressure drop, (c) spatially-resolved 2D maps of current density / concentration / pressure across the electrode (Figs. 6, 7, 8).
  - Units: current in A or A/cm² or A/m³ (volume-specific), pressure in Pa, concentration in mol/m³, overpotential in V.
- **Model architecture (brief):** **No ML model in the paper.** The "model" is the PNM framework: coupled Navier-Stokes (Hagen-Poiseuille on cylindrical throats with hydraulic conductance α = π·S³_T / 8μL_T) + advection-diffusion-reaction (1D analytical Sadeghi 2020 solution per throat) + Butler-Volmer kinetics (with mass-transfer limitations via film theory k_m = 2D/d_p) + charge conservation (Ohm's law on the network with electrical conductance β = σ_l·S_T/L_T). Two half-cells coupled via macroscopic membrane resistance (Δφ_m = R_m·I_m). Iterative scheme with under-relaxation (ω=0.1) + linearization of charge transport source term. ~5×10⁴ max iterations per voltage step; tolerances 5×10⁻⁵ relative + 6×10⁻⁴ A/cm² absolute. ~100 min per polarization curve on single i7-8750H CPU.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: **Custom XTM tomograms of 2 commercial electrodes** (Freudenberg H23 paper + ELAT Cloth woven, both Fuel Cell Store) + **paired single-electrolyte symmetric flow cell polarization measurements** for 2 redox chemistries (aqueous Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ + non-aqueous TEMPO/TEMPO⁺) × 3 inlet velocities (1.5, 5, 20 cm/s) × 3 replicates per system = ~36 polarization curves
  - Size: 2 electrode XTM subsamples (~1 mm³ each) + ~36 experimental polarization curves
  - Source: TU Eindhoven Forner-Cuenca lab + Fuel Cell Store commercial electrodes + Scanco Medical μCT 100 cabinet microCT scanner; **OpenPNM (Gostick lab UWaterloo)** for PNM framework
  - Public? **PARTIAL** — paper does NOT release a separate code/data repository, but **all model parameters are tabulated in Table II + Table SII** (electrolyte properties: ρ, μ, σ_l, α_a, α_c, D, c_in, c_ref; kinetic parameters: j₀ as fitted from experiments per Table SII); **OpenPNM is fully open-source** (github.com/PMEAL/OpenPNM, MIT-licensed, Gostick UWaterloo); supplementary material released online (Sections S1-S6); paper is Open Access (CC BY 4.0). XTM tomograms not separately released. Code for THIS specific paper not separately released.
  - Link: paper at DOI 10.1149/1945-7111/ac5e46; OpenPNM at github.com/PMEAL/OpenPNM; supplementary material via stacks.iop.org/JES/169/040505/mmedia
- **Reported headline metric:** PNM accurately captures TEMPO/TEMPO⁺ symmetric-cell polarization performance for BOTH electrode types (Freudenberg H23 + ELAT Cloth) **WITHOUT fitting parameters** (RMSE within experimental error bars per Table SIII; Fig. 4). Exchange current densities j₀ extracted from experimental fits range 1870–460 A/m² for non-aqueous, 652–98.7 A/m² for aqueous. PNM partially captures aqueous Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ performance for paper electrode ONLY with a fitted km (correction factor 0.11–1, depending on velocity; Table SIV; Fig. 5c) — attributed to incomplete electrode wetting in aqueous experiments (acetonitrile-based electrolytes fully wet carbon fiber; aqueous at contact angle ~80–90° does not). PNM does NOT capture aqueous Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ for cloth electrode even with km fitting — additional resistance correction needed (Fig. 5d) due to multi-scale woven microstructure with threaded fiber bundles that SNOW algorithm cannot fully represent. Velocity sweep at 5/1/0.5/0.2/0.05/0.01/0.005/0.001/0.0005 cm/s (Fig. 9) identifies operating envelopes — kinetically-sluggish electrolytes (j₀ = 1×10⁻² or 1×10⁻⁴ A/m²) reach the "pumping power = electrical power" demarcation at lower velocities than facile electrolytes (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺), and the higher permeability of cloth electrodes enables wider operational ranges.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **OpenPNM** (https://github.com/PMEAL/OpenPNM) — Gostick lab UWaterloo, MIT-licensed; **the entire simulation framework used in the paper is publicly available** — match: **direct, perfect** — access: **easy** (`pip install openpnm`)
  - **PoreSpy** (https://github.com/PMEAL/porespy) — image-based pore-network extraction (the SNOW algorithm + marker-based watershed used in this paper) — match: **direct** — access: **easy** (`pip install porespy`)
  - **Published micro-CT volumes of carbon-fiber GDL/RFB electrodes** (Brushett, Gostick, Eller groups) — methodologically adjacent — match: **close** — access: **medium**
  - **Battery Archive / NREL battery datasets** — wrong scale (cell cycling, not microstructure) — match: **analogy** — access: **easy**
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **Easy-to-medium — OpenPNM is fully open-source** + all model parameters tabulated in Table II + supplementary material online + paper is Open Access (CC BY 4.0). XTM tomograms not released but easily regenerated with OpenPNM-built networks parameterized from the paper's reported geometric properties (porosity, permeability, internal surface area). **Better than Article 1's "data on request"; comparable to Article 2's Source Data + ChemRxiv release in a different way (parameters tabulated vs. raw data released).**
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **OpenPNM** (Python pore network modeling framework — same one needed for Article 1; well-documented; Gostick lab maintains it; ~1 week of self-study); **pore network modeling concepts** (throat conductance, Hagen-Poiseuille on networks, Butler-Volmer kinetics with mass-transfer limitations via film theory, network-in-series approach — all new for a chemistry undergrad with intermediate ML skills, but fundamental to any RFB-electrode portfolio project); **standard ML stack** (PyTorch / sklearn / XGBoost — already familiar). **Optional stretch (GNN route): PyTorch Geometric or DGL** for graph-based ML on extracted pore networks; **Optional stretch (PINN route): same as Article 2's PINN tooling** — DeepXDE or NVIDIA Modulus, bridges to Pulsipher Article 3 PINN methodology.
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** **"ML surrogate for the foundational PNM framework on RFB electrodes."** Reproduce the paper's PNM simulations on Freudenberg H23 + ELAT Cloth via OpenPNM (using the paper's tabulated parameters in Table II + Table SII), generate ~5,000 synthetic (electrode-geometry × electrolyte-chemistry × velocity) → (current, pressure-drop) pairs by varying parameters around the paper's baselines, train a tabular regressor (XGBoost or MLP) or a GNN (if treating networks directly as graphs) to predict performance metrics. Validate against the paper's reported polarization curves (TEMPO + Fe systems, both electrodes) by digitizing Figs. 4 + 5. README headline claim: *"ML surrogate matches OpenPNM physics within ~10% RMSE on held-out electrode-electrolyte combinations, while running ~1000× faster — enabling rapid Pareto-frontier exploration of porous electrode designs across redox chemistries."* **Stretch goal**: combine with the genetic algorithm framework from Maxime's own van Gorp/van der Heijden 2023 *Chem. Eng. J.* unprocessed companion paper to perform GA-driven design optimization with the ML surrogate as the fast fitness evaluator (instead of the slow PNM). **OR**: train a PINN that solves the same Butler-Volmer + Nernst-Planck-Poisson-Stokes physics + validates against both Article 3's PNM results AND Article 2's released ChemRxiv operando concentration data — bridges directly to Pulsipher Article 3 PINN methodology, forming the strongest cross-survey portfolio.

### Article 1: Catalytic and Biocatalytic Degradation of Microplastics (multi-institute REVIEW article, *Exploration*)

- **Full citation:** Zandieh, M., Griffiths, E., Waldie, A., Li, S., **Honek, J.**, Rezanezhad, F., Van Cappellen, P., & Liu, J. (2024). Catalytic and biocatalytic degradation of microplastics. *Exploration*, 4, 20230018. DOI: 10.1002/EXP.20230018. **CC BY** (open access).
- **Authorship caveat:** **REVIEW article**, not primary research. **Honek is 5-of-8 authors** + **one of FOUR co-corresponding authors** (with Juewen Liu for Chemistry, Fereidoun Rezanezhad + Philippe Van Cappellen for Water Institute). First-author Mohamad Zandieh is a postdoctoral fellow in **Juewen Liu's lab** (the chemistry-side senior PI per the explicit author bios — Zandieh's bio reads *"He is currently a postdoctoral fellow under the supervision of Prof. Juewen Liu in the Department of Chemistry at the University of Waterloo"*). Honek's role appears to be **enzymology expertise** (Section 4.1 on enzymatic degradation of PET, PE, PS) consistent with his stated research focus on enzymology + bionanomaterials. **Co-corresponding authorship** is a meaningful PI-class signal but **diluted** by (a) being one of four co-corresponding authors and (b) the paper being a review rather than primary research from his own group. **Compare to Mahadevan A1** (community paper with peripheral authorship) — similar PI-signal weakness, and notably distinct from the strongest authorship classes (Wania-last-corresponding primary research, Galatro-first-corresponding primary research, Pulsipher-last-corresponding primary research).
- **Problem in plain English:** Microplastics (sub-millimeter plastic particles) are pervasive environmental pollutants from PE / PP / PS / PVC / PET that resist natural degradation for centuries. The review surveys the current state of catalytic + biocatalytic strategies for breaking down microplastics — natural enzymes (cutinases / PET hydrolases / laccases / peroxidases / alkane hydroxylases for PET / PE / PS), Fenton chemistry (Fe²⁺ + H₂O₂ → ·OH radicals), nanozymes (Fe₃O₄ + photocatalytic TiO₂ / ZnO / Cu₂O nanomaterials), and microbe-assisted degradation (Bacillus / Pseudomonas / Alcanivorax in marine + freshwater settings). Tables 1-4 compile ~50-100 (enzyme/material × plastic × analysis × weight loss) literature tuples across ~150 references.
- **ML task type:** **The paper has NO ML.** It is a literature review with compiled tables. **Reframing required for any ML portfolio project — and the reframing path is constrained by the review-not-primary-research nature of the source.** The natural ML reframes are: **(1) Protein language model (ESM-2 / ProtBERT) classifier for plastic-degrading enzymes** — train a classifier/regressor on UniProt entries filtered by the paper's identified EC numbers (EC 3.1.1.101 PET hydrolase, EC 1.10.3.2 laccase, EC 1.11.1.13 manganese peroxidase, EC 1.14.15.3 alkane hydroxylase) → predict plastic-degrading activity from protein sequence; **(2) Tabular regression on the paper's compiled Tables 1-4** — features (plastic type, enzyme/catalyst type, source organism, pretreatment, conditions) → label (weight loss % or oxidation extent); **(3) Chemoinformatic property prediction** — combine RDKit polymer descriptors with enzyme/catalyst features → degradation outcome; **(4) Literature text-mining / NLP** for building a structured plastic-degradation database (heavy lift; weak ML angle).
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: **Heterogeneous** — for the protein-language-model reframe, protein amino-acid sequences (FASTA, ~200-700 amino acids per enzyme) from UniProt; for the tabular reframe, plastic-type one-hot + enzyme-class one-hot + source-organism categorical + pretreatment categorical + conditions (pH, T, time) continuous.
  - Shape/size: UniProt has thousands of sequences for cutinases + laccases + peroxidases + alkane hydroxylases combined (filterable by EC number) — adequate for ESM-2 fine-tuning; the paper's Tables 1-4 compile ~50-100 (enzyme × plastic × outcome) tuples — too small for deep learning on its own but useful as a curated test set or weak-supervision training set.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: N/A (review article, no original computational pipeline). For the ML reframe: standard sequence preprocessing (FASTA loading via Biopython, sequence-length filtering, ESM-2 tokenization).
- **Output representation:**
  - **Paper's outputs:** narrative review + compiled tables of literature observations (plastic type × catalyst × analysis method × weight loss % × reference). No quantitative model predictions.
  - For the ML reframe: regression target = weight loss % (0-100); classification target = "plastic-degrading" vs "non-degrading" binary; ranking target = top-K best plastic-degrading sequences.
- **Model architecture (brief):** **No model in the paper.** Reframing options: (i) **ESM-2 + linear probe / MLP head** for sequence-based binary classification (Meta AI's protein language model, freely available on HuggingFace); (ii) **Random Forest / XGBoost** for tabular regression on Tables 1-4 features; (iii) **GNN on polymer molecular graphs** (overkill for the small variety of polymer types — only ~10 distinct polymers).
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: **Compiled literature tables** from ~150 references — Tables 1 (purified enzymes for PE), 2 (TiO₂ photocatalytic degradation), 3 (other photocatalytic nanomaterials), 4 (microbial degradation in marine/freshwater).
  - Size: ~50-100 (catalyst, plastic, conditions, weight loss) tuples across the four tables.
  - Source: Each row sourced from a separate primary-research paper cited in the review.
  - Public? **No** original data — but the review aggregates publicly-discoverable information from primary literature (each row is sourced from an Open Access or paywalled primary paper). For the ESM-2 protein-language-model reframe: **UniProt is fully public + free** (https://www.uniprot.org); **PDB is fully public + free** (https://www.rcsb.org); both have downloadable APIs.
  - Link: paper at DOI 10.1002/EXP.20230018; UniProt at https://www.uniprot.org; PDB at https://www.rcsb.org; ESM-2 weights at https://huggingface.co/facebook/esm2
- **Reported headline metric:** N/A — review article with no quantitative model. Compiled headline observations from the literature: PET enzymatic depolymerization is **commercially close** (Carbios first commercial plant 2025); PE biodegradation is **the hardest** (low surface energy + no heteroatoms + crystalline domains); Fe₃O₄ nanozymes achieve **~100% weight loss** at temperatures near plastic melting point; LMWPE laccase + 1-hydroxybenzotriazole mediator system achieves measurable oxidation; aqueous Fe²⁺/H₂O₂ Fenton chemistry achieves >95% PE weight loss at 140°C with 7.5h treatment; cutinase from *Thermobifida fusca* causes 50% weight loss of commercial PET film.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **N/A — review article with no original dataset.** For the ESM-2 reframe via UniProt: **easy** (free + public + scriptable). For the tabular reframe via the paper's Tables 1-4: **medium** (manual digitization required from PDF tables).
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **PyTorch + HuggingFace transformers** (familiar); **ESM-2 protein language model** (one major new component — well-documented, many tutorials, recently featured in AI-for-biology papers — ~1 week of self-study); **Biopython** for FASTA / UniProt API handling (one minor new piece); **RDKit** for polymer descriptors if going chemoinformatic route (familiar from prior projects); **standard ML stack** (sklearn / XGBoost — already familiar). Rev.* PET hydrolase dataset + recent BRENDA entries to label sequences with known activity / no-activity / unknown. Compute ESM-2 embeddings on the labeled set + train a binary classifier (logistic regression on embeddings, or fine-tuned MLP head). - **Full citation:** Jenkins, T., Persaud, B. D., Cowger, W., Szigeti, K., Roche, D. G., Clary, E., Slowinski, S., Lei, B., Abeynayaka, A., Nyadjro, E. DOI: 10.3389/fenvs.2022.912107. **CC BY** (open access). **Original Research** article (bibliometric meta-analysis).

- **Problem in plain English:** As microplastic pollution research has exploded (~6,608 articles in Web of Science 1964-2021), how openly are the underlying datasets being shared? Are they FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable)? The paper performs a bibliometric meta-analysis on a stratified random sample of 785 microplastic articles + a comprehensive search of 10 data repositories (Dryad, Pangaea, Mendeley, Figshare, Zenodo, etc.) yielding 279 microplastic datasets, to quantify how often microplastic researchers actually share their data + what types of media + geographic regions are represented + what the dominant repository platforms are.

  - Preprocessing in the paper: Web of Science Boolean search (microplastic OR microplastics) + R 4.0.3 / dplyr 1.0.2 stratified random sampling + manual inspection (260 articles removed for irrelevance) + repository site-specific search + duplicate removal (n=21).
- **Output representation:**

  - For the ML reframe: classification target (has data sharing statement yes/no, repository type, data-sharing-category 8-class); regression target (year of publication or media type prediction).
- **Model architecture (brief):** **No model in the paper.** Reframing options: (i) **logistic regression / Random Forest / XGBoost** on tabular metadata for classification; (ii) **BERT / sentence-transformers embeddings + k-means** for abstract clustering (would require scraping abstracts beyond the released metadata); (iii) **collaborative-filtering recommender** on (paper, repository) pairs.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**

### Article 3: Thermodynamic Overview of Bioconjugation Reactions Pertinent to Lysine and Cysteine Peptide and Protein Residues (FIRST Honek-Sole-Corresponding Primary Research Paper)

- **Full citation:** Lopandic, M., Merza, F., & **Honek, J. F.** (2023). Thermodynamic Overview of Bioconjugation Reactions Pertinent to Lysine and Cysteine Peptide and Protein Residues. *Compounds*, 3(3), 464–503. DOI: 10.3390/compounds3030035. **CC BY** (open access). MDPI.
- **Authorship caveat:** **HONEK IS THE SOLE CORRESPONDING AUTHOR + LAST AUTHOR.** Co-first authors Maja Lopandic + Fatima Merza are listed as "These authors contributed equally to this work" with current addresses at EPFL (Lopandic — Polymer Lab, Institute of Materials) + Public Health Ontario (Merza), indicating they are former Honek-supervised trainees (Lopandic was an NSERC CGS M Master's-level recipient per the funding statement). **This is the FIRST Honek-sole-corresponding primary research paper in the survey** — a major positive PI-signal flip after the middle/peripheral Article 1 (1-of-4 co-corresponding) + Article 2 (16-of-21 deep middle). **Funded by Honek's NSERC RGPIN-2017-05232 Discovery Grant** (his core research grant) — NOT the Global Water Futures consortium grant of Articles 1+2 — confirming this paper represents Honek's actual research program (bioconjugation chemistry + enzymology + medicinal-chemistry DFT computation), not the peripheral microplastic-consortium participation.
- **Problem in plain English:** Bioconjugation reactions — covalent attachment of small molecules (drug payloads in antibody-drug conjugates, fluorophores, PEG chains, biophysical probes) to protein side chains — are foundational tools in biological chemistry, antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) development, and biomaterials. Lysine (-NH₂) and cysteine (-SH) side chains are the two most-targeted nucleophilic sites. The paper computes the **thermodynamic favorability** (∆G in water) of >320 bioconjugation reactions as a unified reference compendium — what reagents work well, which cellular intermediates can spontaneously modify proteins (a complication for biological assays + a contributor to non-enzymatic post-translational modifications), and which drug molecules might non-enzymatically acylate proteins as off-target side effects (e.g., aspirin's confirmed acetylation of 523+ proteins in human cancer cells per Wang et al. 2015). Existing literature has fragmented studies at inconsistent levels of theory; this paper provides a unified DFT survey.
- **ML task type:** **NOT an ML paper** — pure DFT computational chemistry. ML reframe options: (1) **regression of reaction Gibbs free energy ∆G(water) on reactant SMILES** via a graph neural network (D-MPNN / Chemprop / GIN); (2) **binary reactivity classification** ("favorable for bioconjugation" if ∆G < −20 kJ/mol); (3) **ML-DFT surrogate** — train a neural network potential on a subset of computed reactions, generalize to held-out reagent classes.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality (paper): SMILES + 3D molecular geometry. Reactants = simple model nucleophiles (methylamine for lysine, methanethiol for cysteine, water for hydrolysis benchmarks) + diverse electrophilic reagents (esters, anhydrides, acyl chlorides, thioesters, NHS esters, fluorophenyl esters, p-nitrophenyl esters, carbonates, isocyanates, isothiocyanates, imidates, sulfonyl chlorides, epoxides, maleimides, DNFB, squarate esters, aldehydes, disulfides, α-bromoacids, α-bromoamides, dibromomaleimides, click reagents, CoA-thioester cellular intermediates, cyclic anhydrides, acyl phosphates, acetyl-L-carnitine + 30+ structural analogs, drug molecules).
  - Modality (ML reframe): SMILES strings → atom-bond molecular graphs (for GNN) OR RDKit descriptors / Morgan fingerprints (for tabular regression).
  - Preprocessing in paper: Conformer search via MMFF (Spartan'20) or OPLS4 (Schrödinger MacroModel) → HF/6-31G(d) or B3LYP/6-31G(d) geometry optimization → DFT single-point energy at higher level. C-PCM (Spartan'20) or COSMO (Jaguar) implicit aqueous solvation.
- **Output representation:**
  - Paper: ∆E, ∆G, ∆H in kJ/mol (gas phase + C-PCM/COSMO water phase).
  - ML reframe target: ∆G(water) in kJ/mol — scalar regression — observed range ≈ −300 to +25 kJ/mol across the reaction set (most favorable: tetrazine + TCO click reaction at −287 kJ/mol; least favorable: methyl acetate hydrolysis at +21.7 kJ/mol; bioconjugation reagents typically −15 to −80 kJ/mol).
- **Model architecture (paper, brief):** Composite thermochemical recipes (T1, G3(MP2)) for gas-phase benchmarking + DFT (M06-2X/6-311+G(2df,2p)//B3LYP/6-31G(d) + M06-2X/cc-PVTZ(-f)++) for diverse reactions in gas + intrinsic aqueous phases; C-PCM (Spartan'20) + COSMO (Jaguar) continuum solvation models. Commercial software: Spartan'20 (Wavefunction, Inc.) + Schrödinger Jaguar / MacroModel / Maestro.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: Custom DFT-computed dataset of >320 bioconjugation reactions (paper text states ">320 reaction computations were undertaken") tabulated in Tables 1–15 + supplementary Tables S1–S10
  - Size: 320+ unique reactions × 3-4 thermodynamic outputs each (∆E gas, ∆E water, ∆G water, ∆H water)
  - Source: Computed in this study using commercial software (Spartan'20 + Schrödinger Jaguar)
  - Public? **NO — Data Availability Statement reads "Computational data are available by directly contacting the corresponding author."** Tables in PDF only (no machine-readable CSV / JSON / Zenodo / FRDR / GitHub release). Supplementary tables S1-S10 available as PDF only.
  - Link: PDF supplementary at https://www.mdpi.com/article/10.3390/compounds3030035/s1; underlying numerical dataset request-only.
- **Reported headline metric:** Validation against experimental thermodynamics where literature values exist. Examples: methyl thioacetate hydrolysis ∆G = −19.81 kJ/mol (computed) vs experimental −17.15 ± 6.28 kJ/mol (Guthrie 1978) — within experimental uncertainty. Methyl acetate hydrolysis ∆G = +21.7 kJ/mol (computed) consistent with Shi et al. 2009. Acetic anhydride aminolysis ∆E = −77.34 kJ/mol (computed) consistent with Kruger 2002 MP2/6-31+G(d,p) value of −74.48 kJ/mol. Click reactions: methyl azide + propyne → triazole ∆G = −238 kJ/mol; trans-cyclooctene + tetrazine ∆G = −287 kJ/mol. Cellular CoA-thioester acylation of methylamine: ∆G ≈ −58 to −61 kJ/mol (consistent with non-enzymatic protein acylation observed in vivo per Trub & Hirschey 2018, Wagner et al. 2017). Aspirin + methylamine ∆G = −75.77 kJ/mol (consistent with aspirin's confirmed off-target acetylation of 523+ proteins per Wang et al. 2015).

### Article 1: Aptamer Array for Discriminating Tetracycline Antibiotics Based on Binding-Enhanced Intrinsic Fluorescence

- **Full citation:** Zhao, Y., Gao, B., Chen, Y., & **Liu, J.** (2023). An aptamer array for discriminating tetracycline antibiotics based on binding-enhanced intrinsic fluorescence. *Analyst*, 148, 1507–1513. DOI: 10.1039/d3an00154g. Royal Society of Chemistry.
- **Authorship caveat:** **Liu is sole corresponding + last author** with trainee Yichen Zhao first. Strongest authorship class — primary research from Liu's own UWaterloo lab. Funded by **NSERC + Strathclyde/Waterloo Joint Transatlantic Funding** (NOT the Global Water Futures consortium grant of Honek's microplastic work, although Liu was the senior PI on Honek's microplastic Article 1).
- **Problem in plain English:** Tetracycline antibiotics (oxytetracycline OTC, tetracycline TC, doxycycline DOX) share a 4-ring core, making them notoriously hard to discriminate — antibodies cross-react at 47–102%. The paper builds a sensor array of three DNA aptamers (none individually fully selective) that **together**, via PCA on their fluorescence-enhancement responses, discriminate all three tetracyclines from each other and from 7 unrelated antibiotics/fluorophores at 50 nM concentrations. Tetracyclines are intrinsically fluorescent; aptamer binding enhances fluorescence — so detection is label-free (no fluorophore tag on the DNA needed).
- **ML task type:** **NOT primarily an ML paper** — uses PCA, which is unsupervised dimensionality reduction (borderline ML). No supervised neural network. ML reframe options: (1) supervised 4-class classifier (RF / SVM / small MLP) trained on (3 aptamer F−F₀ values) → analyte identity, with cross-validation comparing against PCA + k-NN baseline; (2) aptamer DNA sequence (~42 nt) + tetracycline SMILES → predicted Kd or fluorescence fold-change via DNABERT / Nucleotide Transformer fine-tuning; (3) Mfold predicted secondary-structure features (loop sizes, hairpin counts, stem lengths) → Kd regression on the 10-aptamer dataset.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality (paper): 3 aptamer fluorescence enhancement values (F − F₀) × 6 replicates per analyte; 10 aptamers × 3 tetracyclines × titration curves (Kd determination).
  - Modality (ML reframe): for option 1, 3D feature vector → multi-class label; for option 2, DNA sequence + small-molecule SMILES → scalar Kd.
  - Preprocessing: 100 nM antibiotic + titrated aptamer in pH 6.0 MES buffer + 2 mM Mg²⁺; Tecan plate reader (370 nm ex / 535 nm em).
- **Output representation:**
  - Paper: PCA score plots (PC1 vs PC2) — unsupervised cluster IDs.
  - ML reframe target: 4-class label {OTC, TC, DOX, control} OR scalar Kd in nM.
- **Model architecture (paper, brief):** Mfold (secondary structure prediction) + Clustal Omega (sequence alignment + family clustering of top 100 SELEX library sequences) + R PCA on the sensor array fluorescence enhancement matrix.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: Custom-collected aptamer-tetracycline binding dataset
  - Size: 10 aptamers × 3 tetracyclines × 6 replicates fluorescence enhancement matrix; 3 selected aptamers × 10 analytes × 6 replicates selectivity matrix; concentration-dependent titrations
  - Source: Generated in this study via Tecan plate reader experiments
  - Public? **NO** — paper data lives only in figures + ESI PDF. No Zenodo / GitHub / Dryad release.
  - Link: ESI at https://doi.org/10.1039/d3an00154g (PDF only)
- **Reported headline metric:** LOD = 0.7 nM OTC, 0.3 nM TC, 0.4 nM DOX (label-free fluorescence titration). Kd values low nM to ~10 µM range. PCA: PC1 = 84.8% + PC2 = 11.1% variance explained — clear separation of 4 clusters. Linear range 10-200 nM OTC for the array.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **UCI Gas Sensor Array Drift Dataset** — 13,910 measurements × 16 sensors × 6 gases — match: **direct architectural analogue** for the chemical-sensor-array PCA-vs-supervised-classifier reframe (option 1) — access: **easy** (UCI ML repo, one-line CSV download)
  - **AptaNet / AptaDB / RNAcentral** — public DNA/RNA aptamer-target binding databases — match: **direct** for the sequence-based Kd regression reframe (option 2) — access: **medium** (some need account; AptaNet is a 2021 *Brief. Bioinform.* paper with public benchmark)
  - **DNABERT-2 / Nucleotide Transformer pretrained checkpoints** — match: **direct** for fine-tuning option 2 — access: **easy** (HuggingFace one-line load)
  - **MoleculeNet** — broader chemistry ML benchmark including small-molecule property prediction — match: loose — access: easy (DeepChem)
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **Hard** — paper data is only in PDF figures, no machine-readable release. **However the ML reframe is so simple (3 features × ~30 samples) that you can manually transcribe from Fig. 5A**, OR substitute the UCI gas-sensor public dataset for the same architectural reframe with much more data.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **Mfold** (RNA/DNA secondary structure prediction — nucleic-acid specific tool, new; web server available, no local install needed for a small project), **Clustal Omega** (sequence alignment — bioinformatics standard, web-server-available), **scikit-learn** (PCA + LDA + RandomForestClassifier — already familiar), optionally **HuggingFace transformers + DNABERT-2 / Nucleotide Transformer** for sequence-based aptamer-affinity prediction (substantial new component for option 2).
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** **Two viable framings**:

Train PCA + k-NN baseline (replicating Liu's paper approach), then RF / SVM / small MLP supervised classifiers with stratified cross-validation. README headline: *"Supervised classifiers outperform PCA + k-NN on chemical-sensor-array discrimination by X% accuracy with batch-effect robustness."*

Fine-tune DNABERT-2 or Nucleotide Transformer on (aptamer DNA sequence, target SMILES) → log(Kd). Validate on Liu's 10 OTC-targeted aptamers + their measured tetracycline Kd as a held-out test. ### Article 2: Surface Ligand Engineering Ruthenium Nanozyme Superior to Horseradish Peroxidase for Enhanced Immunoassay (Liu MIDDLE Author on China-Led Collaboration)

- **Full citation:** Fan, H., Zheng, J., Xie, J., **Liu, J.**, Gao, X., Yan, X., Fan, K., & Gao, L. (2024). Surface Ligand Engineering Ruthenium Nanozyme Superior to Horseradish Peroxidase for Enhanced Immunoassay. *Advanced Materials*, 36(10), 2300387. DOI: 10.1002/adma.202300387. Wiley-VCH.
- **Authorship caveat:** **Liu is 4-of-8 middle author**, NOT corresponding. **Sole corresponding author = Lizeng Gao** (CAS Engineering Laboratory for Nanozyme, Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing — `gaolizeng@ibp.ac.cn`). Co-first authors marked equal contribution = Huizhen Fan + Jiajia Zheng. **CHINA-LED multi-institute collaboration** — CAS Institute of Biophysics + National Center for Nanoscience China + Zhengzhou University. Liu provides UWaterloo nanozyme/aptamer expertise as a peripheral co-author. **Funded by Chinese government grants** (National Key R&D Program 2019YFA0709200 + National Natural Science Foundation 81930050 etc.) — NOT NSERC. **Analogous authorship class to Honek's Articles 1+2** (peripheral co-authorship on PI-other-led collaborative work).
- **Problem in plain English:** Nanozymes (nanomaterials with enzyme-like activity) are cheaper + more stable than natural enzymes but typically have much lower catalytic activity. The paper engineers Ru nanoparticle surface ligands (PSS / PVA / PVP / PAA polymers) to tune charge transfer between the metal core and the polymer coating, achieving peroxidase (POD)-like specific activity of 2820 U mg⁻¹ for Ru@PSS — **2× higher than horseradish peroxidase (HRP, 1305 U mg⁻¹)**. They demonstrate practical impact via a nanozyme-linked immunosorbent assay (NLISA) for the tumor marker α-fetoprotein (AFP) achieving 1.4 pg/mL LOD — **140× more sensitive** than commercial HRP-ELISA.
- **ML task type:** **NOT an ML paper** — pure experimental + DFT computational chemistry. ML reframe options: (1) **polymer-descriptor regression** — predict POD-activity (U mg⁻¹) from polymer SMILES / RDKit descriptors / functional-group features; small dataset (~5 polymer/Ru pairs + 6 noble metals × 4 ligands ≈ 30 data points); (2) **DFT-property surrogate** — predict E_ads,·OH from metal + ligand combination via small ML model; (3) **inverse design** — generative model proposing new polymer ligands with target charge-transfer properties. All reframes are stretched by tiny dataset size.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality (paper): 6 platinum-group metals (Ru, Rh, Pd, Os, Ir, Pt) × 4 polymers (PSS, PVA, PVP, PAA) → POD activity matrix; XPS Ru 3p binding energies; DFT-computed Bader charges + E_ads,·OH; Michaelis-Menten kinetics (KM, kcat) for TMB + H₂O₂ substrates.
  - Modality (ML reframe): polymer SMILES → RDKit descriptors / Morgan fingerprints; metal identity → one-hot.
- **Output representation:**
  - Paper: specific activity (U mg⁻¹), KM, kcat, Bader charge transfer (e/monomer), E_ads,·OH (eV), AFP detection LOD (pg/mL).
  - ML reframe target: POD activity scalar regression OR E_ads,·OH scalar regression.
- **Model architecture (paper, brief):** No ML. Experimental synthesis (solvothermal, 200 °C, 12 h) + characterization (TEM, XRD, XPS, FTIR, DLS, ESR) + DFT (VASP 5.4.4, PBE-D3BJ functional, 450 eV cutoff, 3×3×1 Monkhorst-Pack k-mesh, slab models of Ru(100)).
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: Custom-collected nanozyme activity dataset
  - Size: ~5 Ru-polymer pairs + ~6 platinum-group metals × 4 polymers ≈ 30 activity measurements + DFT calculations on 2 detailed slab models
  - Source: Generated in this study
  - Public? **NO** — Data Availability Statement: "data available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request." No GitHub / Zenodo / FAIR release.
  - Link: Wiley SI at https://doi.org/10.1002/adma.202300387 (PDF only)
- **Reported headline metric:** Ru@PSS specific activity 2820 U mg⁻¹ (2× HRP); kcat-active-site = 3.23 s⁻¹; E_ads,·OH = −3.06 eV (closer to optimal −2.6 eV than bare Ru's −3.68 eV); NLISA LOD for AFP = 1.4 pg/mL (140× better than HRP-ELISA at 197 pg/mL); 10× better than other reported AFP immunoassays.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **QM9 / ANI-1x** — DFT-property datasets for small molecules — match: **loose** (per-molecule properties, not metal-ligand systems) — access: **easy**
  - **The Materials Project / OQMD** — DFT datasets for solid-state and bulk materials — match: **loose** (different chemistry) — access: easy
  - **Open Catalyst Project (OC20 / OC22)** — 1.2M+ DFT-relaxed catalyst-adsorbate systems — match: **moderate-direct** for the metal-surface adsorption-energy reframe (option 2) — access: **easy** (https://opencatalystproject.org/)
  - **Nanozyme-related datasets** — scarce; some emerging via NanoMine + Chinese nanozyme databases but not standardized
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **Hard** — request-only via Lizeng Gao at CAS Beijing. Commercial VASP DFT software (~$5-15k/year academic license) makes replicating the DFT calculations effectively inaccessible to a student. Public alternative (OC20/OC22) is easy but doesn't directly match the polymer-coated-Ru chemistry.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **VASP** (commercial DFT — not student-accessible), or **psi4 / xtb / GPAW** as open-source alternatives (heavier, optional), **RDKit** (polymer SMILES → descriptors), **scikit-learn** (small tabular regression — familiar), optionally **PyTorch + PyG** for GNN polymer-property prediction (new tooling territory, optional).
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** **"Nanozyme-activity surrogate model — predict POD activity from polymer ligand descriptors."** Manually extract the ~30 (metal, polymer, POD activity) data points from Tables 1 + S1 + S14 + main text + Fig. 4d. Augment by literature mining of nanozyme review papers (Wei et al. 2021 *Nano Today*, Wang et al. 2021 *J. Mater. Chem. B*) to grow the dataset. Train baseline RDKit-descriptor + XGBoost regressor on (metal one-hot, polymer descriptors) → POD activity. Validate via leave-one-metal-out cross-validation. Stretch goal: substitute the polymer-ligand prediction with an Open Catalyst Project surrogate (predict E_ads,·OH for metal-adsorbate systems), then back-calculate POD activity via Sabatier principle. README headline: *"Tabular ML predicts noble-metal nanozyme POD activity from polymer ligand descriptors with R² = X on leave-one-metal-out CV — guides ligand selection without DFT."* **Honest caveat**: dataset is tiny (~30 points), Liu is middle-author (lab-leader signal weak), and commercial VASP dependency makes the original work hard to extend. **Article 2 is structurally weaker as a Liu-anchor than Article 1.**

### Article 1: Ngt-1 — a glycosyltransferase that confers resistance to three distinct antibiotic classes (Wright-corresponding McMaster paper; Sychantha 2nd-of-8 with "supervision"-only CRediT role — research-associate / co-supervisor stage at McMaster, McMaster-based and pre-UWaterloo)

Ngt-1: a glycosyltransferase that confers resistance to three distinct antibiotic classes. *Journal of Biological Chemistry*. DOI: 10.1016/j.jbc.2026.111479. (Journal Pre-proof; received 23 Feb 2026; accepted 12 Apr 2026.)
- **Authorship caveat:** Sychantha is **2nd author of 8** on a **Wright-sole-corresponding** paper. The CRediT statement lists Sychantha's contribution as **"methodology, supervision, writing-review & editing" only** — confirming he was a co-supervisor on the project but **NOT the senior PI**. Gerard D. Wright (McMaster, David Braley Centre for Antibiotic Discovery) is the corresponding author and senior PI; Wright is one of the world's most prominent antibiotic-resistance researchers (D'Costa & Wright 2006/2011, ancient-DNA resistome, glycopeptide-resistance discovery, etc., are all Wright-lab work). **Treat this paper as evidence of the kind of research Sychantha was trained on / co-supervises — NOT as primary research from his independent UWaterloo group.** Combined with Article 2 (Whitney-corresponding 2022 *Molecular Cell* paper, where Sychantha is 2-of-10 with investigation-only CRediT during his CIHR Postdoctoral Fellowship), the 2-article picture is **two McMaster trainee-stage co-authorships in two different labs** — neither Sychantha-corresponding. Until a Sychantha-corresponding paper from his independent UWaterloo Chemistry group is processed, the PI-signal class for his lab remains **structurally unconfirmed**.
- **Problem in plain English:** Antibiotic resistance is one of the largest looming public-health threats. Beyond the clinical pathogens that grab the headlines, soil and environmental bacteria carry a massive untapped reservoir of resistance genes ("the environmental resistome") that may eventually be mobilized into pathogens under selective pressure. The authors screened 200 isolates from a single Nigerian agricultural-soil sample and identified *Bacillus thuringiensis* WAC10774B, which inactivates novobiocin (an aminocoumarin antibiotic) — the **first-ever reported enzymatic inactivation of this antibiotic class**, ~70 years after the drug was discovered. They identified the responsible enzyme — a glycosyltransferase they named **Ngt-1** — and showed it transfers a glucose group from UDP-glucose onto a hydroxyl group of THREE structurally distinct antibiotic classes (novobiocin / aminocoumarin, fidaxomicin / tiacumicin, salinomycin / polyether), inactivating all three. Ngt-1 is a "proto-resistance element" — a gene that does not currently cause clinical resistance but has the structural capacity to evolve into one if mobilized into pathogens.
- **ML task type:** **Paper has NO native ML task** — fundamentally a wet-lab biochemistry + structural-biology paper using FragPipe/MSFragger proteomics, X-ray crystallography (2.0 Å), AlphaFold + Chai Discovery protein-ligand modeling, MUSCLE / IQ-TREE 2 phylogenetics, and steady-state kinetics. Multiple ML reframes are possible (see below); the strongest is **ARG (antibiotic-resistance gene) sequence classification on CARD (Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database)** using protein-language-model embeddings (ESM-2 or ProtBERT).
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: protein sequences (227 aa Ngt-1 + ~100 BLASTP/UniRef90 GT-B fold homologs); small-molecule structures (3 antibiotics + UDP-glucose); 2.0 Å X-ray crystal structure (PDB 10ZG); AlphaFold-predicted structure; MIC fold-changes; steady-state kinetic constants
  - Shape/size if stated: 227 aa Ngt-1 protein; 1 enzyme × 3 antibiotics × 256-fold / 8-fold / 8-fold MIC increases (Table 1); 4 steady-state kinetic curves with ~10 substrate concentrations each (Table 2: KM, kcat, kcat/KM); 1 X-ray co-crystal at 2.0 Å resolution (Rwork 0.1738, Rfree 0.2052, P2₁2₁2₁ space group); 1 Chai-modeled protein-ligand complex (aggregated confidence 0.894, pTM 0.933, ipTM 0.884; RMSD vs crystal 0.653 Å); 100 BLASTP UniRef90 hits used to build IQ-TREE 2 phylogenetic tree
  - Preprocessing in the paper: ammonium sulfate fractionation (20%, 40%, 60%, 80%) + 4-step activity-guided protein purification (Phenyl Sepharose 6 FF + Hydroxyapatite + HiTrap Q HP) + trypsin digest + LC-QToF-MS (Agilent 6545 LC-Q-TOF) DIA auto MS/MS; FragPipe / MSFragger v23.1 peptide mapping vs. *B. thuringiensis* UP000011719 proteome; MUSCLE alignment + trimAl (gt 0.05) + IQ-TREE 2 (v2.2.2.7) + ModelFinder + UFBoot2 (1000 replicates) + iTOL phylogenetic reconstruction; Phaser-MR molecular replacement (PHENIX) + COOT manual model building + PHENIX refinement (X-ray); Chai Discovery + AlphaFold protein-ligand modeling; Michaelis-Menten + Substrate-Inhibition fits in GraphPad Prism v10.6.1
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: in the paper itself, **NO ML model is trained**. Outputs are biochemical: enzyme-mediated antibiotic modification site (benzamide hydroxyl on novobiocin, confirmed by MS/MS + NMR), MIC fold-change (256× novobiocin / 8× fidaxomicin / 8× salinomycin), steady-state kinetic constants (kcat/KM ~10⁷-10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹), proposed catalytic mechanism (His14 catalytic base, Asp326 stabilizes UDP-glucose, Asp106 stabilizes His14 — H14A and D326A mutagenesis abolishes activity, validating mechanism)
  - Units / label space: MIC in µg/mL; kinetics in µM, s⁻¹, M⁻¹s⁻¹; Ramachandran-class statistics for crystal structure; aggregated confidence + pTM + ipTM for Chai model
- **Model architecture (brief):** **No ML model trained in the paper.** The paper uses **Chai Discovery + AlphaFold** for protein-ligand structural prediction (Chai's prediction matches the experimental crystal at 0.653 Å RMSD — a direct demonstration of how well current protein-ligand models work on a real glycosyltransferase·antibiotic complex). For an ML reframe: **ESM-2 (or ProtBERT) sequence embeddings + linear / MLP classifier** on CARD ARG categories is the standard portfolio architecture.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: experimental data deposited across 4 public repositories
  - Size: 1 enzyme × 3 antibiotics (extremely small for direct supervised ML); 100 BLASTP hits for phylogenetic tree
  - Source: NCBI WGS (Bacillus thuringiensis WAC10774B = SAMN57016808; Amycolatopsis sp. WAC10774A = SAMN57036074), PDB **10ZG** (X-ray structure of Ngt-1·novobiocin·UDP), BMRbig139 (NMR of glucosylated novobiocin), Figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.31972497 (proteomics MS data)

- **Reported headline metric:** **Ngt-1 confers a 256-fold increase in novobiocin MIC** (0.5 → 128 µg/mL) when expressed in hypersusceptible *E. coli* BW25113 ∆bamB ∆tolC; 8-fold increases for fidaxomicin (16 → 128 µg/mL) and salinomycin (4 → 32 µg/mL). Glucosylation at the benzamide hydroxyl reduces novobiocin antibacterial efficacy 64-fold. X-ray structure refined to 2.0 Å (Rwork 0.1738, Rfree 0.2052). ### Article 2: An ADP-ribosyltransferase toxin kills bacterial cells by modifying structured non-coding RNAs (Whitney-corresponding *Molecular Cell* paper; Sychantha 2nd-of-10 with "investigation"-only CRediT — pure CIHR Postdoctoral Fellowship-era trainee work at McMaster, EVEN WEAKER PI signal than Article 1)

- **Full citation:** Bullen, N. P., **Sychantha, D.**, Thang, S. S., Culviner, P. H., Rudzite, M., Ahmad, S., Shah, V. S., Filloux, A., Prehna, G., & Whitney, J. C. (2022). An ADP-ribosyltransferase toxin kills bacterial cells by modifying structured non-coding RNAs. *Molecular Cell*, 82(17), 3484–3498. DOI: 10.1016/j.molcel.2022.08.015. (Received 23 May 2022; accepted 11 Aug 2022; published 6 Sep 2022.)
- **Authorship caveat:** Sychantha is **2nd author of 10** on a **Whitney-sole-corresponding** paper. The CRediT statement lists Sychantha's contribution as **"performed radioisotope assays, mass spectrometry, and developed HPLC methods"** — pure **investigation / methodology** role, NO supervision component. The acknowledgments confirm Sychantha was supported by a **Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR) Postdoctoral Fellowship** at the time of this paper (2022) — pure postdoc-stage trainee work in **John C. Whitney's lab at McMaster** (Department of Biochemistry & Biomedical Sciences + David Braley Centre for Antibiotic Discovery). **PI-signal class on Article 2 is even WEAKER than Article 1**: postdoc-investigator (A2, 2022) → research-associate / co-supervisor (A1, 2026) is the trainee-progression trajectory. **This article is fundamentally Whitney-lab work, not Sychantha-independent research.** Notable: Whitney is a Canada Research Chair in Molecular Microbiology and a Burroughs Wellcome Fund Pathogenesis Investigator — Sychantha's training pedigree includes two highly-prominent senior PIs (Whitney + Wright).
- **Problem in plain English:** Bacteria fight each other for resources. One mechanism is the **Type VI Secretion System (T6SS)** — a molecular nano-syringe that injects toxic proteins ("effectors") directly into rival bacterial cells. *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* (a major opportunistic human pathogen) encodes three T6SSs (H1, H2, H3); the H2-T6SS exports a poorly-understood collection of effectors. The authors discover **RhsP2**, a previously uncharacterized H2-T6SS effector, and show it kills target cells by a completely **new biochemical mechanism never described before for ADP-ribosyltransferases (ARTs)**: it transfers ADP-ribose from NAD⁺ onto the **2'-hydroxyl group of double-stranded RNA**, modifying the entire tRNA pool + RNase P (the essential ribozyme that processes tRNA precursors) + 6S RNA + tmRNA + 4.5S RNA + CsrB. Combined, these RNA modifications kill target cells by halting protein translation (modified tRNA can no longer be charged by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases — 91% loss for AlaRS, 62% for SerRS) and disrupting tRNA-precursor processing.
- **ML task type:** **Paper has NO native ML task** — fundamentally a wet-lab biochemistry + structural-biology + molecular-microbiology paper using bacterial competition assays, X-ray crystallography (2.5 Å), Northern blots, anti-ADPr immunoblots, HPLC + ESI-MS/MS, radioisotope metabolic labeling, in vitro aminoacylation kinetics, and Jackhmmer/Clustal Omega/FastTree phylogenetic analysis on 204 RhsP2-tox UniProtKB homologs. Multiple ML reframes are possible (see below); the strongest is **T6SS-effector / ART-substrate-class sequence classification** on the public **SecReT6** database + UniProtKB using protein-language-model embeddings (ESM-2 or ProtBERT) — methodologically identical reframe to the Article 1 ARG classifier (good for a unified portfolio).
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: protein sequences (227 aa RhsP2tox C-terminal toxin domain + 204 Jackhmmer/UniProtKB homologs); 2.5 Å X-ray crystal structure of RhsP2tox·RhsI2 heterodimer (PDB 7RT7); RNA modification readouts (gel shifts, MS/MS, Northern blots); kinetic data (aminoacylation activity, NAD⁺ hydrolysis, in vitro translation rates); *P. aeruginosa* PA14 genome (Lee et al. 2006) for VgrG / effector gene-cluster analysis
  - Shape/size if stated: 227 aa RhsP2tox; 204 BLASTP/Jackhmmer homologs (Table S1); 11 VgrG paralogs in PA14 phylogeny; 1 X-ray crystal structure at 2.5 Å (P3₂21 space group, twin fraction 0.44); 50-base RNA + DNA oligonucleotide modification assays; 13-of-15 dinucleotide-ADPr combinations identified by ESI-MS/MS; 91% / 62% drops in AlaRS / SerRS aminoacylation activity on ADPr-tRNA
  - Preprocessing in the paper: Ni-NTA + on-column denaturation/refolding for toxin-immunity separation + size-exclusion gel filtration; ammonium sulfate precipitation NOT used; sucrose-cushion ribosome isolation; Trizol-based RNA extraction + Monarch RNA cleanup; RNA pull-downs via 5'-biotinylated DNA probes + streptavidin-agarose; nuclease P1 + snake-venom phosphodiesterase I + Antarctic phosphatase digestions for HPLC ribonucleoside analysis; Selenomethionine SAD-phasing for crystal structure (Phenix Autosol + Autobuild + Coot + Phenix.refine); Jackhmmer 3 iterations on UniProtKB; Clustal Omega 1.2.3 alignment + FastTree 2.1.11 phylogeny; ChimeraX electrostatic surface mapping
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: **NO ML model is trained in the paper.** Outputs are biochemical: ART substrate identity (RNA, specifically 2'-OH of dsRNA — first ART of this kind ever described); cellular RNA targets (tRNA pool, RNase P, 6S RNA, tmRNA, 4.5S RNA, CsrB); catalytic mechanism (atypical ART with E1576 invariant glutamate replacing canonical HYE/RSE catalytic glutamate; R1490 + F1513 + Y1524 forming an HYE-like motif modified for RNA recognition; mutagenesis E1576Q, R1490A, Y1524A all abolish toxicity); aminoacylation inhibition (91% AlaRS, 62% SerRS); RNase P substrate-processing inhibition (valU polycistronic tRNA accumulation in rnpA49-equivalent phenotype)
  - Units / label space: ART activity / mechanism class (NADase vs ART vs PARP-like); MIC-equivalent competitive index (log[donor/recipient]); aminoacylation specific activity (pmol/min/µg); X-ray structure quality metrics (Rwork 0.195, Rfree 0.232; Ramachandran 96.63% favored)
- **Model architecture (brief):** **No ML model trained in the paper.** The paper's most ML-adjacent components are (a) **AlphaFold-style structure prediction is NOT used here** (paper predates Chai Discovery; uses traditional X-ray crystallography + SAD phasing via PHENIX), (b) **Jackhmmer iterative profile-HMM search** on UniProtKB (related conceptually to ESM-2 protein-language-model embeddings — both leverage evolutionary conservation, but ESM-2 is the modern parametric replacement). For an ML reframe: **ESM-2 sequence embeddings + linear / MLP classifier** trained on **SecReT6** (T6SS effector public database) + UniProtKB ART homologs is the standard architecture — methodologically identical to Article 1's CARD ARG classifier (which is the key "unified portfolio" angle).
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: experimental data deposited at PDB; most other primary data "shared by lead contact upon request"
  - Size: 1 X-ray crystal structure; 204 BLASTP/Jackhmmer homolog sequences (Table S1); 11 PA14 VgrG protein sequences; aminoacylation + competition + Northern blot datasets are small
  - Source: **PDB 7RT7** (X-ray crystal structure of RhsP2tox·RhsI2 heterodimer); UniProtKB (homolog search); *P. aeruginosa* PA14 genome (NCBI); NCBI for E. coli BW25113 / Keio collection / rnpA49 strains

### Article 3: Targeting bacterial nickel transport with aspergillomarasmine A suppresses virulence-associated Ni-dependent enzymes (Wright-corresponding *Nature Communications* paper; Sychantha **1-OF-5 FIRST AUTHOR who "conceived, performed, and analyzed data for all experiments"** — STRONGEST PI-class signal of his three articles; postdoc CIHR Fellowship + UWaterloo "Present address" transition stage; Sychantha's signature pre-independent-PI paper)

- **Full citation:** **Sychantha, D.**, Chen, X., Koteva, K., Prehna, G., & Wright, G. D. (2024). Targeting bacterial nickel transport with aspergillomarasmine A suppresses virulence-associated Ni-dependent enzymes. *Nature Communications*, 15:4036. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-48232-1. (Received 2 June 2023; accepted 23 April 2024; published online 13 May 2024.) **CC BY 4.0 open access.**
- **Authorship caveat (FUNDAMENTAL UPGRADE FROM A1+A2):** Sychantha is **1st author of 5** on a Wright-corresponding paper. Author contributions: **"D.S. conceived, performed, and analyzed data for all experiments"** + "G.D.W. conceived the project, analyzed data, and directed the work of D.S." — Sychantha is the **lead scientist who designed and executed all experiments**, while Wright supervised + corresponds. **Sychantha is listed with affiliation 5: "Present address: Department of Chemistry, University of Waterloo, Waterloo, ON, Canada"** — confirming this paper is **Sychantha's signature pre-independent-PI paper** at the transition point from McMaster postdoc to UWaterloo assistant professor. Acknowledgments: **"a Canadian Institutes of Health Research Fellowship award (to David Sychantha)"** — his postdoc fellowship. **This is structurally the strongest PI-class signal of his three articles**: A2 (2-of-10 investigation-only) → **A3 (1-OF-5 FIRST AUTHOR conceived/performed/analyzed all)** → A1 (2-of-8 supervision-only). **A3 transforms the PI-signal-class picture from "structurally unconfirmed" (after A1+A2) to "structurally CLEAR DIRECTION + STRONG PEDIGREE"** even though the work itself is still done in Wright's lab at McMaster (not yet from his independent UWaterloo group). **A3 is the kind of postdoc-FIRST-author *Nature Communications* paper that defines what kind of independent research direction Sychantha brings to UWaterloo.**
- **Problem in plain English:** Many pathogenic bacteria (Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, Helicobacter pylori, Proteus mirabilis, Salmonella Typhimurium, etc.) depend on **Ni²⁺-containing enzymes — urease and [NiFe]-hydrogenases — for virulence**: urease hydrolyzes urea to ammonia (causing UTI symptoms, struvite kidney stones, and host-tissue alkalinization), while [NiFe]-hydrogenases enable H₂ metabolism for energy generation under oxidative stress. Bacteria scavenge environmental Ni²⁺ via the **NikABCDE ABC transporter**, with the periplasmic protein NikA binding Ni²⁺ in the form of a Ni-(L-histidine)₂ complex. **The authors repurpose aspergillomarasmine A (AMA)** — a fungal pentadentate metallophore that selectively binds Zn²⁺/Co²⁺/Ni²⁺ — as an **anti-virulence agent**: AMA-Zn²⁺ complexes outcompete Ni-(L-His)₂ for binding to NikA, blocking Ni²⁺ uptake and starving downstream Ni²⁺-dependent virulence enzymes. This avoids the need to inhibit urease or hydrogenase directly (where decades of inhibitor discovery have yielded few clinical leads beyond the 1980 drug acetohydroxamic acid / Lithostat). **Demonstrates in vivo anti-virulence efficacy in *Galleria mellonella* infection model** with K. pneumoniae and S. aureus USA300 (P=0.00008 / P=0.0026 survival improvement at 7.5 mg/kg). Solves the **2.15 Å X-ray structure of NikA·Ni-AMA (PDB 8SPM)** showing how Ni-AMA mimics Ni-(L-His)₂. SAR studies on 4 AMA analogs identify substitutions that improve KD 7-fold but with surprising disconnect from biological activity.
- **ML task type:** **Paper has NO native ML task** — fundamentally a wet-lab biochemistry + structural-biology + drug-discovery paper using ITC, X-ray crystallography (2.15 Å), CETSA, ICP-MS, in vivo *G. mellonella* survival, microtiter biofilm assays, [NiFe]-hydrogenase zymography, and HEK293 cytotoxicity. Multiple ML reframes are possible (see below); **the strongest is structure-activity relationship (SAR) regression on AMA analogs + ChEMBL urease-inhibitor / hydrogenase-inhibitor bioactivity data using RDKit small-molecule descriptors + sklearn regression** — the paper itself contains a 5-analog SAR table (Zn-AMA + 4 analogs with EC₅₀ + KD + ΔG + ΔH + −TΔS values) that can be extended via ChEMBL's ~3,200 known urease inhibitors (per Aniceto 2022 cited in paper).
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: protein sequences (NikA from *K. pneumoniae* + *E. coli*, ~518 aa each; 75% identity / 90.5% similarity); small-molecule structures (AMA + 4 SAR analogs: Zn-AMA(Asn), Zn-AMA(His), Zn-AMB, Zn-Toxin A); 2.15 Å X-ray crystal structure of NikA·Ni-AMA (PDB 8SPM); 4 reference NikA·ligand structures (PDB 4I8C Ni-(L-His)₂ + PDB 1ZLQ Fe-EDTA + PDB 3DP8 Ni-BTC + PDB 1UIU apo); ITC binding affinity panel; whole-cell phenotypic assays (urease activity, struvite crystallization, biofilm formation, [NiFe]-hydrogenase activity, ICP-MS metal content, cellular thermal shift assay); *G. mellonella* in vivo infection survival
  - Shape/size if stated: 1 NikA·Ni-AMA crystal structure at 2.15 Å (P-class space group); ~518 aa NikA × 2 organisms; 5 AMA-analog × Zn²⁺ complex SAR table (Table 1: EC50 0.8-200+ µM, KD 0.8-24 µM, ΔG -6.5 to -8.6 kcal/mol); 6 ITC binding panels (Ni-(L-His)₂, Ni-AMA, Zn-AMA, Co-AMA, Zn-AMA(Asn), Zn-AMA(His), Zn-AMB, Zn-Toxin A); 2 in vivo *G. mellonella* infection models × 3 conditions each
  - Preprocessing in the paper: Strep-Tag-II + N-terminal-tag affinity chromatography for NikA purification; ammonium sulfate + RESOURCE Q anion exchange for E. coli NikA; sparse-matrix crystallization screening with Hampton Research kits; molecular replacement using PDB 4I8C as search model; Phenix.refine + Coot + TLSMD; ITC titrations with detergent (0.1% Triton X-100) to prevent precipitation; Chelex-100 treatment for Ni²⁺-free media; benzyl viologen + tetrazolium chloride zymography for [NiFe]-hydrogenase activity; ICP-MS on HNO₃-digested cell pellets; CETSA with anti-FLAG immunoblotting
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: **NO ML model trained in the paper.** Outputs are biochemical: high-affinity binding of Zn-AMA / Co-AMA / Ni-AMA to NikA (KD 2.2-13 µM); structural basis for AMA-metal complex mimicry of Ni-(L-His)₂ (RMSD 1.16 Å² over 496 residues); EC50 for [NiFe]-hydrogenase inhibition = 50.8 ± 4.4 µM; in vivo *G. mellonella* survival improvement (P=0.00008 K. pneumoniae, P=0.0026 S. aureus USA300); SAR identification of L-Asn and L-His substitutions that improve KD 7-fold; cellular viability of HEK293 unaffected by Zn-AMA at 1.4 mM
  - Units / label space: KD in µM; EC50 in µM; ΔG/ΔH/−TΔS in kcal/mol; survival probability in *G. mellonella* (Log-rank test); MIC fold-change; X-ray structure quality (Rwork 19.5%, Rfree 23.2%; 97% Ramachandran favored)
- **Model architecture (brief):** **No ML model trained in the paper.** For an ML reframe: **(a)** RDKit Morgan/MACCS fingerprints + sklearn random forest / XGBoost / MLP regression on AMA analog SMILES → KD or EC50 (extending the 5-analog table via ChEMBL urease-inhibitor SAR data). **(b)** ESM-2 sequence embeddings + linear classifier on UniProtKB substrate-binding-protein (SBP) families → predict ligand class (metal vs sugar vs amino acid vs peptide). **(c)** AlphaFold2 / Chai Discovery protein-ligand modeling on NikA orthologs (C. jejuni, Y. pestis, H. pylori, S. aureus, E. coli, K. pneumoniae) bound to AMA-metal complexes, validated against PDB 8SPM ground truth — methodologically identical to A1's Chai/AlphaFold reframe.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: experimental data; PDB structure publicly deposited; Source Data files publicly deposited
  - Size: 1 X-ray structure (PDB 8SPM) + 4 reference NikA structures (PDB 4I8C, 1ZLQ, 3DP8, 1UIU) used for structural comparisons; 5-row SAR table; 6+ ITC binding panels; cellular phenotypic readouts; *G. mellonella* infection curves
  - Source: **PDB 8SPM** (X-ray crystal structure of E. coli NikA·Ni-AMA, 2.15 Å); reference NikA structures (PDB 4I8C, 1ZLQ, 3DP8, 1UIU); UniProtKB / NCBI for sequences; *K. pneumoniae* ATCC 33495, *S. aureus* ATCC 23293 + USA300 + USA300 ureC::tn (Tn library mutant); HEK293 (ATCC CRL-1573)
  - Public? **Yes — PDB 8SPM publicly deposited; Source Data files publicly deposited with the paper; CC BY 4.0 open access.** **STRONGEST data deposition discipline of Sychantha's three articles** (vs A1's strong-but-not-CC-BY deposition + A2's request-only most-data deposition).
  - Link: https://www.rcsb.org/structure/8SPM | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-48232-1 (CC BY 4.0 open access + Source Data) | https://www.uniprot.org
- **Reported headline metric:** **Zn-AMA achieves significant in vivo anti-virulence efficacy in *Galleria mellonella* infection model** at 7.5 mg/kg (P=0.00008 vs vehicle for K. pneumoniae; P=0.0026 vs vehicle for S. aureus USA300). **Zn-AMA inhibits [NiFe]-hydrogenase Hyd-3 with EC₅₀ = 50.8 ± 4.4 µM**. **Zn-AMA binds NikA with KD = 6.8 ± 0.4 µM** (vs Ni-(L-His)₂ KD = 0.53 ± 0.02 µM — 14-fold weaker but still strong enough to outcompete in cellular conditions). **2.15 Å X-ray structure of NikA·Ni-AMA (PDB 8SPM)** showing pentadentate Ni-AMA mimicking Ni-(L-His)₂ with His416 occupying the 6th Ni²⁺ coordination site. **SAR optimization** identifies L-AsnAMA and L-HisAMA substitutions yielding KD ~1 µM (7-fold improvement) — but with surprising disconnect from cellular EC50 (suggesting Zn²⁺ affinity, metal selectivity, and cellular accumulation matter).
