Sci.* 9, 1374–1387 (2023). Affiliation discrepancy flagged at intake; assume possible recent move from U Alberta to U Waterloo, or possible namesake confusion. Awaiting Scholar / lab-webpage URL.

**Lab focus (one sentence):** Native mass spectrometry methodology — specifically Concentration-Independent (COIN) and Catch-and-Release (CaR) variants, with Ion Mobility Separation (IMS) — for quantitative measurement of weak carbohydrate–protein binding affinities, including glycan–lectin and glycolipid–Siglec interactions in solution and in lipid nanodiscs.

**Lab webpage / Scholar:** not provided

#### Article 1: Glycolipid recognition and binding by Siglec-6 hinges on interactions with the cell membrane

- **Full citation:** D'Andrea S., Schmidt E.N., **Bui D.**, Singh O., Han L., Mahal L.K., Klassen J.S., Macauley M.S., Fadda E. *Communications Biology* (Nature Portfolio) **9**:333 (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s42003-026-09609-8. Bui is **3rd of 9 authors (middle author)**; corresponding author is **Elisa Fadda (School of Biological Sciences, University of Southampton, UK)**. Author-contribution block places Bui in Methodology + Investigation + Visualisation + Writing-of-original-draft.

- **Problem in plain English:** Human Siglecs (sialic-acid-binding immunoglobulin-type lectins) regulate immune response by recognising sialylated glycans on glycoproteins and glycolipids. Almost all 14 human Siglecs depend on a conserved "canonical" Arg in the V-set Ig domain to bind the sialic-acid carboxylate — but Siglec-6 (and MAG, Siglec-11) bind membrane-embedded monosialylated gangliosides even when that Arg is mutated, implying an alternative recognition mechanism. The paper asks: how does Siglec-6 distinguish GM1 (which it binds) from GM2/GM3 (which it does not) when the ganglioside is embedded in a phospholipid bilayer, and what residues other than the canonical Arg122 mediate that recognition?

- **ML task type:** **Not an ML paper.** The only ML component is AlphaFold (AF-O43699-F1) used as a one-off structure-prediction black box for the Siglec-6 V-set Ig domain (validated by structural alignment to PDB 7AW6 CD33 with backbone RMSD 0.704 Å). No model is trained, no benchmark is reported. **Inspired-by ML reframe (my suggestion, not the paper's):** supervised regression of glycan-Siglec binding affinity (Kd) from glycan structure + Siglec sequence — multi-target regression on this paper's nMS Kd dataset, augmented with binary classification on CFG / UniLectin glycan-array data for the Siglec family.

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** 3D molecular structures (AlphaFold-predicted protein + glycolipid 3D coords) + all-atom MD trajectories of Siglec-6 / GM1 and Siglec-6 / GM2 complexes embedded in a DSPC + cholesterol bilayer + native-MS (nMS) binding-affinity measurements + flow-cytometry liposome-binding cell assays.
  - **Shape / size if stated:** Siglec-6 sequence = 453 aa (extracellular V-set + multiple C2-set Ig domains; 7 N-glycosylation sequons, one in V-set at N103); GM1 ganglioside ≈ 1.5 kDa; symmetric 130 Å × 130 Å lipid bilayer (60% 1,2-distearoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine / 40% cholesterol). MD wall-clock: 2.4 μs single trajectory on non-glycosylated Siglec-6 / GM1; 1.1 + 1.0 μs uncorrelated replicas on N-glycosylated Siglec-6 / GM1; 1.0 + 0.5 μs replicas on Siglec-6 / GM2 control; 1.0 μs each on isolated GM1 and GM3 in the bilayer. Native-MS dataset ≈ 27 Kd measurements (Siglec-6 WT/R122A/W127A × GM1os/GM2os/GM3os, n = 3–7 replicates each).
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** CHARMM-GUI Membrane Builder for bilayer setup; CHARMM36m force field for gangliosides + lipids; AMBER18 (then AMBER22) for MD with 5000-step energy minimisation + six-step CHARMM-GUI equilibration; Langevin thermostat at 315.15 K; Berendsen semi-isotropic barostat at 1 atm; PME electrostatics with 11 Å cutoff; SHAKE; 2 fs timestep. Distance restraint (5 kcal/mol·Å²) on Arg122–Neu5Ac salt bridge for first 400 ns of GM1 production. AlphaFold predictions taken directly from EBI-EMBL AF DB (no in-house re-training).

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** AlphaFold outputs the 3D Siglec-6 structure with per-residue pLDDT (69% of residues > 90; 26% > 70). The MD itself does not "predict" anything supervised — it generates trajectories that the authors analyse for salt-bridge occupancy, residue insertion depth, and tilt angles.
  - **Units / label space:** Å (RMSD, distances); kcal/mol (force-field energies); μs (trajectory length); ° (tilt angle of Neu5Ac relative to bilayer plane); mM (dissociation constant Kd from nMS); % (residue insertion depth into bilayer, salt-bridge occupancy).

- **Model architecture (brief):** AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., *Nature* 2021) as the only ML component, used for structure prediction of Siglec-6 only. The rest is AMBER + CHARMM36m all-atom classical MD — not a learned model.

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** In-house MD trajectories + in-house native-MS Kd dataset + in-house cell-based liposome / nanodisc binding assays (CHO Flp-In stable transfectants).
  - **Size:** ~7 μs of total MD trajectory across systems; ~27 nMS Kd measurements; 8 cell-assay variants (WT + R122A + K126A + W127A + K129A + K126A·W127A + R122A·K129A + untransfected control).
  - **Source:** Maynooth University (Fadda group, original lab pre-Southampton move) + University of Alberta (Klassen + Macauley + Mahal groups) + Southampton.
  - **Public?** **Yes — fully open across multiple repositories.**
  - **Link:**
    - MD trajectories: <https://glycoshape.org/downloads/Siglec-6> + <https://zenodo.org/records/17312619>
    - MD statistical-analysis data: <https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17877366>
    - Raw native-MS data: MassIVE accession **MSV000100484** at <https://doi.org/10.25345/C5028PS8P>
    - Per-experiment numeric data points: Supplementary Data in the paper.

- **Reported headline metrics:**
  - Arg122–Neu5Ac salt bridge occupied **68.5 %** of the 2.4-μs trajectory (i.e. interruptions for ~31.5 % of time without complex dissociation).
  - W127A mutant abolishes liposome binding (≈ 5 % of WT signal in flow cytometry); R122A retains ≈ 75 % of WT binding when GM1 is membrane-embedded.
  - Trp127 sidechain inserts below bilayer surface in 90.7 % (non-glycosylated) / 84.1 % (N-glycosylated) of frames; Lys126 in 80.9 % / 58.7 %; Tyr61 in 35.0 % / 44.0 %.
  - Free-oligosaccharide nMS Kd: Siglec-6 WT × GM1os ≈ 0.12 mM, GM2os ≈ 0.07 mM, GM3os ≈ 0.10 mM (all similarly low); R122A mutant Kd's ≈ 4–5 mM (≈ 40× weaker — binding to free sialosides is Arg122-dependent).
  - AlphaFold model AF-O43699-F1 vs CD33 crystal PDB 7AW6: backbone RMSD = **0.704 Å** (60% sequence identity).

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **GlycoShape Siglec-6 entry + Zenodo 17312619** — *close* match (these ARE the paper's MD outputs); size: multi-GB AMBER trajectories; access: *easy* (direct URL) but needs MDAnalysis / VMD to parse — not pandas-ready. Link: <https://glycoshape.org/downloads/Siglec-6>.
  - **MassIVE MSV000100484** — *close* match (the paper's own nMS data); access: *medium* — MassIVE account + raw files are in Thermo `.raw` / Waters MassLynx proprietary formats requiring conversion via ProteoWizard `msconvert` to mzML before pyteomics / pymzml can read them. Link: <https://doi.org/10.25345/C5028PS8P>.
  - **Consortium for Functional Glycomics (CFG) glycan-array data + UniLectin** — *loose* match (different assay format: printed-glycan microarray fluorescence rather than membrane-bound Kd; but same Siglec family + many overlapping glycans); size: tens of thousands of lectin-glycan pairs; access: *medium* (UniLectin at <https://unilectin.unige.ch/> is the more reliable mirror; CFG itself has had availability churn).
  - **AlphaFold DB (AF-O43699-F1 Siglec-6) + RCSB PDB (1OD9 sialoadhesin, 2ZG3 MAG, 7AW6 CD33)** — *close* match for the structural-prediction baseline used in the paper; size: small (single-structure files); access: *easy* (direct download).

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **medium** — MD trajectories are direct-download but multi-GB and require parsing libraries; native-MS raw files are in proprietary instrument formats requiring `msconvert` to mzML; combining the three Zenodo deposits + MassIVE into a single training table requires non-trivial scripting.

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - **RDKit** — SMILES parsing, molecular fingerprints (Morgan / ECFP), 2D/3D conformer generation.
  - **DeepChem or PyTorch Geometric** — graph neural networks over molecular graphs (GIN, GCN, GAT).
  - **Glycan-specific notation** — SNFG (Symbol Nomenclature for Glycans) + WURCS / GlycoCT serialisations. This is the field's native representation layer and is the most idiosyncratic piece of tooling to learn; conversion utilities exist in `glycowork` (Python library) and at <https://glytoucan.org/>.
  - **ESM-2** (Meta / Facebook) for Siglec protein-sequence embeddings if you want a learned protein representation rather than one-hot Siglec ID.
  - Optional: **MDAnalysis** (if you want to compute features directly from the MD trajectories); **pyteomics / pymzml** (if you want to use the raw native-MS data); **CHARMM-GUI** / **OpenMM** (if you want to run additional MD).

- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** Train a glycan-graph regressor that predicts Siglec × glycan binding affinity from glycan structure + Siglec identity. Anchor the high-quality regression labels on this paper's nMS Kd dataset (~27 datapoints across Siglec-6 × GM1os/GM2os/GM3os × WT/R122A/W127A) and augment with CFG / UniLectin Siglec-family glycan-array data (~tens of thousands of lower-precision binary or relative-intensity binding calls) to handle the small-N problem. Baseline: Morgan-fingerprint glycan features + XGBoost regression. Target model: GIN or GCN over molecular graphs (DeepChem or PyTorch Geometric), with Siglec identity either one-hot-encoded over the 14 human Siglecs or sequence-embedded via ESM-2. **Key evaluation:** hold out Siglec-6 × GM2 / GM3 entirely and ask whether the model recovers the "GM1 selectivity" effect that this paper explains mechanistically — a successful model would predict tight binding for Siglec-6 / GM1 and weak binding for Siglec-6 / GM2 + GM3, *learnt purely from public glycan-array data without seeing the nMS Kd's*. Repo deliverables: data-prep notebook (CFG / UniLectin parsing + SNFG → SMILES conversion via glycowork) + featurisation notebook (RDKit fingerprints + DeepChem graphs) + training notebook (XGBoost vs GIN baselines) + held-out evaluation notebook (Siglec-6 × GM-family prediction comparison vs paper's Kd table) + README with figures. **README headline:** "A glycan-graph regressor that recovers Siglec-6's GM1 preference from public glycan-array data."

- **Ranking for this professor (Article 1):**

| Variable | Score (1–10) | One-line justification |
|---|---|---|
| Data availability | 7 | The paper's own data is fully open across 3 × Zenodo deposits + MassIVE; CFG / UniLectin glycan-array data exists as a loose-but-large public corpus for the same Siglec family. |
| Data access ease | 5 | GlycoShape + Zenodo URLs are direct but MD is multi-GB and needs MDAnalysis; native-MS is in proprietary Thermo / Waters formats needing `msconvert`; CFG / UniLectin needs scripting to combine — no single pandas-ready download covers the whole project. |
| Task tractability on laptop / free GPU | 7 | Fingerprint + XGBoost is trivial on CPU; GIN / GCN over glycans fits comfortably on free Colab GPU; the labelled regression set is small enough (~27 nMS Kd's + thousands of array binding calls) that training is cheap. |

#### Article 2: Absolute Affinities from Quantitative Shotgun Glycomics Using Concentration-Independent (COIN) Native Mass Spectrometry

- **Full citation:** **Bui D.T.**, Favell J., Kitova E.N., Li Z., McCord K.A., Schmidt E.N., Mozaneh F., Elaish M., El-Hawiet A., St-Pierre Y., Hobman T.C., Macauley M.S., Mahal L.K., Flynn M.R., Klassen J.S. *ACS Central Science* **9**, 1374–1387 (2023). DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.3c00294. **Bui is 1-OF-15 FIRST AUTHOR**; corresponding author is **John S. Klassen (sole corresponding, Department of Chemistry, University of Alberta)**. Open access (ACS Author Choice). **This article is Bui's signature paper — the COIN-nMS / COIN-CaR-nMS methodology she first-authored, which Article 1 (*Communications Biology* 2026) applies and explicitly cites as ref. 26.**

- **Problem in plain English:** Native mass spectrometry (nMS) is a powerful screening tool for discovering which glycans bind which glycan-binding proteins (lectins / GBPs), but it has a critical limitation: glycan concentrations in **natural glycan libraries** (extracted from tissues / cells / biofluids by enzymatic digestion of glycoproteins) are unknown, so absolute binding affinities (Kd) cannot be measured directly. Existing approaches use glycan microarrays (qualitative; surface-immobilisation artifacts; false negatives for weak binders during washing) or fluorophore-labelled glycan libraries (non-uniform recovery + non-uniform release efficiencies bias affinity rankings). The paper asks: *can absolute Kd's be measured for hundreds of glycan-lectin pairs from natural libraries at unknown concentrations?*

- **ML task type:** **Not an ML paper** — pure mass-spectrometry methodology development + analytical modelling (advection-diffusion equation for analyte mixing inside the nanoESI emitter). **Inspired-by ML reframe (my suggestion, not the paper's):** multi-target regression of glycan × lectin → Kd, anchored on this paper's Tables S2-S19 (~250+ glycan-lectin Kd pairs across 9 lectins) and benchmarked against the existing **Mahal-group 2022 ML-on-lectin paper** (Bojar D., Meche L., Meng G., Eng W., Smith D.F., Cummings R.D., Mahal L.K., *ACS Chem. Biol.* **17**, 2993–3012, 2022 — cited as ref. 38 of this paper — "A Useful Guide to Lectin Binding: Machine-Learning Directed Annotation of 57 Unique Lectin Specificities").

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** time-resolved native-MS spectra (Orbitrap m/z + abundance, sub-minute time resolution) of GBP and GBP-glycan complexes during slow diffusion-driven mixing inside a nanoESI emitter loaded with 2 layered solutions. For the ML reframe: glycan structures (SNFG drawings in Tables S1-S19 → SMILES / GlycoCT / WURCS) + lectin identity (UniProt sequence or one-hot among 9 lectins).
  - **Shape / size if stated:** 9 lectins (plant: SNA + MAA + RCAI + PHA-E; fungal: AAL; human: Gal-3C + Gal-7 + fCD22 / CD22-Fc / Sig7-Fc; viral: SARS-CoV-2 RBD); N-glycan library = **115 unique molecular weights**; glycopeptide library = **395 molecular weights**; purified glycan set = G1-G34 (34 structurally defined oligosaccharides). Aggregate **~250+ Kd measurements** reported across Tables S2-S19. nanoESI emitter dimensions: L = 2.8 cm tip length, l/L = 0.8-0.85 optimal volume ratio of Solution 2 to total (~2-8 μL volumes), mixing window 0-200 min.
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** N-glycans released from glycoproteins (bovine fetuin + bovine asialo-fetuin + lactoferrin + bovine α1-acid glycoprotein + SARS-CoV-2 RBD) via PNGase F digestion; glycopeptides via pronase digestion; selective α2-3-linked sialic acid cleavage via neuraminidase S (NeuS) for isomer disambiguation; glycan / glycopeptide annotation via HILIC-UHPLC + fluorescence + ESI-MS. All measurements in 200 mM aqueous ammonium acetate (pH 6.8-7.4) at 25 °C; DC-SIGN measurements include 2.5 mM Ca(CH3COO)2.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What is measured:** dissociation constant Kd (μM or mM) for each detected GBP-glycan interaction, extracted by fitting the time-dependent fractional binding occupancy Ft(t) to eq. 12 (COIN-nMS, intact-complex detection) or eq. 13 (COIN-CaR-nMS, ligand-release detection) with the linearised glycan concentration flux C_L · t.
  - **Units / label space:** Kd in μM (or mM for weak binders); abundance ratio R = Ab(PL) / Ab(P) (dimensionless); concentration rate C_L in μM/min; time t in minutes (typical fitting range 0-60 min); fractional binding Ft ∈ [0, 1].

- **Model architecture (brief):** **No learned model.** Closed-form fit of eq. 12 / eq. 13 to time-resolved nMS abundance ratios via nonlinear least-squares regression. Mathematical model = analytical solution of the advection-diffusion equation in the small-Péclet-number limit for a cylindrical nanoESI emitter (full derivation in SI File 2, Theoretical Modeling).

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** in-house COIN-nMS / COIN-CaR-nMS measurements + in-house natural N-glycan + glycopeptide libraries from PNGase F / pronase digestion of commercial glycoproteins (BF + LF + bAGP + RBD).
  - **Size:** **~250+ Kd measurements** across 9 lectins × ~150 unique N-glycan / glycopeptide structures (each from multiple titrations + replicates). N-glycan library = 115 unique MWs (with isomers, ~200 structures); glycopeptide library = 395 MWs.
  - **Source:** Klassen + Macauley + Mahal + Flynn + Hobman + St-Pierre + Cairo collaboration based at University of Alberta + INRS (Laval) + Alexandria University + Cairo University + University of Georgia (RBD gift from Stephen M. Tompkins). Lectins from commercial suppliers (Sigma + Vector Labs + MJS BioLynx + LEE Biosolutions + NIST) + recombinant expression in CHO cells.
  - **Public?** **Partial — Kd tables released as free SI PDF; raw nMS instrument data NOT deposited in a public repository** (unlike Article 1 which has MassIVE MSV000100484 + 3 × Zenodo deposits + GlycoShape). Article 2 has only SI tables.
  - **Link:** Supplementary Information PDFs at <https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acscentsci.3c00294> (free download; Tables S1-S19 with Kd values + SNFG glycan structures + SI File 2 mathematical model derivation). No Zenodo / MassIVE / GitHub for raw MS data.

- **Reported headline metrics:**
  - COIN-nMS Kd's agree within **factor of 2** with direct nMS values (at known concentration) and ITC reference values across validation set (Gal-3C, Gal-7, fCD22, DC-SIGN CRD, SNA, MAA, GNA).
  - **9 lectins screened**: SNA top N-glycan Kd = 0.1-0.4 μM (monosialylated hybrid + biantennary, α2-6 on α3 branch); MAA top Kd = 0.4-1.8 μM (mono- + disialylated bi- + triantennary); AAL top Kd = 0.3-0.7 μM (monosialylated bi- + triantennary); RCA-I top Kd ≥ 0.3 μM (tri- + tetraantennary); PHA-E Kd = 10-40 μM (bisected + biantennary); CD22-Fc Kd ≈ 25 μM (α2-6-disialylated bi- + triantennary); Sig7-Fc Kd = 0.1-0.4 mM (mono- + disialylated biantennary); **SARS-CoV-2 RBD Kd = 50-75 μM (monosialylated hybrid + biantennary)**.
  - **SARS-CoV-2 finding**: kifunensine treatment (blocks complex N-glycan maturation) **decreases SARS-CoV-2 pseudoviral + authentic viral infection** of ACE2+ HEK293 cells concentration-dependently — establishes complex N-glycans as viral attachment factors. Contradicts Lebrilla 2022 (ref. 63) claim that oligomannose N-glycans drive RBD adherence.
  - Method sensitivity: minimum detectable glycan concentration ≈ 50-500 nM (dynamic range of COIN-CaR-nMS).

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**

Link: <https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acscentsci.3c00294>.
  - **Bojar et al., *ACS Chem. Biol.* 2022 (ref. 38 of this paper) — "A Useful Guide to Lectin Binding: Machine-Learning Directed Annotation of 57 Unique Lectin Specificities"** — *close* match for the ML baseline; this is a **published ML benchmark** on lectin-glycan binding from the **Mahal group** (co-author of both Bui A1 and Bui A2); training dataset is CFG glycan-array data for 57 lectins; access: *medium* — paper + code via the **`glycowork`** Python library that Mahal's group maintains: <https://github.com/BojarLab/glycowork>. This is the **most directly aligned public ML resource** for the portfolio angle.
  - **Consortium for Functional Glycomics (CFG) glycan-array data + UniLectin (unilectin.unige.ch)** — *loose-to-close* match (surface-array binding rather than nMS Kd, but same lectin family + many overlapping glycans + same data used by Bojar et al. 2022); access: *medium* — `glycowork` provides loaders.
  - **UniProt / RCSB PDB for the 9 lectin sequences + structures** (SNA / MAA / RCAI / PHA-E / AAL / Gal-3 / Gal-7 / CD22 / Siglec-7 / SARS-CoV-2 RBD) — access: *easy* — useful as lectin-side featurisation input for ESM-2 protein embeddings.

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **medium-to-hard** — the structured Kd dataset exists but only in SI PDF tables with SNFG-drawn glycan structures. Transcribing to machine-readable form (CSV / Parquet with glycan SMILES + lectin UniProt + Kd-μM) is a real engineering task: would need (1) OCR or manual table digitisation via `pdfplumber` / `tabula-py`, (2) SNFG → GlycoCT → SMILES conversion via `glycowork`, (3) cross-referencing against G1-G34 purified-glycan identity table. **No raw nMS data in a public repository** (unlike Article 1 which has MassIVE MSV000100484). The Bojar 2022 + `glycowork` ecosystem partially compensates by providing a parallel ML-ready dataset on the same lectin family.

  - **`pdfplumber` / `tabula-py`** — to digitise the SI PDF tables (Tables S2-S19) into pandas DataFrames.

- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** Anchor the **glycan-graph Kd regressor** project (carried over from Article 1) on **Article 2's ~250-Kd dataset** as the primary regression labels, with the Mahal-group `glycowork` library as the SNFG-handling toolchain and Bojar et al. 2022 as the published baseline. **Data-prep notebook**: (1) digitise Tables S2-S19 from the SI PDF via `pdfplumber` + manual verification into a unified `(glycan-SMILES, lectin-UniProt, Kd-μM, source-table)` schema, (2) convert SNFG glycan IDs to SMILES via `glycowork`, (3) cross-link to G1-G34 purified-glycan reference table for identity confirmation, (4) optionally fold in CFG glycan-array binary binding calls for the same 9 lectins as additional weak labels. **Modelling notebook**: baseline = Morgan-fingerprint glycan + lectin-one-hot + XGBoost regression; target = GIN over glycan molecular graphs + ESM-2 lectin embedding + Siamese / cross-attention fusion → log(Kd) regression. **Evaluation notebook**: held-out *lectin-stratified* split (train on 7 lectins, test on 2 — including SARS-CoV-2 RBD and Siglec-7 as the "hard" out-of-distribution lectins); compare against Bojar et al. 2022's binary-classification baseline. **Repo deliverables**: `data/` (digitised Kd CSV + glycan-SMILES table) + `notebooks/01_digitize_tables.ipynb` + `02_featurise.ipynb` + `03_train_baseline_xgb.ipynb` + `04_train_gin.ipynb` + `05_held_out_eval.ipynb` + README. **README headline:** "Predicting glycan-lectin binding affinity from a Bui-Klassen native-MS Kd dataset — XGBoost baseline + GIN graph neural net, benchmarked against Bojar 2022."

#### Article 3: Quantifying Biomolecular Interactions Using Slow Mixing Mode (SLOMO) Nanoflow ESI-MS

- **Full citation:** **Bui D.T.**, Li Z., Kitov P.I., Han L., Kitova E.N., Fortier M., Fuselier C., Granger Joly de Boissel P., Chatenet D., Doucet N., Tompkins S.M., St-Pierre Y., Mahal L.K., Klassen J.S. *ACS Central Science* **8**, 963–974 (2022). DOI: 10.1021/acscentsci.2c00215. **Bui is 1-OF-14 FIRST AUTHOR**; corresponding author is **John S. Klassen (sole corresponding, Department of Chemistry, University of Alberta)**. Open access. **This article introduces SLOMO — the foundational methodology that Article 2 (COIN-nMS, *ACS Cent. Sci.* 2023) extends to natural glycan libraries**. Article 2 explicitly cites Article 3 as ref. 23 and says COIN-nMS was "inspired by the recently developed Slow Mixing Mode nanoflow ESI (nanoESI)-MS (SLOMO) technique." **Two consecutive Bui-FIRST-AUTHORED *ACS Central Science* methodology papers (2022 + 2023) form a coherent native-MS methodology family.**

- **Problem in plain English:** Native mass spectrometry (ESI-MS) is a powerful label- and immobilisation-free method for measuring biomolecular binding affinities (Kd), but it carries a critical hidden assumption: that the relative ion signals of free protein P and ligand-bound complex PL reflect their relative solution concentrations. This is true only if P and PL have similar ESI response factors (RFs). For most protein–protein and protein–glycoprotein complexes — and essentially all multi-protein and protein-in-membrane complexes — RFs differ significantly, biasing the measured Kd by an unknown factor that can reach ~100×. Existing RF-correction strategies (Gabelica's internal-standard linear-equations, Gross's differential-equation models, Zenobi's global-fitting titrations) all require pump-driven ESI sources with prohibitively large sample amounts — incompatible with the static nanoESI emitters that real biomolecular interaction studies use. The paper asks: *can RF and Kd both be extracted from a single static-nanoESI measurement, so accurate affinities can be obtained for protein–protein, protein–glycoprotein, and lectin–glycolipid-in-membrane systems with the small sample amounts native-MS practitioners are constrained to?*

- **ML task type:** **Not an ML paper** — pure mass-spectrometry methodology + mass-balance / abundance-ratio mathematical derivation. **Inspired-by ML reframe (carrying forward from Article 2):** the Article 3 dataset of 6 validation-quality biomolecular systems — including the **68-glycoform-resolved GAL-3C × SARS-CoV-2 RBD binding-preference table (Table S2)** — serves as a high-confidence held-out evaluation set for the glycan-graph Kd regressor trained on Article 2's ~250-Kd dataset.

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** time-resolved Orbitrap native-MS spectra of biomolecular complexes during slow diffusion-driven mixing inside a static nanoESI emitter loaded with 2 layered solutions (or pH-perturbed solutions for protein homodimers). For the ML reframe: same protein + ligand structure inputs as Articles 1 + 2.
  - **Shape / size if stated:** **6 validation systems**: (1) Van (1448.4 Da) + AcAA dipeptide (202.2 Da); (2) PT trypsin (23.46 kDa) + STI inhibitor (19.99 kDa); (3) BLG monomer (18.3 kDa) ⇌ dimer (36.6 kDa) via pH 6.9 → 10.6 perturbation; (4) GAL-7 galectin (14.94 kDa monomer) + sdAb single-domain antibody / nanobody (19.86 kDa) + tetrasaccharide LNT (707.6 Da) — **multi-equilibrium**; (5) GAL-3C (16.3 kDa) + SARS-CoV-2 RBD (~32 kDa) with **68 distinct N-glycoform MWs resolved**, 36 detected in the complex; (6) CBM (20.74 kDa, family 51 GH98 from *Streptococcus pneumoniae*) + B-triNGL blood-group-B trisaccharide neoglycolipid (1112.5 Da) presented inside a **DMPC nanodisc model membrane** (~120 kDa, ~10% B-triNGL); plus 4 additional specificity-control galectins (GAL-1 + GAL-3 + GAL-13 in addition to GAL-7) tested against sdAb. Concentration ranges: protein 2-9 μM, ligand 0.5-500 μM. Mixing window: 10-250 min.
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** all solutions in 200 mM aqueous ammonium acetate at 25 °C (pH 6.9 default; pH 4.5 for PT-STI; pH 7.4 for RBD + sdAb; pH 10.6 for BLG dimer-dissociation Solution 2); static nanoESI from pulled borosilicate glass capillaries (Sutter P-1000 puller); 1-min time-resolved averaging via **CUPRA-SWARM software** (Kitov et al., *J. Am. Soc. Mass Spectrom.* **30**, 1446-1454, 2019; <https://github.com/pkitov/CUPRA-SWARM>); for the glycoform-resolved RBD analysis, signal areas were obtained via Gaussian-function multipeak fitting in IgorPro + SWARM. **Mass-balance condition for RF extraction**: eq 4 ([P]_t1 - [P]_t2 = [PL]_t2 - [PL]_t1) + eqs 5-7 for ΔAb-ratio-based RF; eq 9 for corrected R = RF_P/PL × R_app; eqs 10-11 for heterocomplex Kd; eqs 13-17 for homocomplex Kd.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What is measured:** dissociation constant Kd (μM) AND relative response factor RF_P/PL (dimensionless) for each biomolecular interaction — BOTH extracted from a single time-resolved nanoESI experiment.
  - **Units / label space:** Kd in μM; RF_P/PL dimensionless (ranges from ~0.4 for similar-MW protein dimers up to ~55 for protein–nanodisc complexes); ΔAb in absolute abundance counts; time t in minutes (typical mixing window 10-250 min).

- **Model architecture (brief):** **No learned model.** Closed-form mass-balance derivation: RF_P/PL = ΔAb(P)/ΔAb(PL) (eqs 5b, 7); R = RF_P/PL × R_app (eq 9); Kd from eqs 10-11 (heterocomplex) or eqs 13, 17 (homocomplex). All fits via nonlinear least-squares regression in IgorPro + CUPRA-SWARM.

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** in-house SLOMO measurements + ITC validation measurements + commercial proteins / glycoproteins / lipids.
  - **Size:** **6 biomolecular systems** with ~50-100 Kd / RF measurements total (replicates + concentration titrations); + 4 specificity-control galectin × sdAb pairs; + ITC validation Kd for Van-AcAA reference (50 ± 14 μM in 200 mM NH4OAc).
  - **Source:** Klassen + Mahal + St-Pierre + Doucet + Tompkins collaboration based at University of Alberta + INRS (Laval) + University of Georgia (RBD plasmid gift from F. Krammer / Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, produced at UGA under NIAID CEIRS contract). Lectins from commercial suppliers (Sigma + Avanti Polar Lipids) + recombinant expression in *E. coli* (CBM, MSP1E1) + HEK293 (RBD).
  - **Public?** **Partial — Kd tables released as free SI PDF; CUPRA-SWARM software open-source on GitHub** (<https://github.com/pkitov/CUPRA-SWARM>); raw nMS instrument data NOT deposited in a public repository.
  - **Link:** SI PDFs at <https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acscentsci.2c00215> (free download; Tables S1-S5 with Kd's + ITC validation data + Table S2 with **68 N-glycoform compositions of free and GAL-3C-bound SARS-CoV-2 RBD**). **CUPRA-SWARM Python tool on GitHub**: <https://github.com/pkitov/CUPRA-SWARM> (Kitov co-author of A2 + A3).

- **Reported headline metrics:**
  - **Apparent vs RF-corrected Kd's**: Van-AcAA Kd_app = 378 ± 36 μM → corrected Kd = 32 ± 1 μM (reported 63 ± 13 μM); PT-STI Kd_app = 27.1 ± 8.4 μM → corrected Kd = 0.8 ± 0.2 μM (reported 0.67 μM); BLG Kd_app = 1.9 ± 0.8 μM → corrected Kd = 3.0 ± 0.5 μM (reported 7.0 μM); GAL-7 homodimer Kd_corrected = 3.1 ± 0.7 μM (reported 1.7 μM); GAL-7 × sdAb Kd_corrected = 3.0 ± 0.1 μM; GAL-3C × SARS-CoV-2 RBD Kd_app = 14.5 ± 0.8 μM → corrected Kd = 5.2 ± 0.4 μM; CBM × B-triNGL-in-nanodisc Kd_app = 1.2 ± 0.2 mM → corrected Kd = 28.1 ± 3.0 μM (reported 20.2 ± 2 μM via competitive assay). **All corrected SLOMO Kd's agree with literature values within factor of 2.**
  - **RF_P/PL range**: 0.4 to 55 across the 6 systems — confirming non-uniform response factors are a major hidden bias in conventional native-MS Kd measurements.
  - **Instrument-parameter robustness**: changing instrumental settings on PT-STI led to a **140× shift in Kd_app**, but RF-corrected SLOMO Kd's were stable across instrument settings.
  - **Glycoform resolution on SARS-CoV-2 RBD**: 68 distinct N-glycoform MWs identified, **36 detected in the GAL-3C–RBD complex**; preferential binding to larger LacNAc-containing N-glycans (consistent with prior glycan-array data).
  - **CBM-nanodisc**: RF_P/PL = 26-55 means the CBM × B-triNGL bound complex is detected with only **2-4% the efficiency of free CBM** — explains why conventional native-MS catastrophically underestimates protein × glycolipid-in-membrane affinities.

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **Article 3's own SI tables (Tables S1-S5)** — *close* match for the 6 biomolecular systems' Kd + RF dataset; access: *medium* — free PDF download, smaller scope than Article 2 but the **GAL-3C × SARS-CoV-2 RBD 68-glycoform table (Table S2)** is uniquely detailed.
  - **CUPRA-SWARM Python tool on GitHub** (<https://github.com/pkitov/CUPRA-SWARM>) — *close* match for the software toolchain; access: *easy* (open-source Python). **The only directly-linked open-source code repository across Bui's three papers**; cited Kitov et al., *J. Am. Soc. Mass Spectrom.* **30**, 1446-1454 (2019).
  - **RCSB PDB structures for the 6 systems' protein components** (STI: 1AVU; BLG: 1B0O; GAL-7: 4GAL; GAL-3C: 1A3K; CBM family 51: 4P3T; SARS-CoV-2 RBD: 6M0J) — *easy* access; useful as protein-side ESM-2 / AlphaFold featurisation.
  - **Bojar et al. 2022 + `glycowork`** (carried over from Article 2 — same Mahal-group ML-on-lectin baseline applies to the GAL-3C × RBD and CBM × B-triNGL portions).

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **medium** — SI PDF tables are direct download, but the 6 validation systems are heterogeneous (peptide-antibiotic + protein-protein + protein homodimer + protein-glycoprotein with 68 glycoforms + protein-glycolipid-in-nanodisc) and each would need to be transcribed into a unified schema. **CUPRA-SWARM on GitHub is the genuine open-source code anchor** — best of the three Bui papers on this criterion.

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - **CUPRA-SWARM** (Pavel Kitov's Python package) — sliding-window adduct removal + abundance extraction for native-MS ion signals; useful for any of the three Bui articles' raw-spectra processing. <https://github.com/pkitov/CUPRA-SWARM>.

#### Summary for this professor

- **Common thread across her work:** Bui's research signature is **native mass spectrometry methodology for measuring weak biomolecular binding affinities** — specifically a **lineage of three closely-linked nanoESI-MS techniques** developed sequentially in the Klassen lab:
  - **Article 3 (2022, SLOMO)** — foundational slow-mixing-mode technique that simultaneously extracts relative response factor (RF) AND Kd from a single static-nanoESI measurement via mass-balance of ΔAb ratios; addresses the bias from non-uniform RF in conventional native-MS Kd measurements. **Bui FIRST author.**
  - **Article 2 (2023, COIN-nMS)** — extension of SLOMO to natural glycan libraries with unknown ligand concentrations; introduces an advection-diffusion analytical model of the slow-mixing emitter; applied to 9 lectins × ~250 glycan-Kd pairs. **Article 2 explicitly cites Article 3 as ref. 23 and says COIN-nMS was "inspired by" SLOMO.** **Bui FIRST author.**
  - **Article 1 (2026, *Communications Biology*)** — application of the COIN-CaR-nMS + IMS-CaR-nMS variants from Article 2 to the Siglec-6 / monosialylated ganglioside system; **Article 1 cites Article 2 as ref. 26**. Bui middle author (3-of-9, under Fadda from Southampton).
- **Authorship trajectory across the 3 articles**: A3 (2022, *ACS Central Science*, **FIRST author** — foundational SLOMO methodology, Klassen lab Edmonton) → A2 (2023, *ACS Central Science*, **FIRST author** — extension to COIN-nMS for natural glycan libraries, Klassen lab Edmonton) → A1 (2026, *Communications Biology*, middle-author — Siglec-6 application, Fadda + Klassen co-collaboration). **TWO consecutive Bui-FIRST-AUTHORED *ACS Central Science* methodology papers (2022 + 2023) is the strongest non-corresponding-author PI-class signal in this survey** — Bui is the developer of a coherent native-MS methodology family, not a one-off methods paper.
- **Dominant data modality:** time-resolved native-MS spectra of biomolecular complexes (Orbitrap m/z + abundance) → fitted Kd + RF values via mass-balance / advection-diffusion modelling of static nanoESI emitters; supporting modalities = AlphaFold-predicted protein structures + all-atom MD trajectories on phospholipid bilayers (Article 1) + ITC validation + nanodisc model membranes + glycan structure annotation via HILIC-UHPLC.
- **Biggest obstacle for me to replicate her work publicly:** Data-access plumbing — Articles 2 + 3 Kd datasets live in SI PDF tables (need OCR + `glycowork` SNFG → SMILES conversion to become ML-ready); Article 1's raw nMS files are in proprietary Thermo / Waters formats needing `msconvert` to mzML. **CUPRA-SWARM on GitHub** (linked from Article 3) is the only directly-runnable open-source artefact across the three papers. The glycan-notation + native-MS-tooling learning curve is significant.
- **Skills I would gain by working with her:** `glycowork` (Mahal-group Python library — de-facto standard for glycan informatics), RDKit + DeepChem / PyTorch Geometric (graph neural nets on glycans), ESM-2 protein-sequence embeddings, **CUPRA-SWARM** (Klassen-lab native-MS abundance-extraction Python tool on GitHub), native-MS data analysis (pyteomics / pymzml + Thermo / Waters `.raw` conversion via `msconvert`), entry points into the **Siglec / immunotherapy** + **SARS-CoV-2 / viral-attachment** + **nanobody / single-domain-antibody therapeutics** literatures, exposure to the Klassen-lab SLOMO → COIN-nMS → IMS-CaR-nMS measurement methodology lineage + advection-diffusion analytical modelling (Flynn co-author on Article 2; Kitov co-author on Articles 2 + 3 + author of SWARM).

#### Article 1: Delta SARS-CoV-2 in free-ranging Quebec white-tailed deer

- **Full citation:** Kotwa JD, Lobb B, Massé A, ..., Doxey AC, Pickering B, Mubareka S (2023). Genomic and transcriptomic characterization of delta SARS-CoV-2 infection in free-ranging white-tailed deer (*Odocoileus virginianus*). *iScience* 26, 108319. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.isci.2023.108319
- **Problem in plain English:** White-tailed deer (WTD) in North America have become a probable non-human reservoir for SARS-CoV-2. The authors sampled 258 deer in southern Quebec (Nov 2021), found 4 Delta-positive nasal swabs (lineage AY.44), sequenced their viral genomes, and ran bulk RNA-seq on the nasal swabs. They then compared the deer transcriptomic response against a human nasopharyngeal-swab RNA-seq cohort to ask whether deer mount a different innate-immune response than humans.
- **ML task type:** No supervised ML in the paper. Closest portfolio reframe: **multi-class sequence classification** (SARS-CoV-2 spike-protein sequence → host species).
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: Illumina amplicon SARS-CoV-2 sequences (ARTIC v3/v4) + bulk Illumina RNA-seq of WTD nasal swabs.
  - Shape/size if stated: 4 viral genomes (3 high-coverage, 1 partial); 8 RNA-seq samples (2 SARS-CoV-2 positive + 6 negative); ~100M reads/sample × 150bp paired-end.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: fastp trimming → Bowtie2 / STAR alignment to *O. virginianus texanus* (GCF_002102435.1) → Salmon quantification → DESeq2 differential expression → DAVID GO enrichment; OrthoFinder for cross-species ortholog mapping to human (GRCh38.p13).
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts (paper's actual output): 316 differentially-expressed deer genes + phylogenetic placement + IFITM1 lineage-duplication discovery (descriptive, not predictive).
  - Units or label space: log2 fold-change values + bootstrap-supported phylogenetic clades.
- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML model in paper; pipeline is fastp → Bowtie2 + STAR → Salmon → DESeq2 → DAVID + OrthoFinder + UShER + IQ-TREE + ggtree.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: 4 Quebec WTD SARS-CoV-2 viral genomes + 8 WTD nasal-swab RNA-seq + 50 SARS-CoV-2-positive + 13 negative human nasopharyngeal RNA-seq (Luc et al. 2023 comparator).
  - Size: 4 viral genomes (3 high-coverage); 8 deer RNA-seq samples; 63 human RNA-seq samples (comparator).
  - Source: this study + Luc et al. 2023 figshare deposit.
  - Public? yes.
  - Link: GISAID EPI_ISL_10168587 / 10169675 / 10170149 (viral); NCBI SRA BioProject PRJNA1025888 (deer RNA-seq); human comparator on figshare DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.22704403.v1; analysis code at https://github.com/CFIA-NCFAD/Delta-SARS-CoV-2-WTD-QC.
- **Reported headline metric:** 1.6% (4/251) WTD nasal-swab prevalence; 316 significant DEGs; weak deer-vs-human innate-immune correlation r = 0.27 (p = 9.49 × 10⁻¹³).
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**

  - GISAID EpiCoV — ≫16 M sequences with rich host metadata — match: close — access: medium (registration + agreement) — https://gisaid.org/

  - This paper's own GISAID + SRA deposits as a held-out test set — match: close — access: easy — links above.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** easy — viral genomes one-click on GISAID after free agreement, RNA-seq one-click on NCBI SRA.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** sklearn (k-mer + LR baseline — known); PyTorch 1D-CNN (known); HuggingFace ESM-2 small fine-tune (new — one major component); biopython for FASTA / GenBank parsing (minor new).
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** Train a multi-class spike-protein → host-species classifier on NCBI Virus + GISAID host-tagged SARS-CoV-2 sequences. Three tiers — sklearn k-mer + logistic-regression baseline, PyTorch 1D-CNN over one-hot spike, ESM-2 small fine-tune. (iScience 2023)."

#### Article 2: Pediatric AOM/URI bacterial WGS + AMR profiling

- **Full citation:** Lobb B, Lee MC, McElheny CL, Doi Y, Yahner K, Hoberman A, Martin JM, Hirota JA, Doxey AC, Shaikh N (2023). Genomic classification and antimicrobial resistance profiling of *Streptococcus pneumoniae* and *Haemophilus influenzae* isolates associated with paediatric otitis media and upper respiratory infection. *BMC Infectious Diseases* 23:596. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12879-023-08560-x
- **Problem in plain English:** Acute otitis media (AOM) is the most common childhood infection requiring antibiotics, driven by *S. pneumoniae* (SPN) + *H. influenzae* (HFLU). Clinical microbiology uses culture + Vitek 2 phenotypic AMR testing, but this can miss strain context + the actual resistance genes. The authors ask: can a WGS-based bioinformatics pipeline classify these isolates (species, serotype, MLST sequence type) AND predict AMR phenotypes well enough to complement or replace clinical testing?
- **ML task type:** No supervised ML in the paper. Closest portfolio reframe: **per-antibiotic multi-label binary classification** (bacterial-genome features → resistant / susceptible per antibiotic) + outlier-detection sub-task.
- **Input representation:**

  - Shape/size if stated: 148 cultured isolates (71 SPN + 76 HFLU + 1 S. mitis); ~2 Mbp assemblies (SPN avg 2.09 Mbp, HFLU avg 1.88 Mbp).
  - Preprocessing in the paper: bcl-convert → fastp → SPAdes (--isolate) → Kraken 2 PlusPF contamination filtering.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts (paper's actual output): MLST sequence type (33 SPN / 29 HFLU STs); 19 SPN serotypes via SeroBA; per-antibiotic resistance label (resistant + intermediate vs susceptible) via Pathogenwatch SPN-PBP-AMR + CARD RGI.
  - Units / label space: categorical (ST, serotype) + binary per antibiotic.
- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML in the paper. Rule-based BLAST-against-CARD/ResFinder/NCBI for AMR-gene presence + *pbp1A/2B/2X* signature-matching for SPN β-lactam MIC inference + Snippy core-genome SNPs → RAxML phylogeny.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**

#### Article 3: ML framework identifies C3/C4-distinguishing plastid-encoded proteins in PACMAD grasses

- **Full citation:** Yogadasan N, Doxey AC, Chuong SDX (2023). A Machine Learning Framework Identifies Plastid-Encoded Proteins Harboring C3 and C4 Distinguishing Sequence Information. *Genome Biology and Evolution* 15(7):evad129. https://doi.org/10.1093/gbe/evad129
- **Problem in plain English:** C4 photosynthesis evolved independently at least 61 times across plants — a classic case of convergent evolution. >50% of C4 species sit in the PACMAD clade of grasses. The authors ask: can ML, by reading patterns across an entire protein sequence simultaneously (rather than position-by-position selection tests), identify which plastid-encoded proteins + specific residues carry C3-vs-C4 distinguishing information — and recover known + novel C4-adaptive sites?
- **ML task type:** Binary supervised classification (C3 vs C4) with feature-importance interpretation.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: MUSCLE-aligned plastid-encoded protein sequences — one model per protein, across 76 plastid-encoded proteins (e.g. RbcL ~475 residues, NdhI ~175 residues).
  - Shape/size: 134 PACMAD grass species (76 C4 + 58 C3) × 76 protein-sequence alignments; alignment positions converted to integer features (predominantly binary [0]/[1]; occasional [2]/[3] for variable positions).
  - Preprocessing: MUSCLE alignment → custom integer encoding per alignment position → standardisation.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: photosynthesis type (C3 vs C4).
  - Units / label space: binary.
- **Model architecture (brief):** scikit-learn `LogisticRegression` classifier (three variants: v1 full-length features, v2 top-10-features per model, v3 RFE-CV-optimal feature subset) with 500-iteration repeated random subsampling cross-validation (70/30 splits) + permutation-test null comparison.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: 135 Poaceae plastomes (134 PACMAD + *Anomochloa marantoidea* for rooting) from the Chloroplast Genome Database (CpGDB); C3/C4 trait labels from Osborne et al. 2014 + Piot et al. 2018.
  - Size: 134 species × 76 plastid-encoded proteins.
  - Source: CpGDB (Singh et al. 2020); Osborne et al. 2014 C4 grass database.

#### Article 1: Transition state analysis of NeuB-catalyzed sialic acid synthesis

- **Full citation:** Mukherjee P, Niu C, Berti PJ (2025). Transition State Analysis of the Aldol-Like Reaction Catalyzed by NeuB, a Sialic Acid Synthase, Reveals a Stepwise Cationic Mechanism. *ACS Bio Med Chem Au* 5(6):882–894. https://doi.org/10.1021/acsbiomedchemau.5c00126
- **Problem in plain English:** NeuB is a bacterial enzyme that builds sialic acid (N-acetylneuraminic acid / NeuNAc), which many pathogenic bacteria (E. coli K1, H. seropedicae, etc.) use to evade the human immune system and cause disease (neonatal meningitis, bloodstream infection). To design antibiotic-like inhibitors of NeuB, you need to know what the **transition state (TS)** — the fleeting highest-energy arrangement of atoms during catalysis — actually looks like, because enzymes bind their TS more tightly than anything else, so TS-mimicking molecules are the most potent possible inhibitors. The authors measure three kinetic isotope effects (KIEs) on the NeuB reaction by NMR, compute candidate TS structures with DFT, and pick the TS structure whose calculated KIEs match the experimental values. They find a **stepwise mechanism through a cationic intermediate**, but the TS itself is reached very early (before much positive charge develops), so cationic-mimic inhibitors are unlikely to work — they recommend **neutral inhibitors that maximize the number of active-site interactions** instead.
- **ML task type:** **No ML in the paper.** Closest portfolio reframes are loose-analogy: (a) regression QSAR for α-CKS-family inhibitor pIC50 from ChEMBL bioassay data; (b) neural-network-potential prediction of TS energies / KIEs from Cartesian coordinates trained on Transition1x.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: small-molecule chemistry (PEP + ManNAc substrates and computational TS / intermediate geometries) + experimental NMR isotope ratios.
  - Shape/size if stated: **31 computational TS / intermediate / reactant DFT structures** with Cartesian coordinates (Supporting Information Table S5); **3 experimental KIEs** (3-13C = 1.023 ± 0.002, 2-13C = 0.994 ± 0.007, 2-18O = 0.999 ± 0.006) + replicates; **3 NeuB crystal-structure dependencies** (PDB 1XUZ, 6PPZ, 6PPW).
  - Preprocessing in the paper: Gaussian 16 DFT geometry optimization at B3PW91/6-31+G** with CPCM water solvent; QUIVER scaled-frequency-based KIE calculation (Cartesian force constants scaled by 0.9139); NMR peak deconvolution via PeakFit (Voigt + Lorentzian); isotope-ratio fits to extent-of-reaction via Bennet eqs 5–6; Bell tunneling correction included.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts (paper's actual output): one **experimental TS structure** (cationic intermediate formation, AN‡ * AN mechanism, C3···C1′ bond order 0.17–0.35) + a design-principle conclusion (avoid cationic mimics, favor neutral high-contact inhibitors).
  - Units or label space: dimensionless Pauling bond orders, KIE values (heavy/light rate ratios, dimensionless), reaction-coordinate frequencies (cm⁻¹).
- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML model in paper. Method stack = NMR-based competitive KIE measurement (Bennet method, 13C / 31P reporter nuclei, incomplete-T1 9× acceleration) + Gaussian 16 hybrid DFT TS optimization (QST3) + QUIVER reduced-partition-function KIE computation + Bell tunneling correction.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house experimental KIE values + in-house DFT TS-structure library + 3 NeuB crystal structures from the literature.
  - Size: 3 experimental KIEs (with replicates) + 31 DFT-optimized structures.
  - Source: this paper (experimental + computational) + RCSB PDB (crystal structures).
  - Public? **partial** — KIE values + Cartesian coordinates are published in the SI PDF only (not as machine-readable files); NeuB crystal structures are fully public on PDB; **no code released**.
  - Link: https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsbiomedchemau.5c00126 (article + SI); https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1XUZ + https://www.rcsb.org/structure/6PPZ + https://www.rcsb.org/structure/6PPW.
- **Reported headline metric:** experimental KIEs 3-13C = 1.023 ± 0.002, 2-13C = 0.994 ± 0.007, 2-18O = 0.999 ± 0.006 → match computational AN‡ * AN TS structures with C3···C1′ bond order 0.17–0.35; 9-fold KIE-measurement speedup via incomplete-T1 NMR relaxation (one spectrum: 6.0 h → 40 min).
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**

  - **Transition1x** — ~9.6M DFT-labeled near-TS molecular geometries from ~10,000 organic reactions — match: loose (general reaction-TS-property prediction, not the NeuB reaction specifically) — access: easy (direct download) — https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/Transition1x/19614120
  - **RGD1-CHNO** (Reaction Graph Database) — ~176,000 elementary reactions with DFT energetics — match: loose — access: easy — https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/model_reaction_database_RGD1/21066901
  - **QM9 / QM7-X / MoleculeNet** — small-molecule DFT-property datasets — match: very-loose (only useful as a sklearn / Chemprop baseline) — access: easy — https://moleculenet.org/datasets-1

#### Article 2: NeuNAc Oxime — slow-binding, effectively irreversible inhibitor of NeuB

- **Full citation:** Popović V, Morrison E, Rosanally AZ, Balachandran N, Senson AW, Szabla R, Junop MS, Berti PJ (2019). NeuNAc Oxime: A Slow-Binding and Effectively Irreversible Inhibitor of the Sialic Acid Synthase NeuB. *Biochemistry* 58, 4236–4245. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.biochem.9b00654
- **Problem in plain English:** This is the paper that **introduced the NeuNAc oxime inhibitor** whose transition state Article 1 (Mukherjee et al. 2025) later dissected — Article 1 cites this paper as its ref 31. NeuB makes sialic acid that pathogenic bacteria need to dodge the immune system, so blocking NeuB is an anti-infective strategy. Most inhibitors are quickly outcompeted by substrate, but this paper shows that **NeuNAc oxime — even though it only binds the enzyme modestly tightly at first (Ki ≈ 36 μM) — then locks itself in via a slow conformational change**, so that the inhibitor's residence time in the active site (>47 days) is longer than the lifetime of a typical bacterial cell, making it "effectively irreversible." The authors also solve four new crystal structures of NeuB (with the oxime, with phosphate + ManNAc, and with two malate-containing complexes), and show that complete inhibition of NeuB only happens when the enzyme is actively catalyzing — direct evidence of allosteric subunit cooperativity in the homodimer.
- **ML task type:** **No ML in the paper.** Closest portfolio reframes are tighter than A1's because the paper releases public PDB structures and explicit kinetic labels: (a) **structure-based virtual-screening / binding-pose ML** on the 4 new PDB structures (regression / pose-ranking); (b) **residence-time / log(tR) QSAR** for slow-binding inhibitors (regression).
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: protein–ligand 3D crystal structures + small-molecule chemistry (NeuNAc oxime as SMILES / 3D conformer) + steady-state enzyme-kinetics time-course data.
  - Shape/size if stated: **4 new PDB depositions** at 1.85–2.40 Å resolution (6PPY, 6PPZ, 6PPX, 6PPW; P21212 space group; ~2670 protein atoms + 9–22 ligand atoms per complex; 191–388 ordered waters); 67 initial-velocity rate measurements fitted globally; 1 known small-molecule inhibitor (NeuNAc oxime) with full kinetic characterization (Ki, k2, kon, residence time).
  - Preprocessing in the paper: HKL 2000 indexing/scaling → Phenix AutoMR molecular replacement (search model 1XUZ) → WinCoot manual rebuilding + Phenix refine; **Dynafit numerical kinetic simulation** of the pre-equilibration/irreversible model (Scheme 1: `E + I ⇌ E·I → E*·I`); 1H + 13C NMR characterization of NeuNAc oxime after Mono-Q anion-exchange purification.
- **Output representation:**

Method stack = X-ray crystallography (Rigaku RU300 + NSLS X25 synchrotron) + HKL 2000 + Phenix + WinCoot + Dynafit kinetic-simulation software + Malachite-green/ammonium-molybdate colorimetric Pi-release assay + Mono-Q anion-exchange chromatography + NMR (1H, 13C, HRMS).

#### Article 3: Slow-binding inhibition of *C. jejuni* KDO8P synthase by KDO8P oxime

- **Full citation:** Gama SR, Balachandran N, Berti PJ (2018). *Campylobacter jejuni* KDO8P Synthase, Its Inhibition by KDO8P Oxime, and Control of the Residence Time of Slow-Binding Inhibition. *Biochemistry* 57(36), 5327–5338. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.biochem.8b00748
- **Problem in plain English:** This paper completes the in-survey Berti-lab "oxime trio" — A2 reported NeuNAc oxime targeting NeuB; here A3 reports **KDO8P oxime targeting a third bacterial α-carboxyketose synthase, KDO8P synthase from the gut pathogen *Campylobacter jejuni***. KDO8P synthase makes a key sugar (KDO) needed to build the lipopolysaccharide outer coat of Gram-negative bacteria, so blocking it is another antibiotic strategy. The authors first nail down the enzyme's basic biochemistry (it's a 4-subunit homotetramer; it needs Mn²⁺; Mn²⁺ binds first, then PEP, then the sugar A5P), then characterize KDO8P oxime as a slow-binding inhibitor. Two findings matter most for inhibitor design: (i) the inhibitor's residence time in the active site varies dramatically (from ~30 min to ~3 days) depending on whether there's free inhibitor sitting around in solution to stabilize the bound state, and (ii) cooperativity analysis (Hill coefficient = 3.5) shows that all four subunits must be occupied simultaneously before the enzyme locks into its tightly-inhibited state — direct evidence that intersubunit communication, not single-site affinity alone, controls how well an oligomeric-enzyme inhibitor actually works in practice.

#### Article 1: PREP-driven inverse design of nanoparticle size for drug delivery

- **Full citation:** Tayebi SS, Dowdall N, Hoare T, Mhaskar P (2025). Data-driven optimization of nanoparticle size using the prediction reliability enhancing parameter (PREP). *Nanoscale* 17, 19767–19784. https://doi.org/10.1039/d5nr01664a
- **Problem in plain English:** When you're making polymer nanoparticles for drug delivery, the particle size controls almost everything that matters — how long the particle circulates in the body, whether it can squeeze through tumor blood vessels, whether the immune system clears it, and whether it can deliver drug inside cells. But hitting an exact target size (e.g., ~100 nm to bypass liver clearance) is hard because the recipe variables (monomer amounts, surfactant concentration, ionic strength) interact in messy nonlinear ways. The standard approach is brute-force trial-and-error, which is slow and expensive. This paper applies a new data-driven optimization method called **PREP** that the same group developed in 2025 — PREP uses latent-variable models (PLS + PCA) to invert the recipe-to-size relationship and predict which next recipes are most likely to hit the target, ranked by a single confidence score. The authors test PREP on two very different nanoparticle systems (smart microgels + DOX-loaded polyelectrolyte complexes) and show that in both cases PREP can hit the size + dispersity targets in **only two experimental iterations**, dramatically beating both the existing dataset and a conventional optimization baseline.
- **ML task type:** **GENUINE supervised regression + inverse design** (no reframe needed). Forward task = recipe (3–4 input variables) → particle size + PDI (1–2 output variables). Inverse task = given target output, find optimal recipe under design constraints. Methods used: PLS (Partial Least Squares Projection to Latent Structure) regression + PCA (Principal Component Analysis) latent-variable modeling + LVMI (latent variable model inversion) + constraint-based numerical optimization (Inversion-by-Optimization, IbO) + PREP equation for ranking candidate recipes by prediction reliability.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: tabular formulation variables.
  - Shape/size if stated: **Case 1** = 15-row × 3-feature table (MBA crosslinker mg, VAA acid comonomer mg, SDS surfactant mg) → 1 output (size in nm). **Case 2** = 19-row × 4-feature table (PBS ionic strength × full strength, total precursor mg/mL, GS:DOX ratio, Dex-GTAC:DOX ratio) → 2 outputs (size + PDI in 1× PBS). Iterations grow the dataset by 2 datapoints per iteration.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: PLS components selected by experimental-knowledge of input-variable interdependence (3 PLS components for both cases); k-nearest-neighbors selection (k = A + 2 = 5) around target output for each iteration; jackknife cross-validation for PLS prediction-accuracy estimation; Hotelling's T² + SPE + score-alignment H computed on both PLS and PCA models for each candidate.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: nanoparticle size (intensity-averaged DLS effective diameter, nm) and PDI (polydispersity index, dimensionless 0–1). PREP score = reliability metric used to rank candidate recipes (lower PREP = higher predicted accuracy; higher PREP = higher uncertainty, used for design-space exploration).
  - Units or label space: nm (size), dimensionless (PDI), dimensionless (PREP score).
- **Model architecture (brief):** Latent-Variable Model (PLS + PCA) → LVMI / IbO numerical inversion → PREP equation (eq 1: linear combination of Hotelling's T²_PLS, SPE_x,PLS, Hotelling's T²_PCA, SPE_PCA, score-alignment H_PLS, score-alignment H_PCA — each raised to an optimized power P_i and weighted by an optimized coefficient C_i). All standard chemometrics, no neural networks.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: 34-datapoint in-house Hoare-lab dataset (15 PNIPAM microgels Table 1 + 19 GS/Dex-GTAC/DOX PECs Table 3) + iteration results (Tables 2 + 4).
  - Size: 15 + 19 = 34 initial datapoints; +6 microgel iteration recipes (Table 2) + 12 PEC iteration recipes (Table 4) = 52 total recipes characterized across both case studies.
  - Source: this paper.
  - Public? **Yes — datasets fully tabulated in the open-access PAPER ITSELF** (Tables 1, 2, 3, 4); raw DLS measurements are request-only; SI contains additional Case 2 iterations 5–6.
  - Link: https://doi.org/10.1039/d5nr01664a (open access CC-BY-NC 3.0).
- **Reported headline metric:** **Case 1**: target = 100 nm microgel; PREP achieved **104 nm in 2 iterations** (98% accuracy), outperforming both the smallest pre-existing microgel (175 nm) and the conventional IbO baseline (170 nm). **Case 2**: target = <200 nm + PDI <0.2 under physiological 1× PBS; PREP achieved **171 nm / PDI 0.19 in 2 iterations** + 182 nm / PDI 0.15 by iteration 4 (matched both targets while no pre-existing sample did); DOX loading 2.3 wt% + 31% encapsulation efficiency.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **The paper itself** — Tables 1 + 3 + 2 + 4 contain the full 34-datapoint primary dataset + iteration outcomes — match: **exact (direct replication)** — access: easy (open access, transcribe tables to CSV) — https://doi.org/10.1039/d5nr01664a

  - **MoleculeNet / QM9 / Materials Project** — for testing the PREP method's scaling claims at the larger-data regime — match: loose (different domain, larger scale) — access: easy — https://moleculenet.org/ + https://materialsproject.org/
  - **scikit-learn PLSRegression + PCA + scipy.optimize.differential_evolution** — for re-implementing the PREP algorithm — match: exact tooling — access: easy (open-source Python) — https://scikit-learn.org/
  - **BoTorch / GPyOpt** — Bayesian optimization baselines for head-to-head PREP comparison — match: close (alternative inverse-design method explicitly discussed in the paper) — access: easy — https://botorch.org/

#### Article 2: Review of microgel/nanogel strategies for poorly water-soluble drug delivery

- **Full citation:** Dave R, Randhawa G, Kim D, Simpson M, Hoare T (2022). Microgels and Nanogels for the Delivery of Poorly Water-Soluble Drugs. *Mol. Pharmaceutics* 19, 1704–1721. https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.molpharmaceut.1c00967
- **Problem in plain English:** Many promising drugs barely dissolve in water (high logP), which is a big problem because the body is mostly water — these drugs don't reach a useful concentration when given conventionally, so they need either much higher doses (causing side effects) or a special carrier. **Microgels** (tiny soft water-swollen polymer gels, ~10–1000 nm) are normally used for water-soluble drugs because they are themselves hydrophilic, but they have unique advantages — they squeeze through tight junctions in tissues, stay in circulation a long time, are easy to chemically modify, and can be made very monodisperse — that make them attractive for hydrophobic drugs *if* you can solve the loading problem. This Hoare-lab review (5 authors, all McMaster ChemE) catalogs every strategy people have used to put hydrophobic drugs into microgels (4 main loading approaches with multiple sub-routes each) and every strategy for then triggering the drug's release at the target site (6 stimulus types), discussing both the chemistry and the open clinical-translation challenges, with 130 cited references and a 5-case-study in vivo summary table.
- **ML task type:** **No ML in the paper — it's a review.** Closest portfolio reframes are loose-analogy literature-meta-analysis: (a) tabular QSAR predicting (encapsulation %, release half-life) from (drug logP + microgel hydrophobization strategy + microgel composition) extracted from the cited literature; (b) NLP/LLM-based structured-data extraction from polymer drug-delivery papers using Table 1 + Table 2 as a labeled seed.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: text (130-reference scientific review) + cited tabular data (logP values for ~30 drugs scattered throughout + Table 1 = 8 nanoparticle-type × hydrophobic-drug-loading-strategy comparison + Table 2 = 5 in vivo case studies with administration route + release trigger + result).
  - Shape/size if stated: ~30 drugs with logP values, ~6 Hoare-lab cited primary research papers visible (Simpson 2020 PhD + Simpson 2018 *Ind. Eng. Chem. Res.* + Mateen 2012 MSc + Jamard 2016 *Drug Deliv Transl Res* + Hoare-Pelton 2008 *Langmuir* + Campea 2021 *Adv. Funct. Mater.*).
  - Preprocessing in the paper: literature synthesis only; no preprocessed dataset released.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the paper "predicts" (review output): a taxonomy of microgel hydrophobization strategies + a taxonomy of release-trigger strategies + a forward-looking list of 5 open clinical-translation challenges.
  - Units or label space: qualitative classification (review framework), not numerical predictions.
- **Model architecture (brief):** None — review paper.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: Hoare-lab + colleagues literature synthesis on microgels/nanogels for hydrophobic drug delivery.
  - Size: 133 cited references + ~30 hydrophobic drugs cataloged with logP values + Table 1 (8-row × 4-column comparison) + Table 2 (5 in vivo case studies with full clinical context).
  - Source: open literature.
  - Public? **Open-access review paper** (CC-not-explicitly-stated; standard ACS access through institutional / individual subscription); cited primary research papers each have their own data-availability status.

- **Reported headline metric:** None — review paper. Key qualitative takeaway: cyclodextrin-functionalized microgels release hydrophobic drugs within <24 h; covalently-hydrophobized microgels can become so collapsed that drug barely releases at all; thermosensitive PNIPAAm microgels with VPTT slightly above body temperature offer the most controllable + clinically-translatable handle for triggered release.

#### Article 3: Multi-scale POEGMA-CNC hydrogel sheets for cell-instructive 2.5D biomaterials

- **Full citation:** De France KJ, Xu F, Toufanian S, Chan KJW, Said S, Stimpson TC, González-Martínez E, Moran-Mirabal JM, Cranston ED, Hoare T (2021). Multi-scale structuring of cell-instructive cellulose nanocrystal composite hydrogel sheets via sequential electrospinning and thermal wrinkling. *Acta Biomaterialia*. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actbio.2021.04.044
- **Problem in plain English:** Cells in your body don't sit on a flat featureless surface — the natural extracellular matrix has structure at multiple length scales (visible micron-scale fibers + nanometer-scale nanofibers), and cells use those cues to decide how to orient and grow. If you want to grow muscle cells in a dish for tissue regeneration, you ideally want a "2.5D" scaffold that mimics those multi-scale cues. Making such a scaffold cleanly out of a soft water-swollen hydrogel is hard. This paper introduces a two-step recipe — first **electrospin** POEGMA-cellulose-nanocrystal nanofibers onto a hydrogel base layer, then **thermally shrink** the underlying plastic to make the whole thing wrinkle — to produce hydrogel sheets that have both 5-12 μm wrinkles AND 300-700 nm fibers, with independent control over fiber alignment (random / parallel-to-wrinkles / perpendicular-to-wrinkles) and wrinkle geometry (biaxial / uniaxial). They then plate C2C12 mouse muscle cells on 6 different sheet morphologies and show that uniaxial wrinkles drive cell elongation along the wrinkle direction (aspect ratio 4.5 vs 1.7 unstructured) and parallel nanofibers reinforce that alignment (12° angular deviation) while perpendicular nanofibers disrupt it (21° deviation).
- **ML task type:** **No ML in the paper.** Closest portfolio reframes are loose-to-medium analogy: (a) **process-parameter QSAR / inverse-design ML** with strong cross-link to A1's PREP method; (b) **SEM image-analysis CV ML** replacing the paper's manual ImageJ workflow; (c) **cell-substrate property prediction QSAR**.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: tabular process parameters (CNC wt%, electrospinning time, collector rotation rate, constraint geometry) + SEM micrographs (cell + fiber + wrinkle morphology) + tabular characterization measurements (compressive modulus, swelling, degradation, protein adsorption).
  - Shape/size if stated: 3 CNC concentrations × 3 electrospinning times × 2 constraint geometries × 2 fiber orientations ≈ 30-50 unique sheet conditions; n=4 replicates per physical property; n≥100 features per SEM image; n≥50 cells per condition for cell aspect ratio + orientation angle.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: ImageJ manual feature extraction (fiber diameter, wrinkle size, cell aspect ratio, cell orientation angle); MicroSquisher 20% strain compression cycles; FITC-BSA fluorescence (Wallac 1420); MTS colorimetric absorbance at 490 nm; confocal CFDA SE + DAPI cell staining; SEM after sputter coat + supercritical drying.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the paper "predicts" (paper's actual output): sheet morphology (fiber diameter, wrinkle size, fiber + wrinkle alignment angle) and cell response (cell aspect ratio, alignment angle, MTS viability) as a function of process parameters.
  - Units or label space: nm (fiber diameter), μm (wrinkle size), dimensionless ratio (cell aspect ratio), ° (cell + wrinkle alignment angle), kPa (compressive modulus), % (water content, BSA uptake), absorbance units (MTS).
- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML model in paper. Method stack = reactive electrospinning (double-barrel syringe co-extrusion of aldehyde-POEGMA + hydrazide-POEGMA + CNCs + PEO aid) + thermal wrinkling on prestressed polystyrene + MicroSquisher cantilever compression + SEM + confocal + ImageJ manual feature extraction + MTS colorimetric assay.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house Hoare-lab + Cranston-lab + Moran-Mirabal-lab characterization of POEGMA-CNC hydrogel sheet morphology + C2C12 myoblast cell-substrate response across 6 sheet morphologies.
  - Size: ~30-50 process-parameter conditions × 4-6 property measurements × n=4 replicates; ~3,000+ measured features (fibers + wrinkles + cells) via ImageJ across all figures.
  - Source: this paper.
  - Public? partial — all quantitative data presented in figures + tables of the open-access paper; SI Figs S1-S11 + Tables referenced but not separately deposited; **NO public dataset deposit**; **NO code release**.
  - Link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actbio.2021.04.044 (CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0).
- **Reported headline metric:** uniaxial wrinkles drive **3-fold cell aspect-ratio increase** (1.7 → 4.5-5.2); parallel nanofibers reinforce alignment to **12° angular deviation** (vs 18° no fibers / 21° perpendicular fibers); 1.65 wt% CNC achieves **25 kPa compressive modulus = 2.5× over 0.2 wt% baseline** + significantly reduced BSA adsorption; multiscale 2.5D morphology achievable by a simple benchtop electrospinning + thermal-wrinkling protocol without lithography.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **The paper itself** — figures + tables contain all quantitative data (open access) — match: exact (literature-meta-analysis or process-parameter QSAR seed) — access: easy + manual CSV transcription needed.
  - **De France 2019 *ACS Appl. Mater. Interfaces* predecessor paper** (2.5D hierarchical structuring of POEGMA-CNC films) — direct predecessor with similar data structure — match: close — access: easy (ACS subscription required).

  - **SEM image datasets from materials-science Kaggle / Zenodo collections** for pretraining / transfer learning — match: loose-to-medium — access: easy.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** medium — Figs 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 + Table summarize all quantitative results; ~30 min CSV transcription per figure; raw SEM micrographs require PDF figure extraction (~50 cell images + ~10 morphology images embedded in figures).
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **scikit-learn** PLS/RF/XGBoost regression (known); **scipy.optimize** for PREP-method implementation (already covered in A1); **OpenCV / scikit-image** for basic image preprocessing (new minor); **Cellpose / nnU-Net** for cell + fiber segmentation (new but well-tooled with pretrained checkpoints); **PyTorch + torchvision** for any custom CV model (known); **ImageJ + Fiji** plugins for ground-truth comparison (new minor); pandas + matplotlib (known).
