### Article 1: Electrochemical Nano-Roughening of Gold Microstructured Electrodes for Enhanced Sensing in Biofluids

- **Full citation:** Eduardo González-Martínez, Sokunthearath (Kevin) Saem, Nadine E. Beganovic, Jose M. Moran-Mirabal*. "Electrochemical Nano-Roughening of Gold Microstructured Electrodes for Enhanced Sensing in Biofluids." *Angewandte Chemie International Edition* 2023, **62**, e202218080. DOI: 10.1002/anie.202218080. Open Access.

- **Problem in plain English:** Miniaturizing electrochemical sensors usually means losing sensitivity because shrinking the working electrode shrinks its electroactive surface area (ESA). The authors show that a flat sputtered-gold electrode on shape-memory polystyrene can be (1) thermally shrunk to ~16% of its original area to produce microscale wrinkles, then (2) further nano-roughened in concentrated sulfuric acid by chronoamperometric (CA) pulsing between 0–2 V (20 ms dwell per step, repeated up to 200 pulses). This 2-step process delivers a 30× ESA enhancement over a planar electrode of the same footprint, plus strong resistance to protein fouling, plus sensitivity sufficient to detect Cu²⁺ in tap water and to perform enzyme-free glucose oxidation in human blood serum at clinical concentrations comparable to two commercial enzyme-based sensors.

- **ML task type:** **None as written** — this is a pure experimental electrochemistry / materials-science paper. ML reframes available to a portfolio project:
  - **(a) Tabular regression**: ESA (cm²) from process parameters {Au-film thickness, pulse count, H₂SO₄ concentration, dwell time}. Figure 2B has ~30 datapoints across 3 thicknesses × ~10 pulse counts × n=3 replicates.
  - **(b) 1D signal regression**: predict glucose concentration (mM) or Cu²⁺ concentration (μM) from cyclic-voltammetry I-vs-V curves. This is a classic 1D-CNN task with public analogue datasets on Kaggle.
  - **(c) Image regression / classification**: predict ESA or surface-quality class ("intact roughened" vs "pinholed/collapsed") from SEM images. Figure 3 = 15 SEM panels; too few for serious image-ML but useful as a teaching notebook.

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** (i) 1D cyclic voltammograms (current vs. potential, ~600 mV span, swept at fixed rate); (ii) chronoamperometric pulse trains (0-2 V step at 20 ms dwell); (iii) SEM images of electrode surfaces (Figure 3 = 3 thicknesses × 5 pulse counts = 15 panels visible).
  - **Shape / size if stated:** ESA measurements averaged across n=3 independently fabricated electrodes per condition. Cu²⁺ calibration: 5–60 μM × 3 electrode types (Planar, MSE, R-MSE), R² ≥ 0.97. Glucose calibration: 6 concentrations × 3 buffer matrices × 3 electrode types. Three human-serum samples assayed against two commercial sensors (Accu-Check Guide Me, Exactive EQ Impulse).
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** Integrate cathodic peak of the CV in sulfuric acid → divide by 386 μC/cm² → yields ESA (Trasatti & Petrii 1991 convention). Linear regression of stripping-voltammetry peak current vs. metal concentration. Linear regression of `ln(current)` vs. `ln(glucose concentration)`. No code or signal-processing scripts provided.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** None in paper. Possible ML outputs: (a) continuous ESA (cm² or normalized) from process parameters; (b) continuous analyte concentration (μM for Cu²⁺, mM for glucose) from CV signal; (c) qualitative surface-quality classification from SEM.
  - **Units or label space:** Continuous regression. ESA 1× to ~4× normalized. Cu²⁺ 5–60 μM. Glucose 0.5–21 mM in PBS / 1.5–7 mM in human serum.

- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML model used. The "model" is electrochemical: anodic stripping voltammetry calibration + Au-OH-mediated glucose electrooxidation mechanism + Cassie-Baxter wettability model (Eq. 1: σ = (cos θᵣ − cos θ)/(cos θ + 1)).

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** Not assigned — in-house tabular + SEM dataset from McMaster Moran-Mirabal lab + Canadian Centre for Electron Microscopy.
  - **Size:** ~30 ESA datapoints in Figure 2B (3 thicknesses × ~10 pulse counts × n=3) + 15 SEM panels in Figure 3 + ~60 voltammetry curves across all sub-experiments (Figures 4-6 + Figures S1-S10).
  - **Source:** Moran-Mirabal lab at McMaster Chemistry & Chemical Biology; electron microscopy via Canadian Centre for Electron Microscopy (CCEM) at McMaster.
  - **Public?** **No.**
  - **Link:** Data Availability Statement reads "The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request." A preprint version exists at ChemRxiv (`https://doi.org/10.26434/chemrxiv-2021-frhb5`), but it contains the manuscript, not a deposited dataset.

- **Reported headline metric:**
  - **30× ESA enhancement** of R-MSE vs. planar gold electrode of identical footprint.
  - **95% signal retention** for R-MSE after 30 min immersion in 2 mg/mL BSA (vs. near-zero signal for planar gold; ~35% for MSE without nano-roughening).
  - **LOQ for Cu²⁺ = 5 μM (0.3 ppm)** in tap water by UPD-ASV (Canadian regulatory limit is 2 ppm; US is 1.3 ppm — well within sensor range).
  - **LOQ for glucose = 1.4 mM** in PBS + 40 mg/mL BSA + 50 μM ascorbic acid (clinical glucose range is 3–7 mM).
  - **Human serum performance**: no statistically significant difference between R-MSE and two commercial enzyme-based sensors (Accu-Check Guide Me + Exactive EQ Impulse); %RSD < 10% across 3 serum samples.

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **Kaggle community electrochemistry datasets** (search terms: "cyclic voltammetry," "glucose CV," "amperometric"). — Size varies (often <1000 curves per dataset, sometimes synthetic). — Match: **loose**. — Access: **easy** direct download but quality is unverified and would require user inspection. — Link: search at `kaggle.com/datasets`.
  - **Materials Project** (`https://next-gen.materialsproject.org/`). — 22,000+ DFT entries with Au surface energies for (100), (110), (111) facets relevant to the paper's facet-dependent glucose electrooxidation discussion. — Match: **analogy** (informs the chemistry, does not reproduce the sensor data). — Access: **easy** via Materials Project REST API + `pymatgen`.
  - **Open Catalyst Project (OC20 / OC22)** (`https://opencatalystproject.org/`). — 1.3M+ DFT adsorption energies on heterogeneous catalysts including Au surfaces with adsorbed OH; directly relevant to the Au(OH)ₐdₛ mechanism for glucose electrooxidation discussed in the paper. — Match: **analogy** (mechanism-informing; the paper does not train a catalysis model). — Access: **easy** via `fairchem` / `torch-geometric` but **heavyweight to train** on free Colab.
  - **D1NAMO continuous-glucose-monitor public dataset** (`https://zenodo.org/record/5651217`). — 9 subjects, ~5 days each of continuous-glucose-monitor time-series. — Match: **analogy only** (different transduction modality — optical CGM, not electrochemical voltammetry). — Access: **easy** direct Zenodo download. — Useful only as a downstream "what to do with the predicted glucose value" demonstration.
  - **OhioT1DM Dataset** (Type 1 diabetes ML benchmark, request-only). — 12 subjects × 8 weeks of CGM + insulin + meals. — Match: **analogy only**. — Access: **medium** (request through Ohio University). — Same caveat as D1NAMO: different modality.

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **hard** — author-only request via `mirabj@mcmaster.ca`, no public deposit, no GitHub repo, no Zenodo DOI. The preprint at ChemRxiv contains the manuscript only.

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - `scipy.signal` for peak detection and integration on cyclic-voltammetry curves (close to your existing signal-processing comfort).
  - Standard `PyTorch` 1D-CNN for signal-to-concentration regression (within your existing PyTorch knowledge).
  - Standard `sklearn` (LinearRegression / RandomForest / XGBoost / GaussianProcessRegressor) for tabular ESA-vs-process-parameter modeling (within your existing sklearn knowledge).
  - `pymatgen` + Materials Project API for any DFT facet-energy lookup informing the mechanism discussion.
  - `fairchem` (Open Catalyst Project tooling) only if you want to incorporate adsorption-energy predictions — heavyweight and probably overkill for a portfolio project.
  - **Nothing chemistry-specific** like RDKit, DeepChem, GNNs, SMILES tokenization, or crystal-graph representations — this is the most "vanilla ML" professor in the survey so far.

- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** Reframe as **"Calibration-free electrochemical glucose sensing via a 1D-CNN that maps raw cyclic voltammetry I-V curves directly to glucose concentration"** — train a small 1D-CNN on simulated and/or scraped CV data, demonstrating that a single learned model can replace per-electrode manual peak-fitting calibration. Repo contents: (a) Notebook 1 — recreate the Moran-Mirabal ESA-vs-pulse-count curve on synthetic CV traces, validating the signal-processing pipeline against Figure 2B; (b) Notebook 2 — train the 1D-CNN end-to-end with PyTorch Lightning; (c) Notebook 3 — compare against the paper's reported sensitivities and LOQs (1.4 mM glucose / 5 μM Cu²⁺); (d) `figures/` folder with confusion-matrix-equivalent regression plots; (e) `data/` folder with the scraped + synthetic CV curves. README headline: "End-to-end calibration-free electrochemical glucose sensing — a 1D-CNN that predicts glucose concentration directly from raw cyclic-voltammetry traces, removing the need for per-electrode peak fitting." Alternative angle: **ESA process-parameter inverse-design** — use Figure 2B as a Gaussian-Process training set (n≈18 if you collapse replicates) and demonstrate optimal-pulse-count prediction for unseen Au thicknesses (this is the "Hoare-PREP-style" portfolio framing, which would directly bridge to Hoare A1 via shared trainee González-Martínez and create a McMaster biosensors-meets-biomaterials portfolio thread).

**One-sentence verdict for Article 1:** Tentatively yes for a chemistry-undergrad → ML-master's pivot — the ESA inverse-design reframe or the 1D-CNN signal-to-concentration reframe are both laptop-tractable with standard PyTorch / sklearn tooling and zero chemistry-specific dependencies (the most "vanilla ML" article in the survey), and the diabetes-tech recruiter-legible framing is strong, but the absence of any public dataset deposit (data only on author request) and the absence of any ML in the source paper itself mean the user has to supply the ML novelty rather than reproducing or extending the authors' own framework — significantly weaker as a portfolio anchor than the Hoare A1 / Pulsipher A1 / Aucoin A1 cluster of genuine-ML papers.

### Article 2: Functionalization of 3D Printed Scaffolds Using Polydopamine and Silver Nanoparticles for Bone-Interfacing Applications

- **Full citation:** Alessandra Merlo, Eduardo Gonzalez-Martinez, Kamal Saad, Mellissa Gomez, Manjot Grewal, Joseph Deering, Liza-Anastasia DiCecco, Zeinab Hosseinidoust, Kyla Sask, Jose M. Moran-Mirabal*, Kathryn Grandfield*. "Functionalization of 3D printed scaffolds using polydopamine and silver nanoparticles for bone-interfacing applications." *ACS Applied Bio Materials* **2023**, *6*, 1161–1172 (venue confirmed via Article 3's reference list, ref [57b] — published, not a preprint); **Moran-Mirabal + Grandfield co-corresponding**.

- **Problem in plain English:** Bone-interfacing implants (e.g., orthopedic prostheses) fail when bacteria colonize their surfaces and form biofilms, which antibiotics cannot easily penetrate. The team develops a simple two-step dip-coating method that (1) deposits a ~22 nm polydopamine (PDA) layer on a 3D-printed UV-resin scaffold, then (2) reduces silver nitrate on top of the PDA to in-situ-nucleate ~71 nm silver nanoparticles (AgNPs). The PDA acts as a universal adhesive primer and as the reducing agent; the AgNPs deliver antibacterial activity. The functionalized scaffolds achieve a 3.5–3.9 log reduction in *S. aureus* biofilm CFU/mL without inducing cytotoxicity in Saos-2 osteoblast-like cells over 7 days, and the method transfers to titanium substrates (smaller 48 nm AgNPs but similar coverage).

- **ML task type:** **None as written** — this is a pure experimental biomaterials / microbiology paper. ML reframes available to a portfolio project:
  - **(a) SEM image regression / classification**: predict AgNP surface coverage (%) and average particle diameter from SEM micrographs (the paper's ImageJ-based analysis pipeline). Standard 2D image-ML task; very small dataset (~10 images per condition × ~6 substrate types).
  - **(b) Tabular meta-analysis of AgNP MIC / cytotoxicity** against *S. aureus* and mammalian cells, using public nanotox databases (NanoMINE, e-NanoMapper, MIC-Database). Predict MIC from {nanoparticle size, shape, surface chemistry, concentration}. This is the strongest single-purpose ML reframe.
  - **(c) Saos-2 viability regression** from {Ag+ concentration, exposure time} — only 4 concentrations × n=3 = 12 datapoints, too few for serious ML, useful only as a teaching demonstration.
  - **(d) Bacterial biofilm SEM image classification** — quantify *S. aureus* colony density from SEM, train binary "biofilm present / absent" classifier or U-Net segmentation of bacterial colonies vs. background.

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** (i) SEM micrographs of AgNP-functionalized surfaces at 10k / 50k / 100k magnification (Figures 3, 4, 5, 6, 9 across resin + titanium substrates); (ii) AFM topography images of the PDA layer (Figure 2, 12×12 μm, 2 measurements × 3 samples); (iii) tabular AlamarBlue fluorescence at 540/580 nm × 3 timepoints × 6 substrate conditions × n=3 biological replicates; (iv) ICP-OES emission intensities at 328 / 338 / 241 nm × 8 calibration points × 1 ppm range; (v) tabular CFU/mL counts × 3 bacterial concentrations × 6 substrate conditions × n=3 biological reps; (vi) Live/Dead confocal microscopy at 4 Ag+ concentrations.
  - **Shape / size if stated:** SEM area threshold for ImageJ analysis = 500 – 55000 nm² per particle; PDA coating thickness measured over 12×12 μm areas. Sample sizes are uniformly small (n=3 biological replicates).
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** Gwyddion 2.55 for AFM thickness extraction. ImageJ for SEM particle counting with size-threshold gating. Linear regression of ICP-OES intensity vs. Ag+ concentration in Microsoft Excel. Two-way ANOVA + Tukey's HSD in GraphPad Prism for cell-metabolism and bacterial-count statistics. No code or scripts provided.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** None in paper. Possible ML outputs: (a) continuous AgNP coverage % and particle diameter from SEM images; (b) continuous MIC against *S. aureus* from nanoparticle descriptors; (c) Saos-2 viability % from Ag+ concentration; (d) binary classification of biofilm formation from SEM micrographs.
  - **Units or label space:** Coverage % (0–100). Particle diameter (nm). MIC (μg/mL). Viability %. Log10(CFU/mL).

- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML model used. Methods are entirely traditional materials-characterization + statistics: AFM line profiling, SEM image analysis via ImageJ, ICP-OES linear calibration, AlamarBlue fluorescence assay, S. aureus biofilm CFU plate counting, Live/Dead Saos-2 staining.

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** Not assigned — in-house multi-modal dataset from McMaster Moran-Mirabal + Grandfield labs.
  - **Size:** ~30+ SEM micrographs across multiple substrate conditions; AFM scans (n=3); AlamarBlue fluorescence values (6 conditions × 3 timepoints × n=3 = 54 datapoints); ICP-OES calibration (8 standards + ~6 samples); CFU/mL counts (6 conditions × n=3 = 18 datapoints); Live/Dead at 4 Ag+ concentrations.
  - **Source:** Moran-Mirabal lab (Chemistry & Chemical Biology) + Grandfield lab (Materials Science & Engineering) + Hosseinidoust lab (microbiology) + Sask lab (BME) at McMaster; SEM via Canadian Centre for Electron Microscopy at McMaster; in vitro studies at Biointerfaces Institute at McMaster.
  - **Public?** **No.**
  - **Link:** The PDF I examined does not include a Data Availability Statement (likely a preprint version where the DAS will be added at acceptance). No GitHub repo. No Zenodo DOI.

- **Reported headline metric:**
  - **3.5–3.9 log reduction in *S. aureus* Newman biofilm CFU/mL** on PDA+AgNP-coated 3D-printed solid + porous resin substrates vs. uncoated controls.
  - **PDA thickness = 22 ± 3 nm** (AFM on silicon wafers).
  - **AgNP diameter = 71 ± 4 nm on resin; 48 ± 4 nm on titanium**; surface coverage 18.3 ± 0.5% on resin, 19.3 ± 0.6% on titanium.
  - **Ag+ leachate = 0.78 ± 0.08 ppm (solid) / 1.0 ± 0.1 ppm (porous)** at 24 h / 37 °C in tryptic soy broth — ~5% of total deposited Ag.
  - **Saos-2 cytotoxicity threshold via Live/Dead**: 95 ± 1% / 86 ± 1% / 75 ± 2% / 58 ± 4% viability at 0 / 0.1 / 1 / 10 ppm Ag+. According to ISO 10993-5, only 10 ppm Ag+ exhibits mild cytotoxicity.
  - **PDA penetration depth ≥ 0.6 cm** within porous scaffold via radial-perfusion scenarios masked with carbon tape.

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **NanoMINE** (`https://nanomine.org/`). — Open-source nanomaterial property database with ~3000+ entries including AgNP toxicity, size, surface chemistry. Curated via NIST + Duke University. — Match: **medium** (loose for the specific *S. aureus* / Saos-2 setup, close for general AgNP MIC prediction). — Access: **medium** (free account; API available).
  - **e-NanoMapper / NanoCommons Knowledge Base** (`https://www.enanomapper.net/`). — EU-funded nanomaterial data integration platform with ~30+ datasets including AgNP cytotoxicity. — Match: **medium**. — Access: **medium** (federated API).
  - **MIC-Database.com** (curated AgNP MIC compilation against *S. aureus* and other pathogens). — Match: **medium**. — Access: **easy** for tabular extraction.
  - **Broad Bioimage Benchmark Collection (BBBC)** (`https://bbbc.broadinstitute.org/`). — Cell-imaging benchmark datasets for image-segmentation / classification ML. — Match: **analogy** (would inform the bacterial-biofilm SEM segmentation reframe, not reproduce the specific *S. aureus* + AgNP experiment). — Access: **easy** direct download.
  - **PubChem Bioassay Records for Antibacterial Compounds against *S. aureus***. — Tabular MIC data for thousands of small-molecule antibacterials. — Match: **analogy only** (compounds, not nanoparticles). — Access: **easy** via PubChem REST API.

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **hard** — no public deposit; likely author-request once published; no DAS visible in the PDF examined.

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - Image processing pipeline equivalent to ImageJ: `scikit-image`, `OpenCV`, or `cellpose` for SEM image segmentation of AgNPs from background and *S. aureus* colonies from substrate.
  - Image augmentation strategies (`albumentations`, `torchvision.transforms`) for small-dataset image-ML (would augment 30 SEM images to ~3000 effective training images).
  - U-Net or Mask-R-CNN if pursuing the bacterial-biofilm segmentation reframe — moderately heavier than vanilla CNN.
  - Standard `sklearn` + `XGBoost` for tabular MIC / cytotoxicity meta-analysis on NanoMINE / e-NanoMapper data.
  - `NanoMINE` + `e-NanoMapper` API tooling — niche but well-documented.
  - **Same caveat as A1**: no chemistry-specific tooling like RDKit, DeepChem, GNNs.

- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** Two viable angles, both weaker than A1's:
  - **(Stronger) "Tabular MIC prediction for silver nanoparticles against *S. aureus*"** — scrape NanoMINE + e-NanoMapper + literature meta-analysis data; train XGBoost / RandomForest / GaussianProcessRegressor with descriptors {AgNP size, shape, surface coating, concentration, exposure time}; demonstrate inverse-design of optimal AgNP coatings for orthopedic-implant-grade antibacterial activity at minimum cytotoxic dose. README headline: "Data-driven inverse design of antibacterial silver nanoparticle coatings — predicting *S. aureus* minimum-inhibitory-concentration from nanoparticle descriptors using public nanotox databases, validated against Merlo/Moran-Mirabal/Grandfield 2024 PDA-AgNP scaffolds."
  - **(Weaker) "SEM image regression of AgNP coverage % from microscopy"** — train a small CNN on heavily augmented SEM micrographs to predict surface coverage % and average particle diameter; demonstrate that the manual ImageJ pipeline can be replaced with an end-to-end learned model. README headline: "End-to-end SEM-to-quantification pipeline for nanoparticle surface coverage analysis." Risk: dataset is too small to argue this is a real ML advance vs. ImageJ.
  - **Pair A2 with A1** for a McMaster Moran-Mirabal-lab portfolio: notebook 1 = A1's 1D-CNN CV → glucose; notebook 2 = A2's tabular MIC prediction → demonstrating that the lab's two threads (biosensors + biomaterials) both yield ML portfolio projects with shared trainee González-Martínez as the human bridge between the labs and the data.

### Article 3: Shrinking Devices — Shape-Memory Polymer Fabrication of Micro- and Nanostructured Electrodes (Review / Umbrella Synthesis of the SMPE Platform)

- **Full citation:** Eduardo González-Martínez, Jose M. Moran-Mirabal*. "Shrinking Devices: Shape-Memory Polymer Fabrication of Micro-and Nanostructured Electrodes." *ChemPhysChem* **2024**, *25*, e202300535. DOI: 10.1002/cphc.202300535. Open Access (CC BY). **This is a Review article, not primary research** — manuscript received July 27, 2023; version of record online January 5, 2024. González-Martínez first author; **Moran-Mirabal sole corresponding**.

- **Problem in plain English:** Miniaturizing an electrochemical sensor shrinks its working-electrode footprint, which shrinks the electroactive surface area (ESA) and therefore the sensitivity. This review surveys roughly a decade of work — much of it from the Moran-Mirabal lab — that uses **shape-memory polymers (SMPs)**, chiefly pre-stressed polystyrene ("Shrinky-Dinks") and polyolefin shrink films, as a cheap bench-top route to fabricate **wrinkled / nano-roughened high-ESA gold electrodes (SMPEs)**. Thermal shrinking buckles a thin sputtered or electroless-deposited gold film into nanoscale-to-microscale wrinkles (film thickness sets the wrinkle wavelength), delivering ~6–32× ESA enhancement over a planar electrode of the same footprint. The review is effectively the **umbrella narrative tying together this professor's whole research program** — it explicitly cites Article 1 (ref [46], the *Angew. Chem.* nanoroughening paper) and Article 2 (ref [57b], the *ACS Appl. Bio Mater.* polydopamine paper) as steps within it.

- **ML task type:** **None as written** — this is a literature review with no model, no task, no labels, and no dataset of its own. ML reframes available to a portfolio project:
  - **(a) [Same as A1] 1D signal regression** — predict analyte concentration (glucose mM / Cu²⁺ μM) from cyclic-voltammetry I–V curves with a 1D-CNN. The review's recurring quantitative thread (sensitivity in µA/mM·cm², LODs) is exactly this.
  - **(b) [Same as A1] Tabular ESA regression** — predict ESA-enhancement fold from {substrate type, gold thickness, fabrication method, shrink temperature, pulse count}.
  - **(c) [Review-specific] Literature-mining meta-analysis** — hand-curate a small tabular dataset across the ~12–15 SMPE sensing studies the review compiles: {substrate, Au thickness, fabrication route, ESA-fold, analyte, LOD, sensitivity} → regression / ranking of which fabrication choices maximize sensitivity. This is the one genuinely *review-enabled* angle and the most distinctive portfolio framing.

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** N/A for the paper itself (review). For the reframes: 1D voltammograms (a); small tabular feature tables (b, c). Figures in the review are SEM micrographs + CV curves + ESA-vs-thickness plots reproduced-with-permission from ~57 cited works.
  - **Shape/size if stated:** No dataset. The literature-mining reframe would yield on the order of tens of rows (one per cited SMPE study / condition).
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** N/A — no data processing; it is a narrative synthesis.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** None in paper. For reframes: analyte concentration (a); ESA-fold (b); sensitivity / LOD ranking across fabrication choices (c).
  - **Units or label space:** Glucose mM / Cu²⁺ µM (a); ESA enhancement ×-fold (b); sensitivity µA/mM·cm² and LOD (c).

- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML model. The review's "models" are the physical ones it cites — CTE-mismatch wrinkling theory, Randles–Ševčík and Levich equations, gold-hydroxide-mediated glucose electro-oxidation.

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** None — review article.
  - **Size:** No dataset.

### Article 1: Deep Learning-Guided Discovery of an Antibiotic Targeting *Acinetobacter baumannii* (Abaucin — Genuine ML Paper)

- **Full citation:** Gary Liu, Denise B. Catacutan, Khushi Rathod, Kyle Swanson, Wengong Jin, Jody C. Mohammed, Anush Chiappino-Pepe, Saad A. Syed, Meghan Fragis, Kenneth Rachwalski, **Jakob Magolan**, Michael G. Surette, Brian K. Coombes, Tommi Jaakkola, Regina Barzilay, James J. Collins\*, Jonathan M. Stokes\*. "Deep learning-guided discovery of an antibiotic targeting *Acinetobacter baumannii*." *Nature Chemical Biology* **2023**, *19*, 1342–1350. DOI: 10.1038/s41589-023-01349-8. (Magolan 11th of 18 authors; **Collins + Stokes co-corresponding**.)

- **Problem in plain English:** *Acinetobacter baumannii* is a multidrug-resistant hospital ("nosocomial") Gram-negative pathogen for which conventional antibiotic screening has been unproductive. The team screened ~7,500 small molecules for growth inhibition of *A. baumannii* in vitro, trained a deep neural network on the resulting active/inactive labels, and used it to predict — in silico, across a public compound library — structurally new molecules likely to be active. This surfaced **abaucin**, a narrow-spectrum antibacterial that inhibits *A. baumannii* (through the lipoprotein-trafficking protein LolE) while sparing other pathogens and human gut/skin commensals, and it controlled an *A. baumannii* infection in a mouse wound model.

- **ML task type:** **Binary molecular-property classification** (supervised) — predict whether a molecule inhibits *A. baumannii* growth (active / inactive) from its chemical structure, then use the prediction score as a virtual-screening ranker over a public library and validate top, structurally-novel hits in vitro. **This is a genuine ML paper — no reframe needed.**

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** Molecular graph derived from SMILES (atoms = nodes, bonds = edges), processed by a directed message-passing neural network (Chemprop), **augmented with 200 RDKit-computed molecule-level features**. (Tanimoto similarity / t-SNE use 2,048-bit radius-2 Morgan fingerprints from RDKit.)
  - **Shape/size if stated:** Training set = **7,684 molecules** (off-patent drugs + Broad Institute screening compounds), labelled by growth inhibition at 50 µM; ~6.2% active (480 active / 7,204 inactive at the 1-SD cutoff). Prediction set = **Drug Repurposing Hub, 6,680 molecules**.
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** Plate growth normalized by interquartile mean, then binarized (active = growth ≥1 SD below dataset mean). SMILES → molecular graph via RDKit. 80/10/10 train/val/test with 10-fold cross-validation; ensemble of 10 models.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** Probability (0–1) that a molecule inhibits *A. baumannii* growth; thresholded (>0.2) and filtered by Tanimoto <0.3 to training actives to prioritize structurally-novel hits.
  - **Units or label space:** Binary {active, inactive}; continuous prediction score for ranking.

- **Model architecture (brief):** Directed message-passing neural network (Chemprop D-MPNN; 3 message-passing steps, hidden size 300, 2 feed-forward layers, dropout 0) + 200 RDKit molecule-level features concatenated to the learned embedding → feed-forward classifier; ensemble of 10. AUROC 0.792 ± 0.042 / AUPRC 0.337 ± 0.088 (RDKit-augmented; the non-augmented baseline was lower at AUROC 0.756 / AUPRC 0.266).

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** In-house *A. baumannii* growth-inhibition screen (7,684 molecules) + public Drug Repurposing Hub (prediction set).
  - **Size:** 7,684 training / 6,680 prediction.
  - **Source:** Broad Institute screening sub-libraries + off-patent drug collections; Drug Repurposing Hub (Broad).
  - **Public?** **Yes (effectively).** Training labels are in Supplementary Data 1 and "Source data are provided with this paper"; the Drug Repurposing Hub is public; resistant-mutant sequences (GenBank OP677864–7) + RNA-seq (GEO GSE214305) are deposited.
  - **Link:** Paper DOI 10.1038/s41589-023-01349-8; code at github.com/chemprop/chemprop + a cloned snapshot at github.com/GaryLiu152/chemprop_abaucin.

- **Reported headline metric:** Model **AUROC 0.792 ± 0.042 / AUPRC 0.337 ± 0.088** (10-model ensemble, RDKit-augmented); downstream, the screen → ML → validation pipeline discovered **abaucin** (MIC ~2 µg/mL vs *A. baumannii*; >128 µg/mL vs *E. coli* / *P. aeruginosa* / *S. aureus* — narrow spectrum), effective in a mouse wound-infection model.

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **The paper's own training set + Drug Repurposing Hub** (Supplementary Data 1 + Source Data + Broad's hub). — ~7,700 + 6,680 molecules. — Match: **close / exact** (it is the paper's data). — Access: **easy** (supplementary download + public hub).
  - **Stokes et al. 2020 *Cell* E. coli growth-inhibition dataset (halicin)** — ~2,335 molecules, public. — Match: **close** (same task family, different organism). — Access: **easy** (published supplementary).
  - **MoleculeNet — BBBP / Tox21 / BACE / HIV** (`moleculenet.org`). — thousands of molecules; standard binary molecular-classification benchmarks. — Match: **close (task) / analogy (target)**. — Access: **easy** via DeepChem or direct download.
  - **ChEMBL antibacterial bioactivity** (`ebi.ac.uk/chembl`). — large; filterable to *A. baumannii* / ESKAPE assays. — Match: **loose-to-close**. — Access: **medium** (API / SQL filtering).

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **easy** — Supplementary Data + Source Data + public Drug Repurposing Hub + open-source code (Chemprop + the abaucin snapshot repo). Among the most reproducible papers in the survey.

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - **Chemprop** (directed message-passing GNN for molecules) — the one major new component; pip-installable, well-documented, CLI + Python API.
  - **RDKit** — SMILES parsing, Morgan fingerprints, molecule-level descriptors (chemistry-specific tooling flagged as new for you).
  - **DeepChem** (optional) for MoleculeNet benchmarks.
  - Standard `scikit-learn` (logistic regression / random forest / XGBoost on Morgan fingerprints) as an accessible baseline that needs **none** of the GNN machinery — a good first step within your current skills before adding Chemprop.

- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** A clean, end-to-end **"ML for narrow-spectrum antibiotic discovery"** repo. Start with an interpretable baseline — RDKit Morgan fingerprints + scikit-learn/XGBoost classifier on the paper's 7,684-molecule training set — reproduce the reported AUROC/AUPRC, then add a Chemprop D-MPNN to match the paper's headline numbers and re-rank the Drug Repurposing Hub to recover abaucin among the top hits. Repo contents: Notebook 1 = data loading + EDA on the screen (class imbalance + t-SNE of chemical space reproducing Fig. 1d); Notebook 2 = fingerprint + sklearn baseline; Notebook 3 = Chemprop train + ensemble + held-out metrics; Notebook 4 = virtual screen of the hub + Tanimoto-novelty filter + "did we recover abaucin?" analysis. README headline: "Reproducing deep-learning antibiotic discovery — a from-scratch Chemprop pipeline that re-discovers abaucin from a public compound library." Recruiter-legible (drug discovery), fully public data + code, laptop/Colab-tractable.

### Article 2: Caffeine Blocks SREBP2-Induced Hepatic PCSK9 Expression to Enhance LDLR-Mediated Cholesterol Clearance (Molecular Pharmacology + Medicinal-Chemistry SAR — No ML)

- **Full citation:** Paul F. Lebeau, Jae Hyun Byun, Khrystyna Platko, Paul Saliba, Matthew Sguazzin, Melissa E. MacDonald, Guillaume Paré, Gregory R. Steinberg, Luke J. Janssen, Suleiman A. Igdoura, Mark A. Tarnopolsky, S. R. Wayne Chen, Nabil G. Seidah, **Jakob Magolan**, Richard C. Austin\*. "Caffeine blocks SREBP2-induced hepatic PCSK9 expression to enhance LDLR-mediated cholesterol clearance." *Nature Communications* **2022**, *13*, 770. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-022-28240-9. Open Access (CC BY). (Magolan 14th of 15 authors; **Austin sole corresponding**.)

- **Problem in plain English:** High blood LDL cholesterol drives cardiovascular disease; PCSK9 is a liver-secreted protein that degrades the LDL receptor (LDLR), so blocking PCSK9 raises LDLR and clears LDL (the basis of the blockbuster anti-PCSK9 antibody drugs). This paper shows that caffeine — at clinically relevant nanomolar-to-micromolar doses — raises hepatic ER Ca²⁺, which blocks activation of the transcription factor SREBP2, which in turn lowers PCSK9 transcription, raising LDLR and LDL uptake. The effect is confirmed in cultured hepatocytes, mice, and a small cohort of healthy human volunteers. Using structure–activity relationships (SAR), the team then designs **xanthine (caffeine) derivatives — MLRA-1812 and MLRA-1820 — that inhibit PCSK9 ~2× more potently than caffeine** without the neuro-excitatory effect. **Magolan's group designed and developed these derivatives.**

- **ML task type:** **None as written** — a wet-lab molecular-pharmacology + medicinal-chemistry paper. ML reframes available to a portfolio project:
  - **(a) QSAR on PCSK9 / cholesterol-pathway small molecules** — predict PCSK9-inhibition (or SREBP2-antagonism) potency from molecular structure. The paper's own compound set is tiny (~8 xanthines: caffeine, theobromine, paraxanthine, PSB603, 8CD, 8CC, MLRA-1812, MLRA-1820), so this must be anchored on **public ChEMBL PCSK9 bioactivity data** — a loose match, because small-molecule PCSK9-inhibitor data is sparse (PCSK9 is famously hard to drug with small molecules).
  - **(b) Xanthine-scaffold property prediction** — RDKit-fingerprint regression on a curated methylxanthine library against a well-populated target (e.g., adenosine-receptor ADORA2A affinity from ChEMBL) as a proxy — analogy only.
  - **(c) Shared tooling with A1** — the same RDKit / SMILES / fingerprint (+ optional Chemprop) QSAR stack, applied to a cardiovascular target instead of an antibacterial one.

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** None in the paper for ML. For reframes: SMILES / molecular graphs of xanthine derivatives + small-molecule PCSK9 modulators (ChEMBL). The paper's experimental modalities are immunoblots, qPCR, ELISA, immunofluorescence, DiI-LDL uptake.
  - **Shape/size if stated:** Paper's SAR series ≈ 8 compounds (far too few for ML); ChEMBL PCSK9-target bioactivity is the realistic training pool (loose).
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** Standard wet-lab quantification (ImageJ densitometry, qPCR ΔΔCt, ELISA standard curves). No cheminformatics pipeline.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** None in paper. For reframe (a): PCSK9-inhibition potency (IC₅₀ / pIC₅₀) or active/inactive from structure.
  - **Units or label space:** pIC₅₀ / IC₅₀ (nM–µM); or binary active/inactive.

- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML model. Methods are molecular-biology assays + organic synthesis (e.g., a one-step 8-substituted-xanthine synthesis for MLRA-1812 / MLRA-1820).

- **Dataset used in the paper:**

### Article 3: A Platform for Predicting Mechanism of Action from Bacterial Transcriptional Responses — Identifying an Unusual DNA Gyrase Inhibitor (Genuine ML / Data-Science Paper; Public Data + Code)

- **Full citation:** Shawn French, Amelia Bing Ya Guo, Michael J. Ellis, Julia P. Deisinger, Jarrod W. Johnson, Kenneth Rachwalski, Zoë A. Piquette, Telmah Lluka, Miranda Zary, Sineli Gamage, **Jakob Magolan**, Eric D. Brown\*. "A platform for predicting mechanism of action based on bacterial transcriptional responses identifies an unusual DNA gyrase inhibitor." *Cell Reports* **2024**, *43*, 114053. DOI: 10.1016/j.celrep.2024.114053. Open Access (CC BY-NC). (Magolan 11th of 12 authors; **Eric D. Brown sole corresponding / lead contact**.)

- **Problem in plain English:** When a new antibacterial molecule is found, figuring out HOW it works (its mechanism of action, MOA) is a major bottleneck. This paper builds a cheap, open-source platform — 3D-printed fluorescence imagers ("PFIboxes") that watch a genome-scale library of ~1,800 *E. coli* promoter-GFP reporter strains respond to >100 antibiotics over 24 h (5-min resolution). Each compound produces a transcriptional "fingerprint," and unsupervised ML (hierarchical clustering, t-SNE, correlation / network graphs) groups compounds by MOA. The platform flagged **metergoline** (a semi-synthetic ergot alkaloid) as behaving like a DNA-replication inhibitor; biochemical assays confirmed it inhibits DNA gyrase, and a potent synthesized analog (**MLEB-1934**, MIC 0.25 µg/mL) is active against quinolone-resistant MRSA via a novel allosteric gyrase pocket. **Magolan's role: he supervised the trainees who designed / synthesized the chemical analogs (medicinal chemistry) — he is not the ML / biology lead and not corresponding.**

- **ML task type:** **Unsupervised learning + MOA classification** (genuine ML, no reframe needed) — cluster / embed high-dimensional bacterial transcriptional fingerprints (compound × promoter-GFP expression time-series) to predict mechanism of action; methods: hierarchical clustering, t-SNE dimensionality reduction, correlation maps, network-connectivity graphs. (Naturally extends to *supervised* MOA classification using known antibiotics' labels with leave-one-out / held-out evaluation, and novelty / outlier detection for unrecognized mechanisms.)

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** Tabular / time-series transcriptional fingerprints — for each compound, the expression trajectories of ~1,800 *E. coli* promoter-GFP fusions imaged over 24 h at 5-min resolution (final-timepoint summation used as a per-promoter feature vector). Not molecular structures — this is **transcriptomics / phenotype data**.
  - **Shape/size if stated:** ~1,800 promoter-GFP strains × >100 antibiotics (in triplicate); 5-min temporal resolution over 24 h.
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** Image processing of PFIbox time-lapse → per-strain GFP expression curves → normalization → fingerprint vectors; hierarchical clustering + t-SNE in R (plus an interactive data explorer).

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** MOA grouping / label of an input compound (which known drug class / target its fingerprint resembles); for novel compounds, separation from known clusters flags novelty.
  - **Units or label space:** Antibiotic MOA classes / target categories (e.g., DNA replication, cell-wall, protein synthesis, folate, OM disruption); unsupervised cluster assignments + 2D/3D t-SNE coordinates.

- **Model architecture (brief):** Unsupervised hierarchical clustering + t-SNE (plus correlation / network graphs) on transcriptional fingerprints; MOA prediction framed as cluster proximity to labeled reference antibiotics (a nearest-reference / dereplication approach), explicitly contrasted with the supervised classifier ensembles used in prior work.

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** PFIbox *E. coli* promoter-GFP transcriptional-response dataset (ab-profiler).
  - **Size:** ~1,800 promoters × >100 antibiotics × time-series.
  - **Source:** Brown lab (McMaster); promoter-GFP library from Zaslaver et al.
  - **Public?** **Yes — fully.** All data and code on **Mendeley Data (https://doi.org/10.17632/kbp7pp2xpy.1)** + **GitHub (https://github.com/sfrench007/ab-profiler)** with an interactive data explorer and PFIbox build files.
  - **Link:** Mendeley DOI 10.17632/kbp7pp2xpy.1; GitHub sfrench007/ab-profiler; paper DOI 10.1016/j.celrep.2024.114053.

- **Reported headline metric:** Not a single ML score — the transcriptional fingerprints cluster antibiotics by known MOA, and as validation the platform correctly predicted metergoline's DNA-gyrase mechanism (confirmed by in vitro supercoiling assays); the synthesized analog MLEB-1934 reaches **MIC 0.25 µg/mL** and is active against quinolone-resistant MRSA.

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **This paper's own ab-profiler data + code** (Mendeley DOI 10.17632/kbp7pp2xpy.1 + GitHub). — ~1,800 promoters × >100 drugs. — Match: **close / exact**. — Access: **easy** (direct download + repo).
  - **MOA-by-transcriptomics RNA-seq datasets** (e.g., the cited efflux-deficient *E. coli* 37-antibiotic RNA-seq set; GEO). — dozens of compounds. — Match: **close** (same task, RNA-seq instead of GFP-reporter). — Access: **medium** (GEO).
  - **Connectivity Map / LINCS L1000** (`clue.io`). — ~1M+ compound expression signatures (human cells). — Match: **analogy** (MOA-by-expression, eukaryotic). — Access: **medium** (registration / API).
  - **EcoCyc / RegulonDB** *E. coli* gene-regulation resources. — Match: **analogy** (annotation, not training data). — Access: **easy**.

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **easy** — Mendeley Data DOI + GitHub repo with interactive explorer + open-source analysis code; one of the most reproducible papers in the survey (alongside A1).

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - **Mostly within your current skills:** `scikit-learn` (AgglomerativeClustering, t-SNE), `pandas` / `numpy`, plotting — vanilla unsupervised ML. The paper's pipeline is in **R**, so light R-reading or a Python re-implementation.
  - **New domain piece (not new ML tooling):** transcriptomics fingerprint preprocessing (promoter-GFP expression curves) — bioinformatics context, but the ML itself is standard sklearn.
  - **No chemistry-specific tooling** (no RDKit / GNN / SMILES) — unlike A1/A2, this article is *not* molecular ML, so it is actually closer to your existing supervised / unsupervised-ML comfort zone.

- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** A strong, self-contained **"predicting antibiotic mechanism of action from transcriptional fingerprints"** repo on the paper's public ab-profiler data. Reproduce the unsupervised pipeline (hierarchical clustering + t-SNE of compound fingerprints, recovering the known-MOA groupings) in Python, then add a **supervised MOA classifier** (logistic regression / random forest / small MLP) with leave-one-compound-out evaluation, plus a **novelty-detection** module (isolation forest / one-class SVM) that re-flags metergoline as an "unusual" hit. README headline: "Predicting antibiotic mechanism of action from bacterial transcriptional fingerprints — reproducing and extending the ab-profiler platform (clustering + supervised MOA classification + novelty detection)." Fully public data + code, laptop-tractable, recruiter-legible (antibiotic resistance / drug discovery), and — unlike A1/A2 — needs **no chemistry-specific tooling**, so it is the most directly within-skillset ML project of Magolan's three articles.

### Article 1: Core-Shell Ir@TiO₂ Nanoparticles via Hydrogen Treatment as Acidic Oxygen Evolution Reaction Catalysts (Experimental Electrocatalysis — No ML)

- **Full citation:** Jihyeon Park, Eric Liu, Shayan Angizi, Ahmed Abdellah, Ecem Yelekli Kirici, Drew Higgins\*. "Formation of Core-Shell Ir@TiO₂ Nanoparticles through Hydrogen Treatment as Acidic Oxygen Evolution Reaction Catalysts." *Advanced Functional Materials* **2024**, *34*, 2408848. DOI: 10.1002/adfm.202408848. Open Access (CC BY). (Higgins sole corresponding + last author.)

- **Problem in plain English:** Green hydrogen made by splitting water in acidic PEM electrolyzers is bottlenecked by the anode's oxygen evolution reaction (OER), which is slow and corrosive and currently needs scarce, expensive iridium catalysts that also degrade. This paper synthesizes a **core-shell Ir@TiO₂ nanoparticle** — a durable TiO₂ core with a thin Ir-rich shell — using a polyol method + urea reduction + annealing in H₂, which drives Ir to migrate to the surface (watched live by in situ environmental TEM). The result uses far less Ir while staying active and far more stable (overpotential 305 mV at 10 mA cm⁻², >600 h stability, ~3× the "S-number" durability metric of commercial IrOₓ, and ~3× the Ir-mass-normalized activity).

- **ML task type:** **None as written** — a pure experimental materials-synthesis / electrocatalysis paper. ML reframes available to a portfolio project (all in the electrocatalyst-discovery space, where public ML datasets are strong):
  - **(a) OER catalyst activity / adsorption-energy prediction** on oxide surfaces using **Open Catalyst Project OC22** (built specifically for oxide OER) — predict adsorption / relaxed energies (a proxy for OER overpotential) from surface structure with a GNN.
  - **(b) Tabular composition → activity regression** — predict OER overpotential / stability from catalyst descriptors (composition, loading, support) using a literature-mined OER dataset + matminer / pymatgen featurization + sklearn / XGBoost (more within current skills than the GNN route).
  - **(c) In-situ TEM image analysis** — segment / quantify the core-shell Ir-segregation transition from the E-TEM image series (small, non-public dataset — teaching demo only).

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** None in the paper for ML. For reframes: 3D crystal / surface structures (OC22; atomic graphs / crystal structures — flagged as new tooling for you) (a); tabular catalyst descriptors (b); TEM images (c). The paper's experimental modalities are TEM / HAADF-STEM + in situ E-TEM, XRD, EDX, XPS, ICP-OES, and electrochemistry (CV, chronoamperometry, S-number).
  - **Shape/size if stated:** OC22 is large (~tens of thousands of DFT relaxations) — heavy. The paper studies a handful of catalyst variants (Core-shell, Mixed, Amorphous, commercial IrOₓ).
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** Standard materials characterization; no cheminformatics / ML pipeline.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** None in paper. For reframes: adsorption / relaxed energy or OER overpotential (regression) (a/b); core-shell vs mixed morphology label (c).
  - **Units or label space:** Energy (eV) / overpotential (mV) / activity (A g⁻¹) regression; or morphology class.

- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML model. The paper's "models" are physical / electrochemical (S-number durability metric, OER kinetics, in situ E-TEM-observed Ir migration).

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** In-house experimental dataset (synthesis + characterization of Ir@TiO₂ variants).
  - **Size:** A handful of catalyst samples + characterization series; not an ML dataset.
  - **Source:** Higgins lab (McMaster Chemical Engineering); microscopy at CCEM.
  - **Public?** **No.** Data "available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request." No code, no deposit.
  - **Link:** Paper DOI 10.1002/adfm.202408848; (for a reframe: Open Catalyst OC22, Materials Project, Catalysis-Hub).

- **Reported headline metric:** **Overpotential 305 mV @ 10 mA cm⁻²; >600 h stability (~0.1 mV h⁻¹ degradation); S-number 3.34 × 10⁶ (vs 1.02 × 10⁶ for commercial IrOₓ); Ir-mass-normalized activity 1,880 A g⁻¹ @ 1.7 V vs RHE (vs 624 A g⁻¹ for IrOₓ).**

### Article 2: Pd/PdHₓ Phase Conversion in Electrochemical CO₂ Reduction via In-Situ TEM + Diffraction (Experimental + DFT / Microkinetics; Public Theory Code; No ML)

- **Full citation:** Ahmed M. Abdellah, Fatma Ismail, Oliver W. Siig, Jie Yang, Carmen M. Andrei, Liza-Anastasia DiCecco, Amirhossein Rakhsha, Kholoud E. Salem, Kathryn Grandfield, Nabil Bassim, Robert Black, Georg Kastlunger\*, Leyla Soleymani, Drew Higgins\*. "Impact of palladium/palladium hydride conversion on electrochemical CO₂ reduction via in-situ transmission electron microscopy and diffraction." *Nature Communications* **2024**, *15*, 938. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-45096-3. Open Access. (First author Abdellah is a Higgins-lab trainee; **Higgins co-corresponding with Georg Kastlunger (DTU, theory)**; "A.A. and D.H. conceived the research.")

- **Problem in plain English:** Electrochemically reducing CO₂ into fuels / chemicals needs catalysts whose behavior under real reaction conditions is understood. Palladium makes formate at low overpotentials and CO/H₂ at high overpotentials, while transforming between metallic Pd and palladium-hydride (PdHₓ) phases — a change that has been hard to watch live. Using **in-situ liquid-phase TEM + select-area electron diffraction**, the team tracks Pd particles changing shape and phase (Pd ↔ PdHₓ, with lattice expansion) as the electrode potential changes, and pairs this with **constant-potential DFT + microkinetic modeling**. The key finding: the selectivity switch from formate to CO/H₂ is driven by potential-dependent reaction energetics, not by the morphology / phase changes; surface-bound *H (whose abundance rises with overpotential) is essential for formate.

- **ML task type:** **None as written** — experimental in-situ microscopy + DFT / microkinetic modeling. ML reframes (CO₂R electrocatalysis is squarely in the Open Catalyst wheelhouse):
  - **(a) Adsorption-energy / selectivity prediction with Open Catalyst OC20** — predict binding energies of CO₂R / HER intermediates (*CO, *H, *OCHO/*HCOO, *COOH) on metal / Pd surfaces via GNN; map to a formate-vs-CO/H₂ selectivity descriptor. **Very close domain match** (OC20 was built for exactly this), and the paper's **public DFT data / code** (github.com/CatTheoryDTU/PdH__formate_vs_CO) can serve as a small validation / comparison set.
  - **(b) Diffraction-pattern → phase classification (most within-skillset)** — classify Pd vs α/β-PdHₓ phase from SAD radial-intensity profiles / lattice spacing (a clean 1D-signal classification; vanilla sklearn / 1D-CNN). The paper's experimental data isn't public, so this would use simulated / curated diffraction profiles.
  - **(c) DFT → microkinetics ML surrogate** — learn a fast surrogate from the public DTU DFT free energies to predict selectivity vs potential.

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** None for ML in the paper. For reframes: 3D metal-surface structures + adsorbates (OC20; crystal / graph — new tooling) (a); 1D SAD radial-intensity / diffraction profiles (b); tabular DFT free energies (c). Paper's modalities: in-situ LP-(S)TEM images, SAD / EDX, electrochemistry (CV, chronoamperometry, Faradaic efficiency), constant-potential DFT (ASE + BEEF-vdW).
  - **Shape/size if stated:** Public DTU DFT dataset is small / specialized (Pd/PdHₓ formate-vs-CO energetics); OC20 is large (~millions of relaxations — heavy).
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** TEM image / diffraction processing (radial intensity profiles), constant-potential DFT energy corrections; no ML pipeline.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** None in paper. Reframes: adsorption energy / selectivity descriptor (a, c); Pd vs PdHₓ phase label (b).
  - **Units or label space:** Energy (eV) regression / selectivity (Faradaic efficiency %); or phase class (Pd / α-PdHₓ / β-PdHₓ).

- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML. Physical / computational: constant-potential DFT (ASE, BEEF-vdW) + microkinetic modeling + in-situ TEM/SAD phase analysis.

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** In-house in-situ LP-TEM / SAD + electrochemistry dataset (experimental) + DTU constant-potential DFT dataset (theory).
  - **Size:** A handful of Pd/PdHₓ conditions / potentials (experimental); a focused DFT set (theory).
  - **Source:** Higgins lab (McMaster ChemEng) experimental + CCEM microscopy; Kastlunger / CatTheory (DTU) DFT.
  - **Public?** **Partial.** Experimental data "available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request"; **theoretical data + analysis is PUBLIC on GitHub (CatTheoryDTU/PdH__formate_vs_CO)**.
  - **Link:** Paper DOI 10.1038/s41467-024-45096-3; theory github.com/CatTheoryDTU/PdH__formate_vs_CO; (reframe: Open Catalyst OC20).

- **Reported headline metric:** Not ML — selectivity shifts from near-exclusive formate at −0.2 V vs RHE to CO + H₂ at −0.5 V vs RHE; DFT + microkinetics attribute the shift to potential-dependent reaction energetics (the CO pathway benefits more from increased cathodic potential), not to PdHₓ lattice expansion; *H intercalation is essential for formate.

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **Open Catalyst OC20** (`opencatalystproject.org`). — millions of DFT adsorption / relaxation calcs incl. CO₂R / HER intermediates on metals. — Match: **close (domain)**. — Access: **medium-hard** (fairchem + torch-geometric; large; GPU). [reframe a]
  - **The paper's own DTU DFT data + code** (github.com/CatTheoryDTU/PdH__formate_vs_CO). — focused Pd/PdHₓ energetics. — Match: **close / exact (theory half)**. — Access: **easy** (public GitHub). [reframe c]
  - **Materials Project / Catalysis-Hub** — Pd / PdHₓ structures + surface-reaction energies. — Match: **analogy-to-close**. — Access: **easy (MP) / medium (Catalysis-Hub)**.
  - **Simulated SAD / XRD diffraction profiles** (pymatgen / ASE generated) for Pd vs PdHₓ. — Match: **analogy** (for the phase-classification reframe). — Access: **easy** (generate yourself). [reframe b]

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **medium** — experimental data is author-request only, but the **theory data + analysis code is public on GitHub**, and the close-match Open Catalyst OC20 is available (medium-hard). Better than A1 (which had no public component).

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - For the close-match route: `fairchem` (Open Catalyst) + `torch-geometric` GNNs + `pymatgen` / `ASE` (crystal-structure + atomistic tooling — new chemistry-specific tooling).
  - For the within-skillset route: vanilla `scikit-learn` / 1D-CNN (PyTorch) for diffraction-profile phase classification; `pandas` + `sklearn` for a DFT→selectivity surrogate on the public DTU data.
  - `ASE` to read the public DTU DFT dataset.

README headline: "Data-driven CO₂-reduction catalysis — phase classification from diffraction + adsorption-energy→selectivity modeling, motivated by in-situ Pd/PdHₓ studies." ### Article 1: Analysing Antimicrobial-Resistance Mobility Patterns Across >8000 Bacterial Species (Large-Scale AMR Genomics; Public Data + Code; Statistics In-Paper, Clean ML Reframe)

- **Full citation:** Baofeng Jia, Brian P. Alcock, Amogelang R. Raphenya, Jason Spence, Finlay Maguire, Robert G. Beiko, **Andrew G. McArthur**, Claire Bertelli, Fiona S.L. Brinkman\*. "Analysing antimicrobial resistance mobility patterns using a diverse dataset of over 8000 bacterial species." **bioRxiv preprint**, posted March 5, 2026. DOI: 10.64898/2026.03.03.709307. CC-BY-NC. (**Not yet peer-reviewed**; corresponding author Fiona Brinkman, SFU; McArthur 7th of 9, CARD/RGI provider + co-funder.)

- **Problem in plain English:** Which antibiotic-resistance (AMR) genes are most likely to *spread* between bacteria? Genes carried on mobile DNA (plasmids, genomic islands) jump between organisms and drive the spread of resistance, while chromosomal genes stay put. This study scans **>8000 bacterial species (~39,000 genomes) from NCBI RefSeq**, identifies AMR genes with **RGI / CARD**, predicts mobile chromosomal regions with **IslandViewer 4** (plus plasmid annotations), and statistically tests whether AMR genes sit in mobile vs non-mobile DNA. Finding: AMR genes are overall enriched in mobile regions (odds ratio ~3), but mobility varies sharply by resistance *mechanism* and bacterial cell-envelope type — specialized mechanisms are more mobile ("ecological public goods"). The paper explicitly aims to "lay the groundwork for **predictive models** of AMR-gene mobility."

- **ML task type:** **None in-paper (statistical analysis: Fisher's exact tests + odds ratios)** — but the paper sets up a textbook-clean supervised reframe: **binary classification — predict whether an AMR gene is "mobile" (plasmid / genomic-island) vs "chromosomal / non-mobile"** from its features (resistance mechanism, drug class / ARO ontology term, bacterial taxonomy + cell-envelope type, optionally gene / protein sequence). Extensions: multi-class location (plasmid / GI / non-GI chromosome), or per-mechanism mobility-risk regression.

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** Tabular AMR-gene features (resistance mechanism, drug class, CARD ARO term, host taxonomy, monoderm / diderm envelope) + optionally protein / DNA sequence of the AMR gene (for a sequence-model reframe, e.g., ESM-2). Not molecular structures.
  - **Shape/size if stated:** **499,319 AMR determinants** identified among 118,144,860 genes across **39,089 accessions (29,793 chromosomal + 9,295 plasmid)**, >8000 species, 45 phyla — a large labelled tabular dataset (with provided sampling-bias-corrected subsets).
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** RGI v6.0.1 + CARD v3.2.9 (`--input_type contig`) for AMR genes; IslandViewer 4 for genomic islands; PSORTdb v4.0 for envelope type; each AMR gene classified into {non-GI chromosome, genomic island, plasmid}; dataset-reduction subsets to correct RefSeq sampling bias.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** None in-paper. Reframe: mobility label (mobile vs chromosomal) or 3-class location; per-mechanism mobility propensity.
  - **Units or label space:** Binary {mobile, non-mobile} / 3-class {plasmid, GI, non-GI chromosome}; or odds-ratio-style mobility score.

- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML model — Fisher's exact tests + odds ratios in R (with ggplot2 visualization). The reframe would be vanilla `scikit-learn` / XGBoost (tabular) and optionally ESM-2 (sequence).

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** RefSeq-derived AMR-gene mobility dataset (RGI / CARD + IslandViewer 4).
  - **Size:** ~39,000 genomes / 499,319 AMR determinants / >8000 species.
  - **Source:** NCBI RefSeq (release 223, 23 May 2024); CARD / RGI; IslandViewer 4; PSORTdb.
  - **Public?** **Yes — fully.** Complete dataset + analysis code on **Open Science Framework (OSF), DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/WE3TX**. Underlying resources (RefSeq, CARD, IslandViewer) are public.
  - **Link:** OSF DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/WE3TX; preprint DOI 10.64898/2026.03.03.709307; CARD at card.mcmaster.ca.

- **Reported headline metric:** Not ML — AMR genes enriched in mobile regions overall (**OR ≈ 3.01, p < 0.001**), with strong heterogeneity by mechanism and envelope type; functionally specialized mechanisms more mobile.

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **This paper's own OSF dataset + code** (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/WE3TX). — ~39k genomes / 499k AMR determinants, labelled by location + mechanism. — Match: **close / exact**. — Access: **easy** (OSF download + code). [primary reframe target]
  - **CARD + CARD Prevalence / Resistomes & Variants** (card.mcmaster.ca). — curated AMR genes + genomic prevalence; CARD 2023 explicitly supports ML / resistome prediction. — Match: **close**. — Access: **easy-medium** (download / RGI).
  - **NCBI Pathogen Detection / RefSeq** + **PLSDB (plasmid database)** + **IslandViewer**. — genomes, plasmids, mobile elements for building / extending the dataset. — Match: **close-to-analogy**. — Access: **medium** (APIs / downloads).
  - **MOB-suite / mobileOG-db** for mobility annotation. — Match: **analogy** (alternative mobility labels). — Access: **easy**.

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **easy** — full dataset + analysis code on OSF, built on public RefSeq / CARD / IslandViewer. Among the most reproducible papers in the survey (alongside Doxey's and Magolan A1/A3).

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - **Within current skills (ML):** `scikit-learn` / `XGBoost` + `pandas` for tabular mobility classification; optionally `ESM-2` / a protein-language model for a sequence→mobility reframe (a transformer, within reach).
  - **New domain pieces (bioinformatics, not ML):** `RGI` / CARD ontology (ARO), IslandViewer / plasmid concepts, basic genome handling — needed to understand features, but the analysis-ready OSF tables let you skip running the pipelines.

- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** A clean, recruiter-legible **"predicting antimicrobial-resistance gene mobility"** repo on the paper's public OSF data. Train a tabular classifier (sklearn / XGBoost) to predict mobile-vs-chromosomal from {resistance mechanism, drug class, ARO term, host taxonomy, envelope type}, with held-out evaluation + SHAP feature importance (recovering the paper's "specialized mechanisms are more mobile" finding); optionally add an ESM-2 sequence model on the AMR-gene proteins and compare. README headline: "Predicting AMR-gene mobility from resistance mechanism and genomic context — a reproducible classifier on 8000+ bacterial species (CARD/RGI + IslandViewer), turning a published statistical analysis into a predictive model." This realizes the paper's own stated goal (predictive AMR-mobility models), uses fully public data + code, is laptop-tractable, and sits in the globally hot AMR space — one of the strongest ML-portfolio sources in the survey.

### Article 2: Evaluating RGI Over- and Underprediction to Improve AMR-Gene Detection Accuracy (CARD/RGI Curation QA — McArthur-Corresponding; No ML)

- **Full citation:** Karyn M. Mukiri, Brian P. Alcock, Amogelang R. Raphenya, Andrew G. McArthur\*. "Increasing the predictive accuracy of the Resistance Gene Identifier by evaluating antimicrobial resistance gene over- and underprediction." **bioRxiv preprint**, posted December 15, 2025. DOI: 10.64898/2025.12.11.693720. CC-BY. (**Not yet peer-reviewed**; **McArthur sole corresponding** — his own lab, trainee Karyn Mukiri first author; AGM holds McMaster's **David Braley Chair in Computational Biology**.)

- **Problem in plain English:** Tools that read a bacterial genome and predict its antibiotic-resistance genes — here, McArthur's **RGI**, powered by the **CARD** database — are only as good as their hand-curated detection thresholds. RGI calls a gene "resistant" when a sequence match scores above a manually set **bit-score cutoff**; cutoffs set too low cause false positives (overprediction), too high cause false negatives (underprediction). This study systematically audits all ~3,900 CARD detection models — using a "percent-positive" alignment metric (70% cutoff) to flag likely Type I / Type II curation errors across 56.7M annotations in CARD's Resistomes-&-Variants dataset. Findings: RGI rarely overpredicts (5/3,900 models with >5% false-positive rate) but somewhat underpredicts (739/3,900 with >5% false-negative rate), with **β-lactamases** the main underpredictors (a systemic curation gap) and **efflux** families the main overpredictors; overall RGI is highly reliable (F1 ≈ 99.98%). Recommends per-subfamily cutoffs + phylogenetic curation.

- **ML task type:** **None in-paper (bioinformatics evaluation: BLAST / DIAMOND alignment + percent-positive thresholds + confusion-matrix metrics + phylogenetics).** ML reframes:
  - **(a) Learned cutoff calibration** — predict an optimal per-model / per-family detection cutoff (regression) that minimizes over / under-prediction, replacing blanket hand-curated cutoffs. Tabular ML on alignment features (bit-score, percent identity, percent positive, family size).
  - **(b) ML-based ARG detection vs BLAST** — train a protein-language-model (ESM-2) classifier to call the AMR gene / family from sequence and compare against RGI's alignment-based calls (the "deep-learning ARG prediction" angle, e.g., DeepARG).
  - **(c) Mis-curation risk classifier** — predict which CARD models / families are prone to Type I / II error from their features (a meta-model on the paper's audit output).

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** Tabular alignment features per annotation (bit-score, percent identity, percent positive, AMR gene family / ARO, model type) + AMR protein sequences (for the ESM-2 reframe). Not molecular structures.
  - **Shape/size if stated:** 3,900 CARD detection models audited; **56,708,241 RGI annotations** re-analyzed (mCARD-R); CARD v4.0.1 = 8,582 ontology terms + 6,442 reference sequences.
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** Re-analysis of CARD-R v3.1.0 with percent-positive recomputed; 70% percent-positive cutoff to label False Strict (FP) / False Loose (FN); per-family stratification; multiple-sequence alignments + phylogenetics.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** None in-paper. Reframes: optimal cutoff (regression) (a); AMR gene / family from sequence (classification) (b); mis-curation risk per model (c).
  - **Units or label space:** Bit-score cutoff (regression); AMR family / ARO class; over / under-prediction risk.

- **Model architecture (brief):** No ML — alignment (BLAST / DIAMOND) + percent-positive thresholding + confusion-matrix evaluation + phylogenetic trees.

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** CARD + CARD Resistomes & Variants (CARD-R) re-analysis (mCARD-R).
  - **Size:** 3,900 models / 56.7M annotations.
  - **Source:** CARD / RGI (McArthur lab, McMaster).
  - **Public?** **Partial.** RGI code public on GitHub (github.com/arpcard/rgi); CARD + CARD-R public (card.mcmaster.ca); supplementary data on bioRxiv. No dedicated OSF deposit for this study's analysis (contrast A1).
  - **Link:** RGI github.com/arpcard/rgi; CARD card.mcmaster.ca; preprint DOI 10.64898/2025.12.11.693720.

- **Reported headline metric:** Not ML — overprediction in 5/3,900 models (>5% FPR), underprediction in 739/3,900 (>5% FNR); reframed as a confusion matrix over 56.7M annotations, RGI shows ~100% accuracy / precision, 99.96% recall, F1 ≈ 99.98%.

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **CARD + CARD-R + RGI** (card.mcmaster.ca, github.com/arpcard/rgi). — the paper's own resources. — Match: **close**. — Access: **easy-medium** (download + RGI). [reframes a/c]
  - **NCBI Pathogen Detection Reference Gene Catalog + ResFinder** — alternative curated ARG databases for cross-tool comparison. — Match: **close**. — Access: **easy-medium**.
  - **DeepARG / public ARG-labelled protein sets** — for the ESM-2 sequence-classifier reframe. — Match: **close (task)**. — Access: **easy-medium**.
  - **A1's OSF dataset** (10.17605/OSF.IO/WE3TX) — pairs naturally (same CARD/RGI ecosystem). — Match: **close**. — Access: **easy**.

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **medium** — RGI code + CARD / CARD-R are public and supplementary data is on bioRxiv, but there's no single packaged ML-ready dataset for this study (you assemble it from CARD-R + RGI output); less turnkey than A1's OSF deposit.

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - ML reframe: `scikit-learn` / `XGBoost` (tabular cutoff calibration / risk classifier) + optionally `ESM-2` (sequence) — within skills / reach.
  - Domain: RGI / CARD ontology, BLAST / DIAMOND alignment outputs, percent-positive — bioinformatics context (shared with A1).

- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** A focused **"learning better AMR-gene detection thresholds"** repo: use CARD / RGI + CARD-R to train a model that predicts per-family optimal cutoffs (or an ESM-2 classifier that calls the AMR gene family from sequence) and benchmark over / under-prediction against RGI's hand-curated cutoffs, reproducing the paper's β-lactamase-underprediction finding. Best **paired with A1** into a single **"ML for the CARD/RGI AMR ecosystem"** portfolio (A1 = predict gene mobility; A2 = predict / calibrate gene detection). README headline: "Calibrating antimicrobial-resistance gene detection with ML — learned cutoffs and sequence models vs hand-curated CARD/RGI thresholds." Narrower and more specialist than A1, but a credible AMR-bioinformatics ML project.

### Article 3: Predicting Severe COVID-19 from Clinical + SARS-CoV-2 Genomic Features with Supervised ML (Genuine ML Paper — Peer-Reviewed)

- **Full citation:** Kuganya Nirmalarajah, Patryk Aftanas, … **Andrew G. McArthur**, … Venkata R. Duvvuri\*, Samira Mubareka\*. "Identification of patient demographic, clinical, and SARS-CoV-2 genomic factors associated with severe COVID-19 using supervised machine learning: a retrospective multicenter study." *BMC Infectious Diseases* **2025**, *25*, 132. DOI: 10.1186/s12879-025-10450-3. Open Access (CC BY). (**Peer-reviewed, not a preprint**; co-corresponding Duvvuri (OAHPP) + Mubareka (Sunnybrook); **McArthur middle author — data acquisition / viral-genomics contribution**, not corresponding.)

- **Problem in plain English:** What makes a COVID-19 patient end up hospitalized — their own characteristics (age, comorbidities, symptoms) or the genetics of the SARS-CoV-2 virus they caught? The team assembled a rare dataset of **617 Greater-Toronto-Area patients with BOTH detailed clinical records AND the whole viral genome**, then trained **supervised ML models to predict hospitalization** from patient demographics + symptoms + comorbidities + viral genomic signatures (amino-acid sequences of spike, nucleocapsid, ORF3a, ORF8). Using **SHAP** to interpret the models, they found clinical features (vascular disease, pulmonary disease, fever, age) dominate; **viral genomic features add little predictive power**. Conclusion: clinical data > viral genomics for predicting COVID severity.

- **ML task type:** **Supervised binary classification (genuine ML, no reframe needed)** — predict hospitalization (inpatient vs outpatient) from integrated clinical + viral-genomic features, with SHAP feature-importance interpretation. Models: logistic regression, LR-LASSO, gradient-boosting machines (GBM), XGBoost, + a stacked meta-model.

- **Input representation:**
  - **Modality:** Tabular clinical features (demographics, one-hot symptoms, comorbidities) + viral-genomic features (amino-acid sequences of spike / N / ORF3a / ORF8 via Nextclade; mutation annotations via CoVEffect). Mixed tabular + sequence-derived.
  - **Shape/size if stated:** **617 patients** (311 inpatient / 306 outpatient — ~50/50, balanced); whole-genome SARS-CoV-2 + matched clinical records.
  - **Preprocessing in the paper:** Genomes → amino-acid sequences per polypeptide (Nextclade); functional regions selected (NTD, RBD, S1/S2 cleavage, ORF3a, ORF8, N); symptoms aggregated / one-hot; binary hospitalization label.

- **Output representation:**
  - **What the model predicts:** Hospitalization (binary: inpatient / outpatient).
  - **Units or label space:** Binary class + SHAP feature attributions.

- **Model architecture (brief):** scikit-learn 1.3.2 + XGBoost 2.0.3 — LR, LR-LASSO, GBM, XGBoost + a stacked meta-model (LR-LASSO meta-learner for regularization); SHAP 0.44.1 for interpretation; evaluated by accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUROC.

- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - **Name:** RISC-CoV / COVIDEO linked clinical + viral-genomic cohort (GTA, 11 institutions, Mar 2020–Apr 2022).
  - **Size:** 617 patients with matched clinical + whole-genome data.
  - **Source:** Greater Toronto Area healthcare institutions; sequencing per Kotwa / Nasir / Quick protocols.
  - **Public?** **Partial.** SARS-CoV-2 **genomes are public on GISAID** (accessions in Additional File 2); **clinical data is RESTRICTED** (de-identified, available on request + ethics approval). Code not explicitly released.
  - **Link:** Paper DOI 10.1186/s12879-025-10450-3; genomes via GISAID.

- **Reported headline metric:** Clinical features outperformed viral-genomic features for predicting hospitalization (SHAP: vascular disease, pulmonary disease, fever, age most important); viral-genomic-only models had limited utility; pre-VOC variants weakly associated with hospitalization. (Per-model accuracy / F1 / AUROC reported in-paper; headline = clinical >> genomic.)

- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this:**
  - **GISAID SARS-CoV-2 genomes** (gisaid.org; the paper's own accessions). — millions of genomes. — Match: **close (genomic half)**. — Access: **medium** (free registration).
  - **Public COVID-19 clinical-outcome datasets** (Kaggle COVID severity sets, Mexico open COVID dataset, CDC). — clinical → severity. — Match: **close (task) / analogy (cohort)**. — Access: **easy**.
  - **ISARIC / N3C** large COVID clinical cohorts. — Match: **close**. — Access: **hard** (controlled access).
  - **Nextclade / CoVEffect** for genomic feature extraction (reproduce the pipeline). — Access: **easy** (open tools).

- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **medium-hard** — genomes are public on GISAID (registration), but the linked **clinical data is restricted** (request + multi-center ethics approval) and code isn't clearly released; the clinical+genomic *linkage* (the paper's key asset) is not openly downloadable.

- **Tooling I would need to learn:**
  - **Almost entirely within current skills:** scikit-learn + XGBoost + SHAP + pandas (stacked classifiers + interpretable ML) — the most standard-ML paper of McArthur's three.
  - **Light domain pieces:** Nextclade / CoVEffect to turn genomes into amino-acid / mutation features (open, lightweight bioinformatics).

- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like:** A clean, recruiter-legible **"interpretable ML for COVID-19 severity from clinical + viral-genomic features"** repo. Because the paper's linked clinical data is restricted, reproduce the *methodology* on a public COVID clinical-outcome dataset (Kaggle / Mexico / CDC) + GISAID genomic features: train LR / GBM / XGBoost + a stacked meta-model to predict severity, run SHAP, and test the paper's central question — do viral-genomic features add predictive value over clinical features? README headline: "Does the virus's genome predict COVID severity? An interpretable clinical-vs-genomic ML study (XGBoost + SHAP), reproducing Nirmalarajah et al. 2025 on public data." Genuine ML, laptop-tractable, standard tooling, hot clinical-ML topic — though the exact dataset linkage isn't public.

### Summary for this professor

- **Common thread across their work (3 articles):** Antimicrobial-resistance & infectious-disease bioinformatics, anchored by McArthur's **CARD / RGI** tooling and pathogen genomics — A1 (Brinkman-led) maps AMR-gene mobility across >8000 bacterial species via CARD/RGI; A2 (McArthur-corresponding, own lab) audits CARD/RGI's AMR-gene-detection accuracy; A3 (Mubareka / Duvvuri-led) uses supervised ML + SHAP to predict COVID-19 severity from clinical + SARS-CoV-2 genomic features. McArthur is the genomics / tooling contributor (corresponding only on A2).

- **Biggest obstacle for me to replicate their work publicly:** **Mixed data access + peripheral authorship on 2 of 3** — A1's data is fully public (OSF), but A2's ML-ready set is unpackaged and A3's clinical data is restricted (genomes public on GISAID); and McArthur is corresponding only on A2, contributing genomics / tools elsewhere.
- **Skills I would gain by working with them:**
  - AMR + infectious-disease bioinformatics (CARD / RGI / ARO, resistome analysis, viral genomics, Nextclade).
  - Interpretable supervised ML (sklearn / XGBoost, stacking, SHAP) on tabular + sequence-derived features.
  - Large-scale pathogen-genome data handling + clinical-genomic data integration.
  - Public-health / AMR / pandemic-surveillance domain context.
