### Article 1: Microplastic Transmission Through Microfiltration Membranes (Fluorescence Measurement)

- **Full citation:** Ryan J. LaRue, Ashleigh Warren, David R. Latulippe. "Evaluation of microplastic particle transmission in a microfiltration process using fluorescence measurements: Effect of pore size and flux." *Journal of Membrane Science* **708** (2024) 123045. (Open access, CC BY-NC-ND.)
- **Problem in plain English:** Microplastics (MPs) escape into waterways largely through wastewater-treatment-plant effluent, and membrane filtration is proposed to capture them — but it is poorly understood how irregularly-shaped MPs (the kind found in real wastewater, ~10 µm) actually pass through membranes. The authors make irregular fluorescent MPs by ball-milling/sieving fluorescent polyethylene spheres, then measure how many transmit through two Durapore PVDF microfiltration membranes (0.45 µm and 5 µm pore sizes) as a function of pore size and permeate flux, quantifying MP amounts via a fluorescence plate reader.
- **ML task type:** **None — this is a wet-lab experimental separations paper, not an ML paper.** No model is trained. (Reframe below is my construction.)
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: physical filtration experiments. Quantification via (i) fluorescence intensity (a.u.) on a microplate reader, (ii) FBRM chord-length distributions, (iii) optical-microscopy + confocal (CLSM) image stacks analyzed in ImageJ/Fiji.
  - Shape/size if stated: irregular M/S-MPs ~10 µm mean Feret diameter (range 2.6–48.2 µm), aspect ratio 1.8 ± 0.7; experiments at fluxes 250–8,000 LMH; all conditions in triplicate.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: milling/sieving (25 µm aperture) to make irregular MPs; Tween-20 dispersion + sonication; ImageJ Feret-diameter measurement; FBRM chord-length binning; CLSM z-stacks (Nile Red membrane stain vs FITC MP signal).
- **Output representation:**
  - What is measured (not "predicted"): permeate fluorescence intensity (proxy for MP concentration), particle-size/chord-length distributions in permeate vs feed, and an approximate rejection coefficient R₀.
  - Units or label space: arbitrary fluorescence units (a.u.); particle sizes in µm; rejection ≈ 100 % for the 0.45 µm membrane, ≈ 99 % for the 5 µm membrane.
- **Model architecture (brief):** None. (A compressible-cake fouling model is fit by least-squares to pressure-vs-time data — classical, not ML.)
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house experimental dataset (no name).
  - Size: small — a handful of conditions (2 pore sizes × ~5 fluxes), triplicate runs; image counts in the hundreds of particles.
  - Source: generated in Latulippe's lab.
  - Public? **No.** Data-availability statement: *"The authors are unable or have chosen not to specify which data has been used."*
  - Link: not provided in paper.
- **Reported headline metric:** ~100 % MP rejection by the 0.45 µm membrane; ~99 % by the 5 µm membrane (with ~2–7 µm MPs detected in the 5 µm permeate); higher flux → greater transmission early in filtration; fouling-mediated rejection increases over time. (No ML metric — these are experimental observations.)
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — these support an *image* reframe, not the paper's transmission question):**
  - **MP-Net dataset (Park et al., PLOS One 2022)** — fluorescence microscopy images of microplastics isolated from clams, with segmentation labels — Kaggle (`sanghyeonaustinpark/mpset`) — [match: close for image segmentation; analogy for the paper's filtration goal] — [access: easy — Kaggle download] — https://www.kaggle.com/sanghyeonaustinpark/mpset
  - **Sewage Microplastic Image Dataset (MDPI *Microplastics* 2024, 3(2):16)** — microscopic images with detection + segmentation labels, classes Fiber / Fragment (tens of thousands of labeled crops) — [match: close — WWTP context like this paper] — [access: easy–medium] — https://www.mdpi.com/2673-8929/3/2/16
  - **Moore Institute "Microplastic Image Explorer"** — 368 microscopic MP images — [match: loose, small] — [access: easy] — (Moore Institute for Plastic Pollution Research)
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **very hard** — the data-availability statement explicitly declines to share; no repository, no code, fluorescence reported in arbitrary units.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** For an image reframe: image segmentation/instance-detection (U-Net, Mask R-CNN or YOLO-seg) — within reach of your CNN background; ImageJ/Fiji for label sanity-checks. **No chemistry-specific ML tooling (no RDKit/SMILES/GNN).**
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** Train a **microplastic detection + segmentation model** on the public MP-Net (fluorescence) and/or Sewage datasets: detect particles, classify Fiber-vs-Fragment, and output a per-image size distribution (particle area → equivalent Feret diameter), echoing the paper's ImageJ-based size analysis but automated with a CNN. README headline: *"Automated microplastic detection and size-distribution estimation from microscopy images (mAP / IoU on a public benchmark),"* with notebooks for training, evaluation, and a size-histogram figure that mirrors the paper's FBRM/image analysis. This is a clean computer-vision project in a recruiter-legible "AI for environmental monitoring" area — but it is **inspired by** rather than a replication of this specific membrane-transmission study.

### Article 2: PLS + Wavelength Selection for Selective Protein Quantification on Continuous Chromatography

- **Full citation:** Ian A. Gough, Sarah Rassenberg, Claire Velikonja, Brandon Corbett, David R. Latulippe, Prashant Mhaskar. "Selective protein quantification on continuous chromatography equipment with limited absorbance sensing: A partial least squares and statistical wavelength selection solution." *Journal of Chemometrics* **38**(7):e3541 (2024). (Open access; **Mhaskar corresponding**, Latulippe 5th of 6 — middle author.)
- **Problem in plain English:** Continuous-chromatography biomanufacturing equipment (e.g., the Sartorius BioSMB PD) can only measure UV-Vis absorbance at **three user-chosen wavelengths**, yet operators need to quantify two proteins (here bovine serum albumin + lysozyme) in real time from those few measurements. The default wavelengths (230/260/280 nm) work poorly. The paper proposes a framework to **pick the best few wavelengths** so a soft-sensor model can selectively quantify the proteins on hardware-limited equipment.
- **ML task type:** **Genuine ML / chemometrics — supervised multivariate regression (soft sensor) + feature (wavelength) selection under a hard feature-count constraint.** Predicts two continuous concentrations from absorbance; the core contribution is the feature-selection pipeline.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: tabular UV-Vis absorbance — full plate-reader spectra 200–900 nm at 1 nm steps (TECAN Spark 10M, path lengths 2.5 + 9.5 mm) for screening, then 3-wavelength in-line measurements (Sartorius BioSMB PD) for verification.
  - Shape/size if stated: two datasets, each a **13-point D-optimal design** (MODDE) of BSA/Lys mixtures, measured in triplicate; X = absorbance matrix, Y = 2 concentrations. Very small.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: mean-centering + unit-variance scaling (automatic in sklearn `PLSRegression`); statistical wavelength refinement via **Welch's t-test** (`scipy.stats.ttest_ind`, p<0.01, vs blank buffer) + an **absorbance-magnitude test** (drop wavelengths >3 AU where Beer–Lambert linearity breaks); absorbance capped at 4 AU for consistency.
  - Wavelength ranking compared three methods: **VIP scores, LASSO** (`sklearn.linear_model.Lasso`), and **sequential forward search (SFS)** (`sklearn.feature_selection.SequentialFeatureSelector`); SFS-PLS won.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: concentrations of BSA and lysozyme.
  - Units or label space: mg/ml (two continuous regression targets).
- **Model architecture (brief):** **Partial least squares regression** with 2 latent variables (`sklearn.cross_decomposition.PLSRegression`), 5-fold CV (`KFold`); LASSO/linear regression used only for the LASSO ranking branch.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: two in-house BSA/Lys mixture datasets (no name).
  - Size: 13-point D-optimal training design × triplicate per dataset + test points — tiny.
  - Source: generated in-house (McMaster, with Sartorius Canada).
  - Public? **No.** Data-availability statement: *"Data available on request from the authors."*
  - Link: not provided in paper.
- **Reported headline metric:** **Sum of RMSE (BSA + Lys) on external test set.** The framework's SFS-selected wavelengths quantified the two proteins **~4× more accurately (lower RMSE)** than the base-case 230/260/280 nm set, in both datasets; a 2-protein system is well-modeled by 2 latent variables + 2–3 wavelengths.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — these support the *method*, PLS + wavelength selection on spectra):**
  - **Corn NIR dataset (Eigenvector "corn" / m5spec)** — 80 corn samples × 700 wavelengths, targets moisture/oil/protein/starch — the canonical wavelength-selection benchmark — [match: close for the PLS+feature-selection method; analogy for the protein-mixture task] — [access: easy — free download] — Eigenvector Research / public mirrors
  - **Tecator meat NIR (OpenML/StatLib)** — 240 samples × 100 absorbance channels, predict fat/protein/moisture — [match: close — multivariate spectral regression] — [access: easy — OpenML download] — https://www.openml.org/d/505
  - **Diesel / soil NIR benchmark sets** — standard public spectra used for waveband-selection papers — [match: loose — different analytes] — [access: easy–medium]
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **hard** — "available on request" only; no repository, no code, requires contacting authors.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** Almost nothing new — pure **scikit-learn** (`PLSRegression`, `Lasso`, `SequentialFeatureSelector`, `KFold`) + `scipy.stats`. PLS / chemometrics framing (latent variables, VIP) is the one mild new concept. **No chemistry-specific ML tooling.**
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** Reproduce the paper's **wavelength-selection-under-a-budget** framework on a public spectral dataset (corn NIR or Tecator): implement Welch's t-test + magnitude filtering, then compare **SFS vs LASSO vs VIP** for picking the best *k* wavelengths, and show a PLS soft-sensor's test RMSE as a function of *k* — exactly the paper's central figure. README headline: *"Constrained wavelength selection for spectral soft sensors — matching full-spectrum PLS accuracy with 2–3 wavelengths."* This is a clean, recruiter-legible chemometrics/feature-selection project squarely inside your sklearn skills, and it directly mirrors the paper's method even though the protein-mixture data itself is request-only.

### Article 3: Model-Based Design of Experiments for Nanofiltration-Membrane Transport Characterization

- **Full citation:** Xinhong Liu, Laurianne Estrada, Jonathan A. Ouimet, Matthew McClure, David R. Latulippe, William A. Phillip,* Alexander W. Dowling.* "Characterizing Transport Properties of Surface Charged Nanofiltration Membranes via Model-Based Data Analytics." *Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research* **64**, 12111–12130 (2025) — ACS special issue "Inverse Design of Materials and Processes for Separations." (**Phillip + Dowling corresponding, both Notre Dame; Latulippe 5th of 7 — middle author**, with McClure also McMaster.)
- **Problem in plain English:** To design better nanofiltration membranes you need accurate values for their transport properties (diffusion + partition coefficients), but standard experiments don't extract these precisely. The authors build a physics-based dynamic model of a diafiltration apparatus (startup dynamics, time delays, concentration polarization) and use **model-based design of experiments (MBDoE)** to find which experimental setup ("lag" vs "overflow" startup, concentrating vs diluting regime) yields the most information per experiment — a step toward "self-driving labs" for membrane discovery.
- **ML task type:** **Not standard ML.** This is **mechanistic ODE/DAE modeling + parameter estimation (weighted least-squares) + optimal experimental design** (Fisher Information Matrix; A-/D-/E-optimality) + model discrimination (AIC). No supervised learning, no neural networks. (The "AI / self-driving lab / digital twin / inverse design" framing is aspirational context, not the method used.)
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: time-series experimental signals — inline conductivity of the retentate (cf) and gravimetric permeate mass/concentration (cv) sampled at 0.2 Hz, plus ICP-OES permeate concentrations; fed into a system of ODEs/DAEs.
  - Shape/size if stated: small in-house diafiltration runs on NF270 membranes (a handful of experiments across startup modes + regimes); no large dataset.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: startup-dynamics modeling, permeate time-delay corrections, concentration-polarization (thin-film) correction, weighted least-squares scaling of residuals.
- **Output representation:**
  - What is estimated (not "predicted" by a learned model): membrane transport parameters — solute diffusion coefficient (Dm) and partition coefficient (H) — plus the information content of each experimental design.
  - Units or label space: cm²·s⁻¹ (diffusion), dimensionless (partition); design quality via A-/D-/E-optimality of the Fisher Information Matrix.
- **Model architecture (brief):** Physics-based convection–diffusion transport ODE/DAE system, solved + fit with **Pyomo 6.8.0 + Pyomo.DAE + Pyomo.DoE** (Python, open-source; Dowling-group framework) — mechanistic, not a learned model.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house diafiltration data (no name; apparatus "DATA" = Diafiltration Apparatus for high-Throughput Analysis).
  - Size: small experimental set on NF270 membranes.
  - Source: generated at Notre Dame (CEST) / McMaster collaboration.
  - Public? **No** — additional datasets appear only inside the Supporting Information PDF; no repository.
  - Link: not provided in paper (SI PDF at the ACS DOI; no GitHub/data repo stated).
- **Reported headline metric:** The **lag** startup mode beat overflow by **8% (A-), 138% (D-), 83% (E-optimality)** in parameter precision; diluting-regime experiments best discriminate competing transport models. (These are experimental-design-quality metrics, not ML performance.)
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — honest caveat: there is no public dataset matching this task):**
  - **Pyomo.DoE example/tutorial problems** (reactor-kinetics MBDoE in the Pyomo docs) — for *learning the method*, not membranes — [match: analogy only — different system] — [access: easy — ships with Pyomo] — https://pyomo.readthedocs.io
  - **No public membrane-transport diafiltration benchmark exists** — any replication needs the authors' in-house data (SI tables) or your own simulated data from the paper's equations.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **very hard** — no repository; data embedded in the SI PDF; reproducing requires re-implementing the ODE model and/or extracting PDF tables.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **Pyomo, Pyomo.DAE, Pyomo.DoE, a nonlinear solver (IPOPT), Fisher-Information / optimal-DoE theory** — all **niche optimization / algebraic-modeling tools outside your CNN/sklearn/transformer skill set** and not transferable to a typical ML portfolio.
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion, with reservations):** The honest take is that **this is the weakest of the three for your goals** — there's no public dataset and the tooling doesn't overlap with your ML skills. If you wanted to engage it, the realistic project is a **simulation study**: implement the paper's transport ODEs, generate synthetic diafiltration data, and use Pyomo.DoE to reproduce the "lag beats overflow" optimality result — a *scientific-computing / optimal-experimental-design* showcase, **not** a machine-learning portfolio piece. README headline would be about MBDoE/parameter estimation, which reads as computational chemical engineering rather than ML. Recommend prioritizing A2 (and A1) over this.

### Article 1: Cationic Block Co-Polymer for Gene Delivery in the Posterior Segment of the Eye

- **Full citation:** Amber Monteiro, Odunayo O. Mugisho, Antonio de Souza, Lina Liu, Yosra Agban, Priyanka Agarwal, Avik Shome, Ilva D. Rupenthal, **Heather Sheardown**. "A Cationic Block Co-Polymer for Gene Delivery in the Posterior Segment of the Eye." *Journal of Biomedical Materials Research Part A* **114**:e70078 (2026). Open access, CC BY. **Sheardown corresponding/senior author.**
- **Problem in plain English:** Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) is currently treated with anti-VEGF biologic injections into the eye every 4–8 weeks — painful, burdensome, and not always effective. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) could silence the disease-causing gene more potently, but unprotected ASOs degrade quickly in the eye. The authors design a **PEG-block-(VEMA-co-DEAEMA)** cationic block copolymer (vitamin-E hydrophobic block + PEG hydrophilic stealth block + DEAEMA tertiary-amine cationic block) that wraps an anti-Cx43 ASO into pH-responsive **polyplex nanoparticles**, then test their cell-compatibility, transfection, knockdown, and distribution after intravitreal injection into ex vivo porcine eyes.
- **ML task type:** **None — this is a wet-lab biomaterials / drug-delivery paper, not an ML paper.** No model is trained. (Reframes below are my construction.)
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: physical/chemical characterization — ¹H NMR spectra (purity), GPC (molecular weight), DLS (size + zeta potential), agarose gel electrophoresis (ASO encapsulation), MTT (cell viability), immunocytochemistry + confocal microscopy (transfection + knockdown), ex vivo porcine-eye fluorescence imaging (biodistribution).
  - Shape/size if stated: polyplexes < 150 nm diameter, slightly negative zeta potential; tested at N/P ratios 1:1 and 10:1; ARPE-19 cell line; ex vivo porcine eyes 4-hour distribution endpoint.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: monomer purification (VEMA synthesis from α-tocopherol + methacryloyl chloride; DEAEMA inhibitor removal via bentonite); flash nano-precipitation polyplex formation; standard cell-culture and tissue-sectioning protocols.
- **Output representation:**
  - What is measured (not "predicted"): polyplex size + zeta potential; encapsulation efficiency; cell viability (% MTT); transfection (Cy3 fluorescence); Cx43 protein knockdown (immunostaining); biodistribution in vitreous/retina/choroid.
  - Units or label space: nm (size), mV (zeta), % (viability/encapsulation), relative fluorescence intensity.
- **Model architecture (brief):** None. (No computational model — pure experimental.)
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house experimental data (no name).
  - Size: small — a handful of formulations × triplicate cell experiments + a few porcine-eye runs.
  - Source: generated in-house at McMaster + Auckland.
  - Public? **No.** Data-availability statement: *"The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request."*
  - Link: not provided in paper.
- **Reported headline metric:** 10:1 polyplexes (N/P) fully complex the ASO at sub-150 nm, are non-cytotoxic to ARPE-19 cells, achieve **superior transfection vs naked ASO**, deliver **significant Cx43 knockdown at 24 h**, and distribute throughout vitreous + retina + choroid within 4 h ex vivo. (No ML metric — these are biological observations.)
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — these support *medical-imaging* and *sequence-ML* reframes, not the polymer-chemistry itself):**
  - **Kermany OCT2017** — 84,484 retinal OCT images, 4 classes **including CNV (the exact pathology of nAMD)** + DME + Drusen + Normal — [match: close for the **disease** context this paper targets (AMD); analogy for the paper's polymer-delivery question] — [access: easy — Kaggle/Mendeley single download] — https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/paultimothymooney/kermany2018 / Mendeley DOI 10.17632/rscbjbr9sj
  - **Huesken et al. siRNA efficacy dataset** — 2,431 siRNAs targeting ~34 human genes with measured knockdown efficacy — [match: close for sequence-based gene-silencing efficacy ML (ASO/siRNA share the antisense mechanism); analogy for the paper's *delivery* aspect] — [access: easy — public CSV/supplementary]
  - **No public dataset matches the paper's polymer-chemistry/polyplex task** — there is no large benchmark of cationic-polymer compositions vs transfection efficacy.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **hard** — "available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request"; no repository.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** For an **OCT reframe (recommended)**: standard CNN classification (ResNet/EfficientNet) in PyTorch — squarely inside your existing skills. For a **siRNA/ASO reframe**: sequence ML (k-mer + LR baseline → 1D-CNN → transformer fine-tune, e.g., DNABERT/Nucleotide Transformer) — slightly newer but within reach. **No chemistry-specific tooling required for either**.
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** **Primary (recommended) — OCT-to-AMD classifier:** train a CNN on Kermany OCT2017 to classify CNV (nAMD's pathology) vs DME vs Drusen vs Normal, report per-class precision/recall + Grad-CAM saliency over retinal layers, and frame the README around: *"Deep-learning triage for age-related macular degeneration — distinguishing CNV (the form Sheardown's polyplexes treat) from other retinal pathologies on a public benchmark."* This connects directly to Sheardown's disease target while sitting squarely in your CNN skill set. **Secondary — ASO/siRNA efficacy prediction:** train a sequence model (1D-CNN or fine-tuned Nucleotide Transformer) on the Huesken siRNA dataset; framed as "computational design of gene-silencing payloads to complement biomaterial-based delivery." Both are *inspired-by* projects on third-party public datasets — neither replicates this exact polymer study.

### Article 2: Mucoadhesive Pre-activated Thiomer Micelles for Cyclosporine A Delivery in Dry Eye Disease

- **Full citation:** Taylor Goostrey, Mitchell Ross, Karim Soliman, Lindsay Sheardown, **Heather Sheardown**. "Mucoadhesive micelles for ophthalmic drug delivery." *Journal of Biomaterials Applications* **40**(8):972–986 (2026). **Sheardown corresponding/senior author.**
- **Problem in plain English:** Topical eyedrops for dry eye disease (DED) work poorly — less than 5% of an applied dose reaches the target tissue because the eye's natural tear turnover washes the drug away, and the most-used drug (cyclosporine A, "cycA") is hydrophobic and stings on application. The authors design **~70 nm amphiphilic block-copolymer micelles** that load cycA into their hydrophobic core and *covalently bond* to mucin via a **pre-activated thiomer** (NAC-conjugated pyridyl-disulfide methacrylate, PDSMA) — the polymer disulfide-exchanges with mucin, releasing the mucolytic NAC and anchoring the micelle. They characterize size, zeta potential, critical micelle concentration (CMC), cycA encapsulation (>90%) and release (~57% over 10 days), and cell viability on human corneal epithelial cells.
- **ML task type:** **None — wet-lab biomaterials / drug-delivery paper, no ML.** (Reframes below are my construction.)
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: physical/chemical characterization — ¹H NMR, GPC, DLS (size + zeta potential), pyrene-fluorescence CMC determination, HPLC for cycA quantification, MTT + Live/Dead on human corneal epithelial cells (HCECs).
  - Shape/size if stated: ~70 nm micelles; CMC = 217 mg/L; cycA >90% encapsulation efficiency; ~57% sustained release over 10 days; tested 1–500 µg/mL on HCECs.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: PDSMA monomer synthesis (PDSOH → methacryloylation), RAFT polymerization with PLA-CDP macroinitiator + AIBN, NAC conjugation, drug loading by co-solvent evaporation, dialysis.
- **Output representation:**
  - What is measured: hydrodynamic diameter (nm), zeta potential (mV), CMC (mg/L), encapsulation efficiency (%), cumulative release (%), cell viability (% MTT).
  - Units or label space: physicochemical/biological measurements; no ML labels.
- **Model architecture (brief):** None. (Pure experimental — no computational model.)
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house experimental data (no name).
  - Size: small — a handful of formulations (LMA, LMS-20, LMP-20) × triplicate cell experiments + release/CMC curves.
  - Source: generated in-house at McMaster.
  - Public? **No.** No explicit data-availability statement; "Supplemental material available online" only.
  - Link: not provided in paper.
- **Reported headline metric:** ~70 nm mucoadhesive micelles with CMC 217 mg/L; >90% cycA encapsulation; ~57% release over 10 days; cell viability is dose-dependent but recovers from 24→48 h. (No ML metric.)
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — these support a *meibography* disease-context reframe and a *CMC* polymer-property reframe):**
  - **Meibography 1000-image dataset (MGD1K)** — 1000 infrared meibography images of meibomian glands with precise segmentation + meiboscores, public on GitHub — [match: close — meibomian-gland dysfunction is the cause of ~80% of DED, the exact disease this paper treats] — [access: easy — GitHub download] — https://mgd1k.github.io/
  - **Public CMC dataset (Brozos et al. 2025 / Springer)** — 2,133 log-CMC values for 1,815 unique surfactants with SMILES (+ temperatures); used as the standard benchmark for surfactant CMC prediction with GNNs — [match: close for the paper's CMC determination angle (paper reports CMC = 217 mg/L)] — [access: easy — public supplementary] — https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13321-025-01112-2
  - **No public dataset matches the paper's micelle-mucoadhesion task itself** — there is no large benchmark of polymer compositions vs mucoadhesive performance.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **hard** — no data-availability statement; only supplementary material; no repository.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** For the **meibography reframe (recommended)**: standard CNN segmentation (U-Net) in PyTorch — within your CNN skills. For the **CMC reframe**: RDKit (Morgan fingerprints / descriptors from SMILES) + sklearn regression as a simple baseline, optionally a GNN (PyTorch Geometric) — RDKit is the one mildly new piece. **No deep niche tooling.**
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** **Primary (recommended) — meibography meiboscore / dropout classifier:** train a U-Net (segmentation) and a CNN (severity classification) on the public MGD1K dataset, output an automated meiboscore + visualize meibomian-gland dropout, and frame the README as: *"Deep-learning meiboscore quantification for dry eye disease — automating the assessment of meibomian-gland dysfunction (the cause of ~80% of DED, the disease Sheardown's mucoadhesive micelles target)."* Recruiter-legible medical-imaging CNN. **Secondary — CMC prediction from polymer SMILES:** train an sklearn regressor on Morgan fingerprints + a small GNN on the 2,133-surfactant public CMC dataset; framed as "computational pre-screening of amphiphilic polymers for self-assembly into micelles" — a chemistry-flavored cheminformatics project. Both are *inspired-by* on third-party public datasets — neither reproduces this micelle/mucoadhesion study exactly.

### Article 3: Tfap2b Deletion in Periocular Mesenchyme → Progressive Glaucomatous Changes (Mouse Model)

- **Full citation:** Aftab Taiyab, Monica Akula, Japnit Dham, Paula Deschamps, **Heather Sheardown**, Trevor Williams, Teresa Borrás, Judith A. West-Mays. "Deletion of transcription factor AP-2β from the developing murine trabecular meshwork region leads to progressive glaucomatous changes." *Journal of Neuroscience Research* **100**(2):638–652 (2022). - **Problem in plain English:** Glaucoma causes irreversible blindness in ~111M people projected by 2040, often due to abnormalities in the eye's aqueous-humor drainage structures (trabecular meshwork + Schlemm's canal). The authors use a **Mgp-Cre.KI mouse line** to conditionally knock out the AP-2β transcription factor (gene *Tfap2b*) in periocular mesenchyme cells that develop into those drainage structures. ### Article 1: Supervised ML for Composite Fiber Orientation from Active Ultrasonic Signals

- **Full citation:** Austin D. Bedrosian, **Michael R. Thompson**, Andrew Hrymak, Gisela Lanza. "Developing a supervised machine-learning model capable of distinguishing fiber orientation of polymer composite samples nondestructively tested using active ultrasonics." *Journal of Advanced Manufacturing and Processing* **e10138** (2022). Open access (AIChE / Wiley). **Thompson corresponding/senior author.**
- **Problem in plain English:** In automotive composite manufacturing (Industry 4.0), you want to know in real time whether the glass fibers inside a thermoset polymer composite are oriented correctly — but no single ultrasonic frequency cleanly maps to fiber angle. The authors emit a sweep of 220–250 kHz ultrasonic waves through epoxy/glass-fiber specimens at six controlled angles (and multi-angle stacks), preprocess the received signal with **FFT / STFT / continuous wavelet transform (CWT)**, and train **PLS, an artificial neural network (ANN), and a CNN** to classify (and regress) fiber orientation directly from the spectrum — aimed at eventually plugging into an extruder for in-line quality monitoring.
- **ML task type:** **Genuine supervised ML.** Multi-class classification (6 fiber-angle classes) for single-orientation specimens, plus regression of angle for multi-orientation specimens; the headline contribution is benchmarking three preprocessing methods × three model families.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: 1D acoustic time-series signals, preprocessed into 1D (FFT) or 2D (STFT, CWT scalograms) spectral representations.
  - Shape/size if stated: 220–250 kHz, 1 kHz step, 700-µs signals; six orientation angles + bi-angle + tri-angle stacks; ≥3 specimens per class; 15 wt% glass fibers. Small in-house dataset.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: FFT / STFT / CWT in Python 3.7 with NumPy + SciPy; FFT amplitudes normalized to unit max; eight derived FFT subsets (frequency-band slicing + 4-of-6-angle restriction).
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: fiber orientation (6 classes; 0°/15°/30°/45°/60°/75°), or continuous angle for multi-orientation samples.
  - Units or label space: degrees; one-hot for classification, scalar for regression.
- **Model architecture (brief):** **PLS** (sklearn-style projection of latent structures, R²/Q² assessment) vs. **3-layer ANN** (RMSprop/Adam/SGD tuned, MAE loss) vs. **CNN** on STFT/CWT scalograms. **Headline: ANN > CNN > PLS; CWT > STFT > FFT for input features; regression > pure classification for multi-orientation.**
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house experimental dataset (no name).
  - Size: small — 6 orientations × ≥3 specimens × multi-angle combinations; per-specimen one 700-µs signal swept over the frequency range.
  - Source: generated in Thompson's CAPPA-D / MMRI lab.
  - Public? **No.** Data-availability statement: *"The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request."*
  - Link: not provided in paper.
- **Reported headline metric:** Single-orientation CNN-on-STFT classification accuracy 50–53% (overfit, poor); ANN-on-STFT classification 70–83% with MAE 8.8°; bi-angle ANN regression near 100% accuracy; tri-angle weakest. CWT-based features beat FFT/STFT for the deepest models. ANN consistently beat the CNN in this small-data regime.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — these support a *1D-signal-classification* method reframe; no public composite-fiber-orientation benchmark exists):**
  - **CWRU Bearing Fault Dataset** (Case Western Reserve University) — the canonical public benchmark for vibration / acoustic signal classification in industrial NDT, ~100s of multi-condition signals across fault types — [match: loose — same modality (1D industrial signals → multi-class), different system (bearings vs composites)] — [access: easy — direct download from CWRU, also Kaggle mirrors] — https://engineering.case.edu/bearingdatacenter
  - **Open Guided Waves (Helmholtz / Cantwell) — CFRP plate guided-wave datasets** for composite NDT — [match: closer to this paper's composite context, but smaller community] — [access: medium — university hosting] — https://openguidedwaves.de
  - **UORED-VAFCLS** — natural-fault bearing acoustic + accelerometer dataset, used as a cross-domain complement to CWRU — [match: loose — same as CWRU] — [access: easy]
  - **No public benchmark matches the exact task** (active-ultrasonic spectrum → glass-fiber orientation in epoxy) — analogues only.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **hard** — request-only; no repository; no code.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** Almost nothing new — **Python + NumPy + SciPy** (paper's stack), plus **PyWavelets** for CWT scalograms (the one mildly new piece) and **Keras/TensorFlow** or **PyTorch** for the ANN/CNN — all within your existing skills. PLS via sklearn `PLSRegression`.
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** Reproduce the paper's **preprocessing × model bake-off** on the public **CWRU bearing-fault dataset** — FFT vs STFT vs CWT × PLS vs ANN vs CNN — and show test-set accuracy + MAE curves for fault-type classification (a clean public analogue of the paper's "spectrum → discrete category" task). README headline: *"Signal-representation bake-off for industrial fault classification — FFT/STFT/CWT × PLS/ANN/CNN on the CWRU benchmark, reproducing the wavelet-preprocessing advantage seen in composite ultrasonic NDT."* This is squarely in your sklearn/CNN skills, has zero chemistry-specific tooling, runs on free Colab, and maps directly onto Thompson's paper without depending on his proprietary composite dataset.

### Article 2: Image-Based Model Predictive Control of Batch Rotational Molding via CNN + PCA + SSID + PLS

- **Full citation:** Aswin Chandrasekar, Hassan Abdulhussain, **Michael R. Thompson**, Prashant Mhaskar. "Utilizing Neural Networks for Image-based Model Predictive Controller of a batch Rotational Molding process." *IFAC-PapersOnLine* — **2024 IFAC ADCHEM** (12th IFAC Int'l Symposium on Advanced Control of Chemical Processes), Toronto, July 14–17, 2024, pp. 472–477. Open access (CC BY-NC-ND). **Senior author is Prashant Mhaskar** (process-control PI; Chandrasekar is his trainee per the cited foundational Corbett+Mhaskar 2016 SSID paper); **Thompson is co-PI / 3rd of 4 — middle author** providing the rotational-molding domain. (Same pattern as Latulippe A2.)
- **Problem in plain English:** Batch processes (here: bi-axial rotational molding of hollow plastic parts) often only let you measure product quality *after* the batch finishes — destructively. The team uses a **thermal camera through a slit in the oven** as the only online sensor and wants to close a feedback loop that produces good-quality parts (low sinkhole-area %, high impact strength). They build a multi-stage data-driven model — CNN object detection of "is the mold in frame?", PCA to crush each 90×120-pixel image to one latent variable, subspace-identified state-space model of (heater input → image latent), and PLS regression from terminal states to the two destructive quality variables — and plug it into a Model Predictive Controller.
- **ML task type:** **Genuine ML *plus* classical control.** ML pieces: (a) CNN binary classification + YOLOv3-style object detection ("is the mold in frame?"); (b) PCA dimensionality reduction; (c) PLS regression (latent → quality). Control pieces: subspace identification (SSID) → LTI state-space model + Model Predictive Control (MPC) closed-loop. The headline contribution is the integrated pipeline, not any single ML model.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: thermal-camera images (90×120 = 10,800 pixels) sampled over a batch; heater-input time series; quality measurements at end-of-batch (sinkhole area % via ImageJ; impact strength via ASTM D256 pendulum).
  - Shape/size if stated: small dataset (a handful of batches); explicitly noted "limited experimental data."
  - Preprocessing in the paper: CNN frames in-mold detection → cropping; PCA on in-frame images → 1 latent variable; SSID on (input → latent) sequence; PLS terminal states → quality.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model predicts: end-of-batch sinkhole area % and impact strength.
  - Units or label space: % and joules (continuous regression targets); MPC then drives heater input toward desired quality.
- **Model architecture (brief):** **CNN** (classifier + YOLOv3-style detector) → **PCA** (1 latent variable) → **LTI state-space model** identified by SSID (A, B, C, D matrices in Appendix A) → **PLS** quality model (R, P matrices in Appendix B) → **MPC** closed loop.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house experimental batches (no name).
  - Size: small — a handful of rotational-molding batches.
  - Source: McMaster Mhaskar + Thompson labs (HDPE donated by Imperial Oil).
  - Public? **No.** Conference paper; no formal data-availability statement; no code release.
  - Link: not provided in paper.
- **Reported headline metric:** Open-loop quality-prediction RMSEs presented (sinkhole area + impact strength); closed-loop MPC demonstrably drives products toward user-specified quality targets; outperforms PI control on the same setup. (No standard ML benchmark — in-house validation.)
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — no exact image-based-MPC benchmark exists; only loose component analogues):**
  - **Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) dataset** — the canonical public benchmark for data-driven process control / soft-sensing in chemical engineering; multiple Python implementations on GitHub — [match: loose — same field (chemical process control + soft sensing), different system, no images] — [access: easy — public CSVs + Python sims] — https://github.com/camaramm/tennessee-eastman-profBraatz
  - **COCO** / open YOLO detection benchmarks — for the CNN sub-component (object detection in industrial scenes) — [match: analogy only — generic detection task, no batch-control context] — [access: easy — `torchvision.datasets`] — https://cocodataset.org
  - **No public dataset matches image-based MPC for batch processes** — the paper's exact contribution has no benchmark.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **very hard** — not released; reproducing requires building the rotational-molding rig.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** **Mixed.** CNN classification + YOLOv3-style detection + PCA + PLS are in your sklearn/PyTorch skills. **But subspace identification (SSID) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) are classical-control niche tooling** — typically MATLAB-based, with Python alternatives (`do-mpc`, `python-control`, `casadi`). This is the **one major unfamiliar component** for your portfolio.
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** **Be selective.** Reproduce *only* the **PCA + PLS soft-sensor** sub-component on the public **Tennessee Eastman Process** benchmark — a clean "high-dimensional sensor → quality variable" regression pipeline that recruiters will recognize as ML-for-process-engineering — and *optionally* layer a CNN object-detection demo on top using COCO. **Skip the MPC closed-loop** unless you specifically want to learn classical control. README headline: *"Data-driven soft sensors for chemical batch processes — PCA + PLS pipeline on the Tennessee Eastman benchmark, with CNN-based image preprocessing inspired by image-based MPC."* This is honest about which parts of the paper you can leverage given your CNN/sklearn skill set, without committing you to a months-long detour through classical control theory.

### Article 3: Genetic-Programming-Derived Attenuation Model for Fiber-Reinforced Thermoplastic Composites

- **Full citation:** Austin D. Bedrosian, Andrew Hrymak, Gisela Lanza, **Michael R. Thompson**. "Developing a Heterogeneous Attenuation Model for Fiber Reinforced Thermoplastic Composites in the Kilohertz Region of the Ultrasonic Spectrum." *Polymer Composites* (Society of Plastics Engineers / Wiley) **2026**:1–11. DOI 10.1002/pc.70918. Open access (CC BY-NC). **Thompson corresponding/senior author** (same Bedrosian/Hrymak/Lanza team as A1).
- **Problem in plain English:** When you send ultrasound through a fiber-reinforced plastic composite, the signal weakens (attenuates) due to a mix of the polymer dampening it, fibers scattering it, and tiny entrapped air bubbles scattering it further. Existing physics-based attenuation models assume the material is homogeneous and ignore how attenuation changes with **fiber content** and **porosity** — so they don't generalize across composite formulations. The authors want a single mathematical expression that captures all three effects (frequency, fiber content + type, porosity) in the kHz region used by smart-factory acoustic NDT. They use **genetic programming (symbolic regression)** to *discover* the right functional form from experimental data, rather than guessing it.
- **ML task type:** **Genuine ML — symbolic regression via genetic programming.** Target: ultrasonic attenuation α(f, porosity, fiber-content, fiber-type). The output of the model is not a number predicted by a neural net but a **mathematical expression** evolved by GP — interpretable scientific ML.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: tabular features — frequency f (kHz), porosity (vol%, measured via micro-CT on every plaque at the test location), fiber content (5/15/25 vol%), fiber type (E-glass vs carbon).
  - Shape/size if stated: small — 3 fiber loadings × 2 fiber types × multiple plaques × frequency-binned attenuation values (~tens of data points per region).
  - Preprocessing in the paper: micro-CT porosity quantification in VGStudioMax; active-ultrasonic spectrum acquisition (250–500 kHz, R15 emitter + F30 receiver); attenuation α calculated per frequency bin.
- **Output representation:**
  - What the model produces: a closed-form mathematical expression for α as a function of f, porosity, fiber content, and fiber type.
  - Units or label space: attenuation in dB or nepers per unit length; the actual contribution is the *equation*, not a per-sample number.
- **Model architecture (brief):** **Symbolic regression** via **GPlearn** (sklearn-compatible Python library for genetic programming) — Python 3.11 + NumPy + SciPy + GPlearn; hyperparameter sweep over mutation/crossover probabilities; candidate expressions ranked by R².
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house experimental composite-plaque dataset (no name).
  - Size: small — six formulations × ~3 frequency regions × CT-measured per-plaque porosity.
  - Source: McMaster CAPPA-D + KIT micro-CT facility (Bedrosian's PhD work, 2025).
  - Public? **No.** Data-availability statement: *"Data will be made available on request."*
  - Link: not provided in paper.
- **Reported headline metric:** Two-regime attenuation model derived; first regime (250–310 kHz) depends on porosity + fiber content (S1 dispersion mode), with porosity-fit R² = 0.73 (glass) / 0.30 (carbon); second regime (310–500 kHz) shows linear frequency dependence with fiber-type-only dependence. Modest fit quality on a small dataset — the contribution is the *form* of the equation, not high predictive accuracy.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — these support a *symbolic regression / scientific-ML* method reframe):**
  - **PySR / AI Feynman benchmark (100 Feynman Lectures equations)** — the canonical public benchmark for symbolic regression; rediscovers known physics equations from data — [match: close for the *method* (symbolic regression with R² evaluation), analogy for the composite-physics target] — [access: easy — `pip install pysr` and built-in benchmarks] — https://github.com/MilesCranmer/PySR
  - **SRBench (Symbolic Regression Benchmark)** — 252 tabular regression problems (~130 real-world + ~120 synthetic) standardized for SR comparison — [match: close for general SR method] — [access: easy — public Python framework] — https://github.com/cavalab/srbench
  - **CWRU / Open Guided Waves** — the same ultrasonic-NDT public datasets recommended for A1, where you could swap symbolic regression in for neural nets — [match: closer for the composite-NDT context, but doesn't give you a symbolic regression task per se]
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **hard** — request-only; no repository; no code.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** Almost nothing new — **GPlearn** is **sklearn-compatible** (the usual `fit` / `predict` / `score` interface), so you'd just `pip install gplearn` and use it like any other sklearn estimator; alternatively the more modern **PySR** is similar with a richer feature set. Otherwise pure Python + NumPy/SciPy. **No deep niche tooling.**
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** **Symbolic-regression bake-off project.** Run **GPlearn vs PySR vs a small sklearn baseline (random forest / XGBoost)** on a public regression task — either **AI Feynman equations** (rediscover known physics formulas) or a CWRU-style 1D-signal feature-regression task — and report R², expression complexity, and "interpretability vs predictive accuracy" trade-offs. README headline: *"Symbolic regression for interpretable scientific ML — GPlearn / PySR baselines on the AI Feynman benchmark, reproducing the genetic-programming methodology used in composite-NDT attenuation modeling."* Squarely sklearn-territory, runs on free Colab, and gives you an "interpretable AI" angle that pairs well with Thompson A1's signal-processing bake-off in a combined repo.

### Summary for this professor

- **Common thread across their work (3 articles):** Industry-4.0 data-driven monitoring + modeling of polymer processing — A1 (Thompson-corresponding): supervised classification/regression of fiber orientation from ultrasonic spectra; A2 (Mhaskar-corresponding, Thompson co-PI on the molding domain): image-based MPC of batch rotational molding with CNN + PCA + SSID + PLS; A3 (Thompson-corresponding, same Bedrosian/Hrymak/Lanza team as A1): **genetic-programming symbolic regression** to derive a heterogeneous ultrasonic attenuation model. A1 + A3 are clearly the **Thompson lab's NDT-of-composites thread** (same trainee Bedrosian, same international team); A2 is a Mhaskar-led collaboration.
- **Dominant data modality:** Sensor signals + small tabular feature sets — 1D ultrasonic spectra → scalograms (A1), thermal-camera images (A2), and tabular (frequency, porosity, fiber content/type) → symbolic expressions (A3). Strong overlap with your sklearn skills throughout (PLS, PCA, GPlearn — all sklearn-compatible) and with your CNN skills on the image / scalogram side; the **SSID + MPC** stack in A2 is the only major out-of-skill-set piece.
- **Biggest obstacle for me to replicate their work publicly:** **No data, no code on any of the three** — A1 + A3 data request-only, A2 conference paper with no data-availability statement. Portfolio projects all rebuild the *method* on public benchmarks (CWRU for A1, Tennessee Eastman + COCO for A2, AI Feynman / SRBench for A3) rather than reproducing the actual studies.
- **Skills I would gain by working with them:** signal processing (FFT/STFT/CWT + PyWavelets, scalograms; A1); image-based soft sensing + dimensionality reduction (PCA, PLS; A2); **interpretable scientific ML via symbolic regression (GPlearn / PySR; A3)**; polymer processing + composite manufacturing + rotational molding domain. The cleanest ML transfer to your portfolio is the **A1 + A3 NDT-of-composites pair** — both Thompson-corresponding, both sklearn-style ML, both squarely in your skill set.

### Article 1: ALD ZnO-Enhanced Anode for Lithium-Ion Batteries — Mechanism via ⁷Li Solid-State NMR

- **Full citation:** Zoya Sadighi, Jeffrey S. Price, Jingyi Qu, **David J. H. Emslie**, Gianluigi A. Botton, Gillian R. Goward. "Atomic Layer Deposition ZnO-Enhanced Negative Electrode for Lithium-Ion Battery: Understanding of Conversion/Alloying Reaction via ⁷Li Solid State NMR Spectroscopy." *Journal of The Electrochemical Society* **170**, 010512 (2023). Open access (CC BY 4.0, IOP Publishing for ECS). **Corresponding author: Goward** (Chemistry & Chemical Biology, McMaster). **Emslie is 4th of 6 — peripheral co-author providing ALD precursor expertise.**
- **Problem in plain English:** Lithium-ion battery (LIB) anodes need higher capacity than graphite — but candidate alternatives like ZnO suffer from poorly-understood reaction mechanisms during cycling. The team grows an ultrathin ZnO film by **atomic layer deposition (ALD)** onto carbon-paper current collectors, builds it into half-cell + full-cell LIBs, then uses **⁷Li MAS solid-state NMR (60 kHz)** (which can see both crystalline and amorphous Li environments unlike XRD) to track exactly what happens to lithium during charge/discharge — finding that ZnO undergoes an irreversible *conversion* step that leaves zinc nanograins, which then alloy reversibly with Li to give the cycling capacity (and improve cycling by 40% over uncoated carbon paper).
- **ML task type:** **None — wet-lab electrochemistry / materials-characterization paper, no ML.** (Reframes below are my construction.)
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: physical/chemical characterization — ⁷Li MAS ssNMR spectra (chemical shift + relaxation), XRD diffractograms, SEM micrographs, cyclic voltammetry curves, galvanostatic charge/discharge profiles.
  - Shape/size if stated: in-house ALD-deposited samples on carbon paper substrates; half-cell and full-cell coin cells; cycling at multiple current densities; 100-cycle full-cell test.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: thermal ALD of ZnO from diethylzinc + H₂O at 150 °C; cell assembly; standard battery cycling protocols; NMR with rotor synchronization at 60 kHz MAS.
- **Output representation:**
  - What is measured (not "predicted"): cycle capacity (mAh/g), Coulombic efficiency (%), ⁷Li chemical shift identification of Li environments (LixZn alloy, Li intercalated in carbon, Li in SEI), morphological evolution.
  - Units or label space: mAh/g, %, ppm; physical battery + spectroscopy measurements.
- **Model architecture (brief):** None. (Pure experimental — no computational model.)
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house experimental data (no name).
  - Size: small — a handful of cells × cycling curves + NMR + XRD + SEM characterization.
  - Source: McMaster Chemistry & Chemical Biology + Materials Science & Engineering + Canadian Light Source.
  - Public? **No.** No explicit data-availability statement; supplementary material only.
  - Link: not provided in paper.
- **Reported headline metric:** ZnO ALD coating boosts half-cell capacity by ~40%; full-cell averages 98.8% Coulombic efficiency over 100 cycles; ⁷Li ssNMR identifies LixZn alloy formation during discharge + atomic Zn nanograins after charge (not re-oxidized). (No ML metric — these are battery + spectroscopy measurements.)
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — these support a *Li-ion battery cycle-life ML* reframe, not the ALD/NMR mechanism question):**
  - **Severson et al. 2019 (Nature Energy) — MIT-Stanford-Toyota 124-cell LFP/graphite dataset** — the canonical public benchmark for Li-ion battery cycle-life ML; cells cycled 150–2,300 cycles; published with code — [match: close for the *battery* context this paper studies; analogy for the paper's ZnO-anode chemistry] — [access: easy — GitHub + Kaggle download] — https://github.com/rdbraatz/data-driven-prediction-of-battery-cycle-life-before-capacity-degradation / https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/itshpark/data-driven-prediction-of-battery-cycle
  - **Materials Project** — DFT-computed properties for ~140,000+ inorganic materials including battery cathodes/anodes; API access — [match: close for materials discovery; analogy for the paper's anode-specific question] — [access: easy — free API + Python client] — https://next-gen.materialsproject.org
  - **NASA Battery Dataset (Prognostics Center of Excellence)** — older but classic Li-ion cycling dataset for state-of-health prediction — [match: loose — different chemistry, different fault modes] — [access: easy]
  - **No public dataset matches the paper's exact ALD ZnO anode + ⁷Li NMR task** — these are inspired-by reframes anchored to the LIB context.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **hard** — no explicit data-availability statement; only supplementary; no repository.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** For the **Severson battery-cycle-life reframe (recommended)**: standard sklearn (Ridge / RandomForest / XGBoost) for the linear/GBM baselines + optionally a 1D-CNN on early-cycle voltage curves — within your existing PyTorch/sklearn skills. For the **Materials Project route**: pymatgen + matminer (chemistry-specific cheminformatics) — slightly newer but well-documented. **No deep niche tooling required.**
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** Train a **battery cycle-life predictor on the Severson public dataset** — reproduce the paper's headline result of predicting cycle life from the first 100 cycles' voltage-vs-capacity curves with sklearn linear models, then push to 1D-CNN on the early-cycle voltage curves and compare. Frame the README as: *"Early-cycle prediction of lithium-ion battery cycle life — sklearn + CNN baselines on the MIT-Stanford-TRI Severson 2019 benchmark, motivated by ALD anode design (Emslie/Goward-lab context)."* This is a clean, recruiter-legible "AI for energy storage / EVs" portfolio piece using a real public benchmark, anchored to the *battery* domain Emslie's collaboration targets even though the paper itself has no ML.

### Article 2: Gold(I) Alkoxide and Thiolate ALD Precursors for Thin Gold Films

- **Full citation:** Nicholas A. Hoffman, **David J. H. Emslie**. "Gold(I) alkoxide and thiolate complexes as potential atomic layer deposition precursors." *Dalton Transactions* (Royal Society of Chemistry) **55**:1234–1247 (2026). Open access (CC BY-NC 3.0). **Emslie corresponding/senior author** (emslied@mcmaster.ca) — **this is Emslie's own lab paper**, with Hoffman as trainee first author.
- **Problem in plain English:** Thin gold films are used in microelectronics, photonic devices, and biosensors, and atomic layer deposition (ALD) is the only thin-film technique that can coat high-aspect-ratio surfaces uniformly. But existing gold ALD precursors all have problems — either they need ozone or hydrogen plasma (which damages substrates), or they're not volatile enough to deliver cleanly. The authors design and synthesize a family of **linear gold(I) alkoxide and thiolate complexes** bearing perfluoro-*tert*-butoxide / *tert*-butylthiolate ligands and trialkylphosphine donors, then characterize their thermal stability + volatility + reactivity with hydroborane/hydrosilane co-reactants (HBpin, H₃SiPh) to find a candidate that gives gold deposition without plasma or ozone. Compound **3** ([Au{OC(CF₃)₃}(PiPr₃)]) emerges as the best combination of thermal stability + volatility + reactivity, and preliminary ALD reactor experiments at 124 °C demonstrated gold deposition.
- **ML task type:** **None — pure synthetic inorganic / organometallic chemistry paper.** Precursor design, NMR characterization, X-ray crystallography, TGA / DSC, sublimation studies, reactor demonstrations. No ML, no computation.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: synthetic chemistry + solid/solution-state characterization — multinuclear NMR (¹H, ¹³C, ¹⁹F, ³¹P), single-crystal X-ray diffraction, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), powder XRD, AFM of ALD films, reactor depositions.
  - Shape/size if stated: 6 new compounds (1–6) + a decomposition product 7 + a comparison [Au(η¹C-hfac)(PiPr₃)] — small, individual compounds, no large dataset.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: Schlenk / glovebox synthesis under N₂ or Ar; precursor purification by sublimation; ALD reactor with HBpin as co-reactant at 124 °C.
- **Output representation:**
  - What is measured (not "predicted"): melting points (°C), sublimation conditions (°C / mTorr), thermal decomposition kinetics (% over time at T), crystal structures, NMR shifts, deposition outcomes (Au metal formation).
  - Units or label space: physical/chemical measurements; no ML labels.
- **Model architecture (brief):** None. (Pure experimental — no computational model.)
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house synthetic compounds (no name).
  - Size: tiny — 6 new compounds + a few related structures.
  - Source: generated in Emslie's lab at McMaster.
  - Public? **Crystallographic data deposited at CCDC** (CCDC 2503049–2503054 + 2505331) — publicly searchable via the CCDC free service. Synthesis + characterization details in supplementary information; no machine-readable ML-ready dataset.
  - Link: CCDC deposits (free public access via https://www.ccdc.cam.ac.uk); SI at DOI 10.1039/d5dt02836a.
- **Reported headline metric:** Compound 3 has melting point 59–61 °C, sublimes cleanly at 5 mTorr, decomposes only 4% after 72 h at 85 °C; reacts within minutes with HBpin and H₃SiPh to give gold metal + volatile byproducts; preliminary ALD at 124 °C demonstrated. (No ML metric — these are chemistry measurements.)
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — these support only a *very loose* ML-of-organometallics reframe, since no public ALD-precursor benchmark exists):**
  - **PubChem** — millions of small molecules with computed and measured physicochemical properties; can be filtered to organometallic / gold complexes — [match: very loose — generic molecular-property prediction, not ALD-specific] — [access: easy — Python clients, REST API] — https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  - **Materials Project** — DFT-computed properties for inorganic materials (less coverage for molecular organometallic precursors) — [match: loose — solid-state materials rather than discrete molecular precursors] — [access: easy — API + pymatgen] — https://next-gen.materialsproject.org
  - **CCDC Cambridge Structural Database** — ~1.3 M organic + organometallic crystal structures (free for academic use via WebCSD; full programmatic access requires institutional license) — [match: closer for organometallic chemistry, but not a clean ML benchmark and not fully open] — [access: medium — academic registration; full API behind paywall]
  - **No public benchmark exists for ALD precursor thermal-stability / volatility / reactivity prediction** — any ML project would be on a small custom dataset (e.g., scraping PubChem properties for organometallics) and would be only very loosely related to the paper.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **medium-hard** — crystal structures publicly retrievable from CCDC by ID (good); but no machine-readable dataset of properties, no code, only PDFs/SI for the synthesis + characterization.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** For an organometallic-property ML reframe: **RDKit** (SMILES handling) + sklearn / XGBoost on Morgan fingerprints — RDKit is the one mildly new piece, otherwise sklearn-standard. The actual *chemistry* (Schlenk / glovebox synthesis) is a year-plus skill set in its own right.
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** Honest take — **A2 is a weak ML-portfolio anchor for you**. The paper is excellent synthetic chemistry but has no ML target and no public ML benchmark. If you wanted to engage it, the realistic project would be a **molecular-property prediction toy project**: scrape ~few-thousand organometallic / metal-complex entries from PubChem with melting point + boiling point + molecular weight labels, train RDKit-fingerprint → sklearn regression for "predict melting point from SMILES," and frame the README as: *"Cheminformatics baseline for organometallic precursor screening — predicting melting point and volatility proxies from SMILES, motivated by ALD precursor design."* This is *very loosely* connected to the paper and won't read as a faithful representation of Emslie's work — **A1 is the better portfolio anchor** despite the peripheral authorship; A2 is more informative about Emslie as a *PI* than as a source of ML projects.

### Article 3: Rh and Ni Complexes of an Ambiphilic Phosphine-Thioether-Borane Ligand

- **Full citation:** Bradley E. Cowie, **David J. H. Emslie**. "M·H·BR₃ and M·Br·BR₃ Interactions in Rhodium and Nickel Complexes of an Ambiphilic Phosphine-Thioether-Borane Ligand." *Canadian Journal of Chemistry* (2018, manuscript ID cjc-2017-0758.R1). **Emslie corresponding/senior author**, just two authors — Cowie is his PhD trainee. **This is again Emslie's own lab work** (his second clean own-lab paper in the survey).
- **Problem in plain English:** "Ambiphilic" ligands carry both an electron-donor (phosphine, thioether) and an electron-acceptor (borane) group, so they can grab metal centres and also coordinate to atoms hanging off the metal. The authors wanted to characterize how a hydride or bromide bridges between a metal (Rh or Ni) and the borane group of the **TXPB** ligand (a phosphine-thioether-borane built on a thioxanthene backbone). They synthesize **[Rh(μ-H)(CO)(TXPB)]** (2) and **[NiBr(μ-Br)(TXPB)]** (6), determine X-ray crystal structures, and use multinuclear / variable-temperature NMR + DFT-calculated Mayer bond orders to characterize the M–H–B and M–Br–B bonding regimes.
- **ML task type:** **None — pure synthetic inorganic / organometallic chemistry paper**, same flavor as A2.
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: synthetic chemistry + characterization — single-crystal X-ray diffraction, multinuclear NMR (¹H, ¹¹B, ³¹P, including VT-NMR), DFT for Mayer bond orders.
  - Shape/size if stated: 2 new compounds (Rh hydride 2 + Ni dibromide 6); tiny.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: Schlenk / glovebox synthesis; standard NMR + crystallography; DFT geometry optimization in supplementary.
- **Output representation:**
  - What is measured: bond distances + angles, ¹¹B and ³¹P NMR chemical shifts, Mayer bond orders, fluxional behavior (square-planar ↔ tetrahedral equilibrium).
  - Units or label space: Ångströms / degrees / ppm / bond-order numbers; no ML labels.
- **Model architecture (brief):** None for ML; DFT (program not specified in extract) for ground-state geometry + Mayer bond orders.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house synthetic compounds (no name).
  - Size: tiny — 2 new compounds.
  - Source: generated in Emslie's lab at McMaster.
  - Public? **2 crystal structures deposited at CCDC** (CCDC 1827160 + 1827159) — publicly retrievable. No ML-ready dataset.
  - Link: CCDC deposits via https://www.ccdc.cam.ac.uk/data_request/cif.
- **Reported headline metric:** Compound 2 has Rh–H 1.84(5) Å, Rh–B 2.456(6) Å, B–H 1.59(6) Å (elongated); Mayer bond orders Rh–H = 0.58, Rh–B = 0.23, Rh–Cipso = 0.27 — bonding sits between an η²BC-coordinated borane and a σ-hydroborate interaction. Compound 6 has B–Br = 2.311(6) Å; VT-NMR shows square-planar ↔ tetrahedral equilibrium in solution.
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — same as A2; no public benchmark for this exact task):**

  - **CCDC Cambridge Structural Database** — has the relevant transition-metal organometallic complexes, but the open-access portion (WebCSD) is limited; full programmatic access requires institutional license — [match: closer for the actual chemistry, weaker for clean ML benchmarking] — [access: medium]
  - **No public benchmark exists** for ambiphilic ligand binding-mode prediction or M–(co-ligand)–Lewis-acid bridging-bond characterization.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **medium-hard** — 2 crystal structures publicly retrievable from CCDC (good); but no machine-readable dataset, no code.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** Same as A2 — **RDKit** (SMILES) + sklearn for any cheminformatics reframe; DFT (Gaussian / ORCA / etc.) if you wanted to push into quantum chemistry, but that's a year-plus skill set away from ML.
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** Honest take — **A3 reinforces A2**: Emslie's own-lab work is exclusively synthetic organometallic chemistry, with a small DFT component for bonding analysis. There's no ML reframe that closely matches this work. The only realistic portfolio piece would be the same cheminformatics toy project as A2 (PubChem organometallic property prediction). **A3 strengthens the conclusion that Emslie's lab is structurally a poor ML-thesis fit but a fine synthetic-chemistry training option.** If you want to acknowledge A3 in the same portfolio repo as A2, you could add an "interpretable bonding analysis" sub-notebook that loads CCDC structures and visualizes them in NGLview / py3Dmol — chemistry-flavored visualization, not really ML.

### Summary for this professor

- **Common thread across their work (3 articles):** Synthetic inorganic / organometallic chemistry — A1 (Goward-corresponding, **Emslie peripheral** providing ALD chemistry): ALD ZnO on carbon paper → Li-ion battery anode → mechanism via ⁷Li ssNMR. A2 (**Emslie-corresponding own lab**): design + synthesis of new Au(I) ALD precursors for thin gold films. A3 (**Emslie-corresponding own lab**): Rh and Ni complexes of an ambiphilic phosphine-thioether-borane (TXPB) ligand — fundamental M–(co-ligand)–Lewis-acid bonding studies. **A2 + A3 cleanly establish Emslie's lab focus: air-sensitive synthetic organometallic chemistry** — ALD precursors (A2) and fundamental ambiphilic-ligand metal-complex chemistry (A3), with A1 a battery-applied collaboration via Goward.
- **Dominant data modality:** Wet-lab synthesis + chemical characterization (multinuclear NMR / single-crystal XRD / TGA / DSC + a touch of DFT for bonding analysis in A3). **No native ML modality** in any of the three papers; closest reframes are **Li-ion battery cycling (Severson 2019)** for A1 and **organometallic property prediction (PubChem + RDKit/sklearn)** for A2 + A3 — neither closely matches the actual papers.
- **Biggest obstacle for me to replicate their work publicly:** **Emslie's actual research is fundamentally not ML-flavored** — A2 and A3 both confirm this. The lab does air-/moisture-sensitive organometallic synthesis + ALD reactor work + bonding studies, which has no public ML benchmark. Every portfolio project becomes an *inspired-by* reframe on a tangentially related public dataset; the science you'd actually do under Emslie would be wet-lab synthesis + crystallography + multinuclear NMR + occasional DFT.
- **Skills I would gain by working with them:** organometallic / inorganic synthesis (Schlenk technique, glovebox, air-/moisture-sensitive chemistry); ALD precursor design + thin-film growth + reactor operation; multinuclear NMR (¹H/¹¹B/¹³C/¹⁹F/³¹P + VT-NMR) + single-crystal X-ray crystallography + TGA / DSC; light DFT for bonding analysis (Mayer bond orders); *no native ML / CS skills* — any ML on your portfolio side is entirely on you to bring in.

## Gillian R. Goward

**Affiliation:** McMaster University, Department of Chemistry and Chemical Biology, Hamilton, ON, Canada (corresponding-author email goward@mcmaster.ca confirmed on Emslie A1 in this survey).

### Article 1: Inverse Modeling of Phase Transformations in Graphite LIB Anodes from In-Situ MRI

- **Full citation:** José Morales Escalante, William Ko, Jamie M. Foster, Sergey Krachkovskiy, **Gillian Goward**, Bartosz Protas. "Discerning models of phase transformations in porous graphite electrodes: insights from inverse modelling based on MRI measurements." McMaster Math/Stats + Portsmouth + Faraday Institution + McMaster Chemistry (preprint dated April 23, 2020; venue not explicit in extract). **Senior author Protas (math); Goward 5th of 6 — peripheral co-author providing the MRI experimental side.** Funded by NSERC CRD with General Motors R&D collaboration + Faraday Institution (UK).
- **Problem in plain English:** Graphite is the standard anode in Li-ion batteries, but Li intercalation into graphite isn't a smooth "fills up evenly" process — it goes through several discrete *stages* (separated phases) as the battery charges. Standard mathematical battery models (Newman + Fickian diffusion) can't reproduce these sharp phase transitions, which limits how well anyone can simulate a real battery. The authors take **in-situ MRI scans** of an operating graphite anode (Goward's lab provides this data) and use **inverse modeling** — fit competing PDE models (Newman + nonlinear diffusion vs Newman + Cahn–Hilliard) to the MRI concentration profiles + cell voltage — to figure out which physics is right. Headline: **Fickian diffusion fails**; nonlinear (concentration-dependent) diffusion + Cahn–Hilliard both fit; Cahn–Hilliard is more economical because it captures the phase behavior without needing weird state-dependent diffusivities.
- **ML task type:** **Not standard ML — PDE-constrained parameter estimation + multi-objective optimization** (similar in flavor to Latulippe A3's Pyomo.DoE work). The authors infer concentration-dependent diffusion coefficients and Cahn–Hilliard parameters by minimizing a model-vs-data error functional; they use Pareto-front analysis for the multi-objective version. **No neural networks, no sklearn-style supervised ML.**
- **Input representation:**
  - Modality: in-situ MRI concentration profiles c(x, t_k) along the through-thickness of a graphite anode at multiple time-points + cell voltage V(t).
  - Shape/size if stated: a single in-situ MRI experiment with multiple time-snapshots (k = 2…11); standard battery half-cell.
  - Preprocessing in the paper: MRI data is fed directly into the inverse-problem cost functional; PDE models are discretized and solved at each candidate-parameter evaluation.
- **Output representation:**
  - What is inferred: model parameters — concentration-dependent diffusivity Q_N(c_s) (piecewise representation with N break-points), Cahn–Hilliard chemical-potential coefficients, electrode kinetic parameters (k_0, ν, etc.).
  - Units or label space: physical units (m²/s for diffusivity, etc.); the contribution is the *fitted functional form* of Q(c), not a per-sample number.
- **Model architecture (brief):** Newman battery model + (i) nonlinear diffusion or (ii) Cahn–Hilliard dynamics for graphite; numerical optimization with Pareto-front analysis for multi-objective (concentration + voltage) fits.
- **Dataset used in the paper:**
  - Name: in-house in-situ MRI measurements (no name).
  - Size: small — a handful of time-snapshots from a single MRI experiment.
  - Source: Goward + Krachkovskiy groups at McMaster.
  - Public? **No.** No explicit data-availability statement; no code release stated.
  - Link: not provided in paper.
- **Reported headline metric:** Fickian diffusion: high residual error in concentration profiles; Q_N nonlinear-diffusion (N = 3, 5) and Cahn–Hilliard: residuals near measurement noise; Cahn–Hilliard wins on parsimony (no state-dependent transport needed). (No ML benchmark metric — these are inverse-problem error functionals.)
- **Public alternatives to replicate or approximate this (my suggestion — same situation as Emslie A1, plus a PINN angle for the inverse-modeling part):**
  - **Severson et al. 2019 (Nature Energy) — MIT-Stanford-TRI 124-cell LFP/graphite dataset** — the canonical public benchmark for Li-ion battery cycle-life ML, with code on GitHub + Kaggle — [match: close for the *battery* context; analogy for the inverse-modeling target] — [access: easy] — https://github.com/rdbraatz/data-driven-prediction-of-battery-cycle-life-before-capacity-degradation
  - **DeepXDE PINN library** — modern ML approach to PDE-constrained parameter inference; includes diffusion / Allen-Cahn / Cahn-Hilliard tutorials and battery-relevant examples — [match: close for the *method* (PDE inverse problems via neural nets); the paper's inverse problem could be re-cast as a PINN] — [access: easy — `pip install deepxde`] — https://github.com/lululxvi/deepxde
  - **PyBaMM (Python Battery Mathematical Modelling)** — open-source DFN/SPM/Newman battery simulator backed by the Faraday Institution (same UK consortium that co-funded this paper); useful for generating synthetic data + benchmarking inverse algorithms — [match: closer to the paper's PDE side; not a labeled ML benchmark] — [access: easy — `pip install pybamm`] — https://github.com/pybamm-team/PyBaMM
  - **No public benchmark matches the exact MRI-of-graphite inverse-problem task** — only loose analogues.
- **Data access difficulty (for the paper's own dataset):** **very hard** — MRI data not released; in-situ MRI on operating cells is also not easily replicable without specialized NMR / MRI infrastructure.
- **Tooling I would need to learn:** Mixed. For the **Severson reframe**: pure sklearn / PyTorch — in your skills. For the **PINN / PyBaMM reframe**: **DeepXDE** (PyTorch-based — within reach for a CNN/PyTorch user but a new paradigm) + **PyBaMM** (well-documented Python battery simulator) — both mildly new but well-supported. **No deep niche tooling.**
- **Portfolio angle — what a good GitHub project based on this would look like (my suggestion):** Two clean options. (1) **Severson 2019 cycle-life ML** — same as Emslie A1, anchored to the battery context (recommended as the safer recruiter-legible choice). (2) **PINN-based inverse problem on a toy Cahn–Hilliard intercalation model**: generate synthetic "MRI-like" concentration data with PyBaMM, then use DeepXDE to recover the diffusivity Q(c) — this directly mirrors the paper's inverse-modeling approach, frames as "physics-informed ML for battery materials parameter estimation," and gives you exposure to PINNs (an active area in AI-for-science). README headline option: *"Physics-informed neural networks for Li-ion battery transport — recovering concentration-dependent diffusivity in graphite anodes from simulated in-situ concentration profiles, inspired by inverse-modeling work on the Goward/Protas MRI dataset."*
